board_events.text: Three families, one oxygen

board_events.caption: Alcohol, phenol and ether compared
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">The three oxygen families</text><text x="95" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2933">CH3–CH2–OH</text><text x="95" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">O H on an sp3 carbon</text><text x="95" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">ALCOHOL  R–OH</text><polygon points="300.0,102.0 275.8,116.0 275.8,144.0 300.0,158.0 324.2,144.0 324.2,116.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="300" cy="130" r="16.8" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="300.0" y1="102.0" x2="300.0" y2="78.0" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><text x="300.0" y="72.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#c05621">OH</text><text x="300" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#c05621">PHENOL  Ar–OH</text><text x="300" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">O H straight on the ring</text><text x="520" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2933">C2H5–O–C2H5</text><text x="520" y="145" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">no O–H bond at all</text><text x="520" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">ETHER  R–O–R'</text></svg>

board_events.text: Alcohol: an $-OH$ group on an $sp^3$ carbon, written R$-$OH.
Phenol: an $-OH$ bonded directly to an aromatic ring carbon, written Ar$-$OH.
Ether: oxygen bridging two carbon groups, R$-$O$-$R$'$. There is no O$-$H bond.
Same OH, different neighbourhood, completely different chemistry.
That O-H pair hydrogen-bonds, donates and accepts electrons, and rewrites boiling point and solubility.
Three families, one shared element: oxygen.

segments.text: <curious>Strip one hydrogen off a hydrocarbon, bolt on an oxygen hydrogen group, and you have manufactured a whole new personality.</curious> Let us meet the three families this chapter is built on.
Here they are side by side. On the left an alcohol, in the middle a phenol, on the right an ether. Watch where the oxygen sits in each one, because that single detail decides everything that follows.
First, the alcohol. The oxygen hydrogen group is bolted to an ordinary saturated carbon, an s p three carbon. We write it R minus O H. Picture a small shop attached to a quiet residential flat.

Second, the phenol. That very same oxygen hydrogen group now sits directly on a benzene ring carbon. We write it A r minus O H. Ring and oxygen start sharing electrons, and that sharing makes phenol behave quite differently, notably more acidic.
Third, the ether. Here oxygen is not a shop at all, it is a flyover linking two separate carbon colonies, R minus O minus R prime. There is no oxygen hydrogen bond, so ethers stay aloof.
<whisper>Hold on to this one line: the same O H group in a different neighbourhood gives completely different chemistry.</whisper>

That little oxygen hydrogen pair is the most sociable group in beginner organic chemistry. It hydrogen bonds, it donates and accepts electrons, and it completely rewrites boiling points and solubility.
So the whole chapter is really three families built around one shared element, oxygen. Get their differences clear now and everything downstream falls into place.
<curious>Hydrocarbon से एक hydrogen हटाओ और एक O H group जोड़ दो, पूरी personality ही बदल जाती है।</curious> इस chapter की तीन families से मिलते हैं।
ये देखिए तीनों साथ में, बाईं ओर alcohol, बीच में phenol, दाईं ओर ether। ध्यान दीजिए oxygen हर एक में कहाँ बैठा है, क्योंकि यही एक बात आगे सब कुछ तय करती है।
पहला, alcohol। O H group एक साधारण saturated carbon पर लगा है, यानी s p three carbon। इसे लिखते हैं R minus O H। इसे ऐसे सोचिए जैसे एक छोटी दुकान किसी शांत flat की दीवार पर लगी हो।

दूसरा, phenol। वही O H group अब सीधे benzene ring के carbon पर बैठा है। इसे लिखते हैं A r minus O H। ring और oxygen अपने electrons share करने लगते हैं, और यही sharing phenol को अलग बनाती है, खासकर ज़्यादा acidic।
तीसरा, ether। यहाँ oxygen कोई दुकान नहीं, बल्कि एक flyover है जो दो carbon colonies को जोड़ता है, R minus O minus R prime। यहाँ कोई O H bond नहीं है, इसलिए ethers काफ़ी aloof रहते हैं।
<whisper>ये एक line पकड़ लीजिए, वही O H group, अलग neighbourhood, तो बिल्कुल अलग chemistry।</whisper>
ये छोटा सा oxygen hydrogen pair beginner organic chemistry का सबसे सामाजिक group है। ये hydrogen bond बनाता है, electrons देता और लेता है, और boiling point तथा solubility को पूरी तरह बदल देता है।
तो पूरा chapter असल में तीन families हैं जो एक ही element oxygen के इर्द गिर्द बनी हैं। इनका फ़र्क़ अभी clear कर लीजिए, आगे सब आसान हो जाएगा।

sections.title: When an OH is not an alcohol

board_events.text: When an OH is NOT an alcohol
Alcohol: $-OH$ on an $sp^3$ carbon (R$-$OH). Phenol: $-OH$ on a ring carbon (Ar$-$OH). Ether: R$-$O$-$R$'$.

board_events.caption: The neighbourhood test
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="320" y="26" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Is the OH really an alcohol OH?</text><rect x="40" y="55" width="230" height="150" rx="10" fill="#fff4f2" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="155" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">CH3–COOH</text><text x="155" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">the OH carbon is also</text><text x="155" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">double-bonded to O</text><text x="155" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">NOT an alcohol</text><text x="155" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c53030">(carboxylic acid)</text><rect x="370" y="55" width="230" height="150" rx="10" fill="#f0fff4" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="485" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">CH3–CH2–OH</text><text x="485" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">OH carbon carries only</text><text x="485" y="138" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">H and C</text><text x="485" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">a true alcohol</text><text x="320" y="235" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">Same visible “OH” — the label depends on the neighbourhood</text></svg>

board_events.text: An OH carbon double-bonded to O ($-COOH$) or carrying $-NH_2$ is NOT an alcohol.
The label depends on what else the OH carbon is bonded to, not just on seeing an O and an H.
A saturated monohydric alcohol and its isomeric ether share this formula, so they are functional isomers.
The alkoxy unit is the OR fragment; it names ethers, as we will see shortly.

segments.text: So we saw the analogy. But here is the trap that analogy hides, and examiners love it. Just seeing an O and an H does not make something an alcohol.

Keep the three definitions crisp. An alcohol has its oxygen hydrogen group on an s p three carbon, R minus O H. A phenol has it on a ring carbon, A r minus O H. An ether is R minus O minus R prime, oxygen bridging two carbon groups.

Now look at these two. On the right, ordinary ethanol, a genuine alcohol, because the carbon wearing the O H is bonded only to hydrogen and carbon. On the left, acetic acid. It clearly shows an O H, and yet it is not an alcohol.

Why not? Because that same carbon is also double bonded to a second oxygen, making it a carboxylic acid. The moment the O H carbon is double bonded to oxygen, or carries an amino group, the compound stops being an alcohol.

So the rule to internalise is this. The label depends on the neighbourhood of the O H carbon, on what else that carbon is bonded to, and not merely on spotting an oxygen and a hydrogen in the formula.
There is one general formula worth memorising. A saturated, open chain compound with a single oxygen fits C n H two n plus two O.

And here is a fact J E E loves. A monohydric alcohol and an ether with the same number of carbons both fit that same formula, so an alcohol and its matching ether are functional isomers of each other.
One last piece of vocabulary. The O R fragment inside an ether is called an alkoxy group, and it is exactly what we will use to name ethers a little later.
तो analogy तो देख ली। लेकिन अब वो trap जो analogy छुपा देती है, और examiners इसे बहुत पूछते हैं। सिर्फ़ एक O और एक H दिखना किसी चीज़ को alcohol नहीं बना देता।

तीनों definitions crisp रखिए। Alcohol में O H group एक s p three carbon पर होता है, R minus O H। Phenol में वो ring carbon पर होता है, A r minus O H। Ether है R minus O minus R prime, oxygen दो carbon groups को जोड़ता हुआ।

अब इन दोनों को देखिए। दाईं ओर साधारण ethanol, एक असली alcohol, क्योंकि O H वाला carbon सिर्फ़ hydrogen और carbon से जुड़ा है। बाईं ओर acetic acid। इसमें साफ़ O H दिख रहा है, फिर भी ये alcohol नहीं है।

क्यों नहीं? क्योंकि वही carbon एक दूसरे oxygen से double bonded भी है, जो इसे carboxylic acid बना देता है। जैसे ही O H वाला carbon oxygen से double bond बनाए, या amino group रखे, वो compound alcohol नहीं रहता।
तो असली rule ये है। label O H carbon के neighbourhood पर depend करता है, यानी उस carbon के बाकी bonds पर, न कि सिर्फ़ एक oxygen और hydrogen देख लेने पर।
एक general formula याद रखने लायक है। एक saturated, open chain compound जिसमें एक ही oxygen हो, वो C n H two n plus two O में fit होता है।
और ये fact J E E को बहुत पसंद है। एक monohydric alcohol और उतने ही carbon वाला ether, दोनों उसी formula में fit होते हैं, इसलिए alcohol और उसका matching ether एक दूसरे के functional isomers हैं।
आख़िरी vocabulary। ether के अंदर O R fragment को alkoxy group कहते हैं, और ठीक यही हम थोड़ी देर बाद ethers के नाम रखने में इस्तेमाल करेंगे।

board_events.text: Three ways to classify an alcohol

board_events.caption: Number of OH, carbon type, and position

board_events.text: By number of OH groups: monohydric (one), dihydric (a glycol), trihydric (glycerol), polyhydric (many).
By the OH carbon: bonded to one other C is $1^\circ$, to two is $2^\circ$, to three is $3^\circ$.
$1^\circ / 2^\circ / 3^\circ$ decides oxidation product, dehydration ease and Lucas speed. Internalise it now.
By position: allylic (OH next to C=C), benzylic (OH next to a ring), vinylic (OH on a C=C carbon).
Vinylic alcohols are enols; they are unstable and tautomerise to carbonyl compounds. OH straight on the ring is a phenol.
Ethers classify simply: simple/symmetrical (identical groups) or mixed/unsymmetrical (different groups).

segments.text: Alcohols get classified three independent ways, and exam questions cheerfully mix all three in one line. Let us keep them separate in our heads.
Here is the whole scheme on one board. Three columns for alcohols, and below, the two simple classes of ethers. Take them one at a time.
First way, count the oxygen hydrogen groups. One makes it monohydric, two makes it dihydric, a glycol for example, three makes it trihydric, like glycerol, and many make it polyhydric.
Second way, look at the carbon actually wearing the O H. If that carbon is bonded to one other carbon it is primary, to two other carbons it is secondary, and to three it is tertiary.

<whisper>This second distinction is the one that keeps paying off.</whisper> Primary, secondary, tertiary will later decide the oxidation product, how easily the alcohol dehydrates, and how fast it responds to the Lucas test. So lock it in right now.

Third way, look at the position relative to unsaturation. An O H on the s p three carbon next to a carbon carbon double bond is allylic, next to a ring is benzylic, and directly on a double bond carbon is vinylic.

Now a built in warning. Vinylic alcohols are called enols, and they are generally unstable, tautomerising into carbonyl compounds. And when the O H sits directly on the aromatic ring, that is not an alcohol at all, that is a phenol.

Ethers are far simpler. If both groups on oxygen are identical, the ether is simple or symmetrical, like diethyl ether. If they differ, it is mixed or unsymmetrical, like ethyl methyl ether or anisole.
Alcohols को तीन अलग अलग तरीक़ों से classify किया जाता है, और exam एक ही line में तीनों को मिला देता है। इन्हें दिमाग़ में अलग अलग रखते हैं।
पूरा scheme एक ही board पर है। alcohols के लिए तीन columns, और नीचे ethers की दो simple classes। एक एक करके लेते हैं।
पहला तरीक़ा, O H groups गिनिए। एक हो तो monohydric, दो हों तो dihydric, जैसे glycol, तीन हों तो trihydric, जैसे glycerol, और कई हों तो polyhydric।
दूसरा तरीक़ा, उस carbon को देखिए जो असल में O H पहने है। अगर वो carbon एक और carbon से जुड़ा है तो primary, दो से जुड़ा है तो secondary, और तीन से जुड़ा है तो tertiary।

<whisper>यही दूसरा distinction बार बार काम आता है।</whisper> primary, secondary, tertiary आगे तय करेगा oxidation का product, alcohol कितनी आसानी से dehydrate होगा, और Lucas test में कितनी जल्दी react करेगा। तो इसे अभी पक्का कर लीजिए।
तीसरा तरीक़ा, unsaturation के relative position देखिए। double bond के बगल वाले s p three carbon पर O H हो तो allylic, ring के बगल हो तो benzylic, और सीधे double bond carbon पर हो तो vinylic।

अब एक built in warning। vinylic alcohols को enols कहते हैं, और ये आम तौर पर unstable होते हैं, carbonyl compounds में tautomerise हो जाते हैं। और जब O H सीधे aromatic ring पर बैठे, तो वो alcohol नहीं, phenol है।

Ethers कहीं ज़्यादा simple हैं। अगर oxygen पर दोनों groups एक जैसे हों, तो ether simple या symmetrical है, जैसे diethyl ether। अगर अलग हों, तो mixed या unsymmetrical, जैसे ethyl methyl ether या anisole।

sections.title: The C-O framework: angles and lengths

board_events.text: Bond angles and bond lengths

board_events.caption: C-O geometry across the three families
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="660" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="330" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">The C–O framework: angles & lengths</text><text x="120" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">Alcohol</text><text x="120" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#1f2933">C–O–H</text><text x="120" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c05621">angle < 109°28'</text><text x="120" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">lone pairs squeeze inward</text><text x="120" y="203" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">C–O ≈ 143 pm</text><polygon points="330.0,104.0 307.5,117.0 307.5,143.0 330.0,156.0 352.5,143.0 352.5,117.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="330" cy="130" r="15.6" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="330.0" y1="104.0" x2="330.0" y2="82.0" stroke="#c05621" stroke-width="2.4"/><text x="330.0" y="76.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#c05621">OH</text><text x="330" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">Phenol</text><text x="330" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c05621">C–O ≈ 136 pm (shorter)</text><text x="330" y="203" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">conjugation + sp2 carbon</text><text x="545" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">Ether</text><text x="545" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="#1f2933">C–O–C</text><text x="545" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c05621">angle ≈ 111.7°</text><text x="545" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">bulky R groups push apart</text><text x="545" y="203" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">C–O ≈ 141 pm</text></svg>

board_events.text: In an alcohol the oxygen is $sp^3$; the C$-$O$-$H angle is slightly less than $109^\circ 28'$.
Reason: the two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bond pairs inward, closing the angle.
In phenol the C$-$O bond is about $136$ pm, shorter than the $\sim 143$ pm in methanol.
Two causes: partial double-bond character from lone-pair conjugation, and the sp2 ring carbon.
In an ether the C$-$O$-$C angle opens to about $111.7^\circ$; bulky R groups push apart. C$-$O $\approx 141$ pm.
These specific numbers are exam-quotable, so keep them at your fingertips.

segments.text: This subtopic has almost no formulas, but it has a handful of geometry numbers that examiners quote directly. Let us walk the C to O framework across all three families.
Here they sit together. Alcohol on the left, phenol in the middle, ether on the right, each with its angle and its bond length labelled. Read them off as we go.
In an alcohol the oxygen is s p three hybridised. The carbon oxygen hydrogen frame has a bond angle slightly less than the tetrahedral value of one hundred nine degrees twenty eight minutes.
Why less? Because oxygen carries two lone pairs, and those lone pairs push harder than bond pairs, squeezing the bond pairs inward and closing the angle a little below tetrahedral.
Now phenol. Its carbon oxygen bond is about one hundred thirty six picometres, noticeably shorter than the roughly one hundred forty three picometres in methanol.

That shortening has two causes. First, a lone pair on oxygen conjugates into the ring, giving the bond partial double bond character. Second, the ring carbon it attaches to is s p two, and s p two carbons form shorter bonds. Both pull the length in.

And the ether. Here the carbon oxygen carbon angle actually opens up, to about one hundred eleven point seven degrees, because the two bulky R groups on oxygen repel each other and push apart. The carbon oxygen length, about one hundred forty one picometres, is close to that in alcohols.

Keep these three numbers handy. Angle just under tetrahedral for the alcohol, a shortened carbon oxygen bond for phenol, and a slightly opened angle for the ether. They are exactly the kind of one mark facts a paper drops in.
इस subtopic में formulas लगभग नहीं हैं, लेकिन कुछ geometry के numbers हैं जो examiners सीधे पूछते हैं। तीनों families में C to O framework देखते हैं।
ये देखिए तीनों साथ में। बाईं ओर alcohol, बीच में phenol, दाईं ओर ether, हर एक के साथ उसका angle और bond length लिखा है। साथ साथ पढ़ते चलिए।
Alcohol में oxygen s p three hybridised होता है। carbon oxygen hydrogen frame का bond angle tetrahedral value यानी one hundred nine degrees twenty eight minutes से थोड़ा कम होता है।
कम क्यों? क्योंकि oxygen पर दो lone pairs हैं, और ये lone pairs bond pairs से ज़्यादा ज़ोर लगाते हैं, bond pairs को अंदर की ओर दबाते हैं और angle थोड़ा tetrahedral से नीचे ले आते हैं।
अब phenol। इसका carbon oxygen bond लगभग one hundred thirty six picometres है, जो methanol के करीब one hundred forty three picometres से साफ़ छोटा है।

इस shortening के दो कारण हैं। पहला, oxygen का एक lone pair ring में conjugate करता है, जिससे bond को partial double bond character मिलता है। दूसरा, जिस ring carbon पर ये जुड़ा है वो s p two है, और s p two carbons छोटे bonds बनाते हैं। दोनों length को अंदर खींचते हैं।

और ether। यहाँ carbon oxygen carbon angle असल में खुल जाता है, लगभग one hundred eleven point seven degrees तक, क्योंकि oxygen पर दो bulky R groups एक दूसरे को repel करके दूर धकेलते हैं। carbon oxygen length, लगभग one hundred forty one picometres, alcohols जैसी ही है।
ये तीन numbers याद रखिए। alcohol के लिए tetrahedral से ज़रा कम angle, phenol के लिए छोटा carbon oxygen bond, और ether के लिए ज़रा खुला angle। यही तो वो one mark facts हैं जो paper में आ जाते हैं।

board_events.text: IUPAC naming: alcohols

board_events.caption: Four steps to an alkanol name
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="660" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="330" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Naming an alcohol (alkanol)</text><text x="330" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="17" fill="#1f2933">CH3–CH2–CH2–CH2–OH</text><text x="150" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2b6cb0">4</text><text x="230" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2b6cb0">3</text><text x="315" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2b6cb0">2</text><text x="405" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c53030">1</text><text x="330" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">1. longest chain THROUGH the OH carbon</text><text x="330" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">2. alkane “-e” → “-ol”   (keep -e for diols: ethane-1,2-diol)</text><text x="330" y="181" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#5a6570">3. number so OH gets the LOWEST locant</text><text x="330" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">butan-1-ol</text></svg>

board_events.text: Step 1: pick the longest continuous chain that contains the carbon bearing the OH.
OH is a principal group, so the chain MUST include it, even if a longer chain exists elsewhere.
Step 2: replace the alkane's final $-e$ with $-ol$. Keep the $-e$ for diols and triols: ethane-1,2-diol.
Step 3: number to give OH the lowest locant, then place that number just before the suffix: butan-2-ol.
If a higher-priority group (acid, ester, carbonyl) is present, OH becomes a hydroxy- prefix instead.
Seniority: acid $\gt$ ester $\gt$ carbonyl $\gt$ OH/phenol $\gt$ amine $\gt$ ether $\gt$ $C=C$ / $C\equiv C$ $\gt$ halo, nitro, alkyl.

segments.text: The first of our two procedural systems is naming. Let us master alcohols first, and there is a clean four step routine.
Follow along on the board with butanol as our test case. Four numbered steps take any alcohol from structure to name.
Step one, pick the parent chain. It is the longest continuous carbon chain, but with one non negotiable condition: it must contain the carbon that carries the O H.

<whisper>This overrides plain longest chain.</whisper> The oxygen hydrogen is a principal characteristic group, so if a longer chain exists somewhere that skips the O H carbon, you ignore it. The chain has to run through the O H.

Step two, take the parent alkane name and swap its final letter e for o l. Ethane becomes ethanol. But keep that e before a consonant suffix and for di and tri ols, so it is ethane one comma two diol, never ethandiol.
Step three, number the chain so the O H gets the lowest possible locant, and write that number right before the o l suffix in modern style. So we get butan two ol, or here, butan one ol.
One more case. If a group that outranks O H is present, such as an acid, an ester, or a carbonyl, then the O H stops being the suffix and becomes a hydroxy prefix instead.

And here is the seniority ladder to memorise. Carboxylic acid beats ester, beats carbonyl, beats hydroxyl and phenol, beats amine, beats ether, beats carbon carbon double or triple bonds, beats halogen, nitro, and alkyl. Whoever is highest claims the suffix.
हमारे दो procedural systems में से पहला है naming। पहले alcohols master करते हैं, और इसके लिए एक साफ़ चार step का routine है।
board पर butanol को test case मानकर साथ चलिए। चार numbered steps किसी भी alcohol को structure से name तक ले जाते हैं।
Step one, parent chain चुनिए। ये सबसे लंबी continuous carbon chain है, पर एक शर्त पक्की है: इसमें वो carbon होना ही चाहिए जो O H पहने है।

<whisper>ये सादे longest chain के ऊपर है।</whisper> oxygen hydrogen एक principal characteristic group है, तो अगर कहीं और लंबी chain हो जो O H carbon को छोड़ दे, तो उसे नज़रअंदाज़ कीजिए। chain को O H से होकर गुज़रना ही है।

Step two, parent alkane का नाम लीजिए और उसके आख़िरी अक्षर e को o l में बदल दीजिए। Ethane बनता है ethanol। पर वो e रखिए किसी consonant suffix से पहले और di तथा tri ols के लिए, तो ये है ethane one comma two diol, कभी ethandiol नहीं।
Step three, chain को इस तरह number कीजिए कि O H को सबसे lowest locant मिले, और वो number modern style में सीधे o l suffix से पहले लिखिए। तो मिलता है butan two ol, या यहाँ, butan one ol।
एक और case। अगर कोई group मौजूद हो जो O H से senior है, जैसे acid, ester, या carbonyl, तो O H suffix नहीं रहता, बल्कि hydroxy prefix बन जाता है।

और ये seniority ladder याद रखिए। carboxylic acid ऊपर ester से, फिर carbonyl, फिर hydroxyl और phenol, फिर amine, फिर ether, फिर carbon carbon double या triple bond, फिर halogen, nitro, और alkyl। जो सबसे ऊपर है वही suffix लेता है।

board_events.text: Naming phenols and ethers
"Phenol" is itself the accepted IUPAC name for hydroxybenzene; substituents are named as derivatives.
2-methylphenol (o-cresol), 3-methylphenol (m-cresol), 4-methylphenol (p-cresol).

board_events.text: Matching a common name to its IUPAC form is a frequent one-mark NEET item.
Ethers are alkoxyalkanes: the larger group is the parent alkane, the smaller becomes the alkoxy substituent.
CH$_3$-O-C$_2$H$_5$ is methoxyethane; C$_6$H$_5$-O-CH$_3$ is methoxybenzene (anisole).
Common names: list both groups alphabetically plus ether, with di- if identical (diethyl ether).

segments.text: Phenols and ethers each have their own naming habit. Both are quick once you see the pattern, so let us take phenols first.
The word phenol is itself the accepted I U P A C name for hydroxybenzene. Everything with a substituted ring is then named as a derivative of phenol.
So a methyl group on the ring gives two methylphenol, also called ortho cresol, three methylphenol or meta cresol, and four methylphenol or para cresol. The cresols are just methyl phenols.

Now the ones worth memorising outright, the benzenediols on the board. Two hydroxyls adjacent is benzene one comma two diol, catechol. In a one three pattern it is resorcinol. Directly across in a one four pattern it is hydroquinone. And the trihydric benzene one two three triol is pyrogallol.
<whisper>Why bother with the trivial names?</whisper> Because papers quote either form, and matching a common name to its I U P A C name is a classic one mark N E E T item you should never lose.

Ethers switch to a different logic, the alkoxyalkane system. Treat the ether as a hydrocarbon in which one hydrogen has been replaced by an O R group. The larger group becomes the parent alkane, and the smaller one becomes the alkoxy substituent in front.

So methyl on oxygen with ethyl gives methoxyethane, the ethane is the parent and methoxy is the prefix. And methyl on oxygen with a phenyl ring gives methoxybenzene, whose famous trivial name is anisole.

The older common system is even simpler. Just list both groups alphabetically and add the word ether, using di if the two groups are identical, as in diethyl ether. Recognise it, because question papers still use it.
Phenols और ethers की अपनी अपनी naming habit है। pattern दिख जाए तो दोनों जल्दी हैं, तो पहले phenols लेते हैं।
phenol शब्द ख़ुद hydroxybenzene का accepted I U P A C name है। फिर substituted ring वाली हर चीज़ को phenol के derivative की तरह name करते हैं।
तो ring पर एक methyl group देता है two methylphenol, यानी ortho cresol, three methylphenol या meta cresol, और four methylphenol या para cresol। cresols बस methyl phenols हैं।

अब वो जो सीधे याद करने लायक हैं, board पर benzenediols। दो hydroxyl बगल बगल हों तो benzene one comma two diol, catechol। one three pattern में resorcinol। ठीक सामने one four pattern में hydroquinone। और trihydric benzene one two three triol है pyrogallol।

<whisper>trivial names की परवाह क्यों करें?</whisper> क्योंकि papers दोनों form में पूछते हैं, और common name को उसके I U P A C name से match करना एक classic one mark N E E T item है जो कभी नहीं छोड़ना चाहिए।
Ethers अलग logic पर चलते हैं, alkoxyalkane system। ether को एक hydrocarbon मानिए जिसमें एक hydrogen की जगह O R group आ गया। बड़ा group parent alkane बनता है, और छोटा group आगे alkoxy substituent।
तो oxygen पर methyl के साथ ethyl देता है methoxyethane, यहाँ ethane parent है और methoxy prefix। और oxygen पर methyl के साथ एक phenyl ring देता है methoxybenzene, जिसका मशहूर trivial name है anisole।

पुराना common system और भी simple है। बस दोनों groups को alphabetically लिखिए और ether शब्द जोड़ दीजिए, di का इस्तेमाल तब जब दोनों groups एक जैसे हों, जैसे diethyl ether। इसे पहचानिए, क्योंकि question papers में अब भी आता है।

sections.title: Alcohols from alkenes I: acid-catalysed hydration

board_events.text: Adding water across a C=C: three routes, one goal
All three routes add H and OH across a double bond, but differ in WHICH carbon gets the OH, and whether a carbocation forms.

board_events.text: Step 1 (protonation): C=C $+$ H$_3$O$^+$ gives a carbocation on the carbon that makes the more stable cation.
Step 2 (capture): water attacks the carbocation to give a protonated alcohol. Step 3: it loses a proton.
Proton adds to give the more stable C+, so OH lands on the more substituted carbon = Markovnikov.
A free carbocation forms, so rearrangements are possible and can spoil the yield.
Remember this as the route that is Markovnikov but MAY rearrange.

segments.text: Now the second procedural system, making these compounds. We start with alcohols from alkenes, and there are three routes worth knowing. All three add the elements of water across a carbon carbon double bond.

But do not lump them together. The three routes differ on two axes: which carbon ends up wearing the O H, and whether a naked carbocation appears along the way. Those two differences are the entire exam story.
Route one is acid catalysed hydration. Watch propene on the board go across in three steps to propan two ol.

Step one, protonation. The alkene picks up a proton from hydronium ion, and it does so on the carbon that leaves behind the more stable carbocation. For propene that gives a secondary cation on the middle carbon.
Step two, capture. A water molecule attacks that carbocation, giving a protonated alcohol. Step three, it simply loses a proton to give the neutral alcohol.
Because the proton added so as to make the more stable cation, the oxygen hydrogen ends up on the more substituted carbon. That is Markovnikov addition, and it is the default outcome to expect here.

<whisper>But there is a catch.</whisper> A genuinely free carbocation sits in the middle of this mechanism, and free carbocations can rearrange to something even more stable, which quietly spoils the yield.
So file this route under one label. Acid hydration gives the Markovnikov alcohol, but it may rearrange. Keep that phrase, because the next two routes will each fix a different weakness of this one.
अब दूसरा procedural system, इन compounds को बनाना। शुरू करते हैं alkenes से alcohols, और तीन routes जानने लायक हैं। तीनों carbon carbon double bond पर पानी के elements जोड़ते हैं।
पर इन्हें एक साथ मत मिलाइए। तीनों routes दो axes पर अलग हैं: कौन सा carbon O H पहनेगा, और क्या बीच में कोई नंगा carbocation आता है। यही दो differences पूरी exam की कहानी हैं।
Route one है acid catalysed hydration। board पर propene को तीन steps में propan two ol बनते देखिए।
Step one, protonation। alkene hydronium ion से एक proton लेता है, और उस carbon पर लेता है जो पीछे ज़्यादा stable carbocation छोड़े। propene के लिए ये बीच वाले carbon पर एक secondary cation देता है।
Step two, capture। एक water molecule उस carbocation पर attack करता है, जिससे protonated alcohol बनता है। step three, ये बस एक proton खोकर neutral alcohol बन जाता है।
चूँकि proton ने ज़्यादा stable cation बनाने के लिए add किया, oxygen hydrogen ज़्यादा substituted carbon पर आता है। यही Markovnikov addition है, और यहाँ यही default outcome expect कीजिए।
<whisper>पर एक catch है।</whisper> इस mechanism के बीचोंबीच एक सचमुच free carbocation बैठा है, और free carbocations rearrange होकर और भी stable चीज़ बन सकते हैं, जो चुपके से yield ख़राब कर देता है।
तो इस route को एक label के नीचे रखिए। acid hydration Markovnikov alcohol देता है, पर rearrange हो सकता है। ये phrase याद रखिए, क्योंकि अगले दो routes इसकी अलग अलग कमज़ोरी ठीक करेंगे।

board_events.text: Hydroboration-oxidation (HBO)
Reagents: diborane B$_2$H$_6$ (or BH$_3\cdot$THF), then H$_2$O$_2$ in OH$^-$.

board_events.text: Boron is electron-deficient, so the electrophilic boron attaches to the LESS substituted carbon (less crowding).
On oxidation, oxygen replaces boron with retention, so OH ends up on the less substituted carbon.
Result: anti-Markovnikov alcohol. The addition is concerted and stereospecifically syn.
There is no carbocation anywhere, so there is NO rearrangement, ever.
Signature cue in a question: anti-Markovnikov, or syn, or no rearrangement points straight to HBO.

segments.text: Route two is hydroboration oxidation, which everyone shortens to H B O. This is the route that flips the regiochemistry.
The reagents come in two stages. First diborane, or borane complexed with T H F, and then hydrogen peroxide in base. Two flasks, two steps.
Follow the board. Boron leads in the first step, and then oxidation swaps that boron for an oxygen hydrogen group.

Here is the logic. Boron is electron deficient, so the electrophilic boron attaches to the less substituted, less crowded carbon. The partial positive charge that develops sits on the more substituted carbon during a single concerted, syn addition.
Then in the oxidation step, oxygen replaces boron with retention of position. So the oxygen hydrogen ends up exactly where the boron was, on the less substituted carbon.

That is the anti Markovnikov product, the mirror image of acid hydration. And because the whole first step is concerted, the addition is stereospecifically syn, both new bonds forming on the same face.
<excited>And here is the beauty of it.</excited> There is no carbocation anywhere in this mechanism, which means there is no rearrangement, ever. The skeleton you start with is the skeleton you keep.
So the exam cue is unmistakable. The moment a question says anti Markovnikov, or says syn addition, or insists on no rearrangement, your hand should already be reaching for H B O.
Route two है hydroboration oxidation, जिसे सब short में H B O कहते हैं। यही वो route है जो regiochemistry को पलट देता है।
reagents दो stages में आते हैं। पहले diborane, या T H F से complexed borane, और फिर base में hydrogen peroxide। दो flasks, दो steps।
board देखिए। पहले step में boron आगे रहता है, और फिर oxidation उस boron को एक oxygen hydrogen group से बदल देता है।

logic ये है। boron electron deficient है, इसलिए electrophilic boron कम substituted, कम भीड़ वाले carbon पर जुड़ता है। जो partial positive charge बनता है वो एक ही concerted, syn addition के दौरान ज़्यादा substituted carbon पर बैठता है।
फिर oxidation step में oxygen boron की जगह position की retention के साथ ले लेता है। तो oxygen hydrogen ठीक वहीं आता है जहाँ boron था, कम substituted carbon पर।
यही anti Markovnikov product है, acid hydration का उलटा। और चूँकि पूरा पहला step concerted है, addition stereospecifically syn है, दोनों नए bonds एक ही face पर बनते हैं।
<excited>और यही इसकी ख़ूबसूरती है।</excited> इस mechanism में कहीं कोई carbocation नहीं है, यानी कभी कोई rearrangement नहीं। जिस skeleton से शुरू करते हैं वही रहता है।
तो exam cue साफ़ है। जैसे ही कोई question कहे anti Markovnikov, या कहे syn addition, या ज़ोर दे no rearrangement पर, आपका हाथ पहले ही H B O की ओर बढ़ जाना चाहिए।

board_events.text: The intermediate is a bridged mercurinium ion, NOT an open carbocation.
Water opens the bridge at the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov), and no free cation ever exists.
This is the rearrangement-free way to get a Markovnikov alcohol.
Summary: acid $\rightarrow$ Markovnikov, may rearrange; oxymercuration $\rightarrow$ Markovnikov, no rearrangement; HBO $\rightarrow$ anti-Markovnikov, syn, no rearrangement.
Memorise this three-row table; almost every alkene-hydration MCQ tests exactly one cell of it.

segments.text: Route three is oxymercuration demercuration. Think of it as acid hydration with the danger surgically removed.
The reagents are mercuric acetate in a tetrahydrofuran and water mix, followed by sodium borohydride in base. That second step swaps the mercury out cleanly.
On the board, the scheme runs across the top and, below it, the summary table that ties all three routes together. Let us earn that table.
The key is the intermediate. Instead of an open, flat carbocation, this route forms a bridged mercurinium ion, a three membered ring where mercury straddles both carbons.

Water then opens that bridge at the more substituted carbon, which gives the Markovnikov placement of the oxygen hydrogen. And crucially, because a bridged ion, not a free cation, is the intermediate, no rearrangement can occur.
<whisper>So this is your disciplined tool.</whisper> When you need a Markovnikov alcohol but cannot risk a rearrangement, oxymercuration is the answer, not acid hydration.
Now read the summary as one block. Acid hydration, Markovnikov but may rearrange. Oxymercuration, Markovnikov with no rearrangement. And H B O, anti Markovnikov, syn, no rearrangement.
Photograph this three row table in your mind. Almost every alkene hydration multiple choice question is really asking you for the contents of exactly one cell of it.
Route three है oxymercuration demercuration। इसे acid hydration ही समझिए जिसमें से ख़तरा precisely हटा दिया गया हो।
reagents हैं tetrahydrofuran और water के mix में mercuric acetate, फिर base में sodium borohydride। वो दूसरा step mercury को साफ़ तरीक़े से हटा देता है।
board पर scheme ऊपर चल रही है और उसके नीचे वो summary table है जो तीनों routes को जोड़ती है। चलिए उस table को कमाते हैं।
असली बात intermediate में है। एक खुले, flat carbocation की जगह ये route एक bridged mercurinium ion बनाता है, एक तीन membered ring जहाँ mercury दोनों carbons पर फैला होता है।

फिर water उस bridge को ज़्यादा substituted carbon पर खोलता है, जो oxygen hydrogen को Markovnikov position देता है। और अहम बात, चूँकि intermediate एक bridged ion है, कोई free cation नहीं, इसलिए कोई rearrangement नहीं हो सकता।
<whisper>तो ये आपका disciplined tool है।</whisper> जब Markovnikov alcohol चाहिए पर rearrangement का risk नहीं ले सकते, तो जवाब है oxymercuration, acid hydration नहीं।
अब summary को एक block की तरह पढ़िए। acid hydration, Markovnikov पर rearrange हो सकता है। oxymercuration, Markovnikov बिना rearrangement। और H B O, anti Markovnikov, syn, बिना rearrangement।
इस तीन row वाली table को दिमाग़ में photograph कर लीजिए। alkene hydration का लगभग हर multiple choice question असल में इसी table के किसी एक cell का content पूछ रहा होता है।

board_events.text: A Grignard reagent R-MgX adds to the carbonyl carbon; aqueous work-up then gives the alcohol.
Methanal $\rightarrow$ 1$^\circ$; any other aldehyde $\rightarrow$ 2$^\circ$; a ketone $\rightarrow$ 3$^\circ$.
Reagents and apparatus must be scrupulously DRY; any active hydrogen destroys the Grignard.
So the same reagent gives 1, 2 or 3 degree simply by choosing the carbonyl partner.

segments.text: We can also build alcohols without any alkene at all, by starting from carbonyl compounds. Two big methods here, reduction and Grignard addition.

Reduction first. An aldehyde reduces down to a primary alcohol, and a ketone down to a secondary alcohol. Your reducing agent can be catalytic hydrogen over nickel, platinum or palladium, or a hydride like sodium borohydride or lithium aluminium hydride.
Carboxylic acids and esters are tougher customers, harder to reduce. For those you bring out the strong hydride, lithium aluminium hydride, which drives them all the way to primary alcohols.
Now the elegant part, on the board. The class of alcohol you get is decided entirely by the carbonyl partner you feed in.
With a Grignard reagent, an alkyl or aryl magnesium halide, the carbon of R minus magnesium halide adds straight onto the carbonyl carbon. A quick aqueous work up afterwards releases the alcohol.
And the pattern is clean. Start from methanal and you get a primary alcohol. Start from any other aldehyde and you get a secondary. Start from a ketone and you get a tertiary.

<whisper>One warning that ruins many practical marks.</whisper> Grignard reagents are destroyed by any active hydrogen, even a trace of water. So the reagents and the apparatus must be scrupulously dry, or there is no reaction to speak of.
So notice the leverage. One Grignard reagent, and you can dial the product to primary, secondary or tertiary just by choosing whether the partner is methanal, another aldehyde, or a ketone.
हम बिना किसी alkene के भी alcohols बना सकते हैं, carbonyl compounds से शुरू करके। यहाँ दो बड़े methods हैं, reduction और Grignard addition।

पहले reduction। एक aldehyde घटकर primary alcohol बनता है, और एक ketone घटकर secondary alcohol। reducing agent हो सकता है nickel, platinum या palladium पर catalytic hydrogen, या sodium borohydride तथा lithium aluminium hydride जैसा hydride।
carboxylic acids और esters ज़्यादा ज़िद्दी हैं, reduce करना कठिन। उनके लिए strong hydride निकालिए, lithium aluminium hydride, जो उन्हें पूरा primary alcohol तक ले जाता है।
अब elegant हिस्सा, board पर। आपको कौन सी class का alcohol मिलेगा ये पूरी तरह आपके दिए carbonyl partner से तय होता है।
Grignard reagent के साथ, यानी एक alkyl या aryl magnesium halide, R minus magnesium halide का carbon सीधे carbonyl carbon पर add हो जाता है। बाद में एक quick aqueous work up alcohol छोड़ देता है।
और pattern साफ़ है। methanal से शुरू करें तो primary alcohol मिलता है। किसी और aldehyde से शुरू करें तो secondary। ketone से शुरू करें तो tertiary।

<whisper>एक warning जो कई practical marks ख़राब करती है।</whisper> Grignard reagents किसी भी active hydrogen से नष्ट हो जाते हैं, पानी की एक बूँद से भी। इसलिए reagents और apparatus बिल्कुल सूखे होने चाहिए, वरना reaction होगी ही नहीं।
तो leverage देखिए। एक ही Grignard reagent, और आप product को primary, secondary या tertiary पर set कर सकते हैं, बस ये चुनकर कि partner methanal है, कोई और aldehyde, या ketone।

board_events.text: Dow process: chlorobenzene $+$ aqueous NaOH at about 623 K under high pressure ($\sim$300-320 atm).
The signature of the Dow route is 623 K and high pressure.
Alkali fusion: benzene is sulphonated with oleum to benzenesulphonic acid, then fused with molten NaOH.
Both routes give sodium phenoxide, which is acidified to phenol.
C B S E reliably asks a prepare-phenol equation, so write conditions on every arrow.

segments.text: Phenol is such an important molecule that four different preparations are worth knowing, and examiners test the conditions, not just the products. Let us take the first two now.
Here is a helpful pattern before we start. Several routes funnel through the same intermediate, sodium phenoxide, and the last step is simply acidifying that salt to free phenol.
On the board, the top row is the Dow process and the bottom row is alkali fusion. Read the conditions off each arrow as we go.

The Dow process starts from chlorobenzene. You heat it with aqueous sodium hydroxide at about six hundred twenty three kelvin under high pressure, around three hundred to three hundred twenty atmospheres.
<whisper>Tag this route by its conditions.</whisper> Six hundred twenty three kelvin plus high pressure is the fingerprint of the Dow process. If a question quotes those numbers, it wants Dow.
The second route is alkali fusion. First you sulphonate benzene with oleum to give benzenesulphonic acid. Then you fuse that acid with molten sodium hydroxide, which replaces the sulphonic group.
And notice, both of these deliver sodium phenoxide. A quick acidification with any acid then converts the phenoxide salt into phenol itself.

C B S E reliably asks you to prepare phenol from chlorobenzene or from benzene, worth two or three marks. So train yourself to write the reagent and temperature on every single arrow, because that is where the marks live.
Phenol इतना ज़रूरी molecule है कि इसकी चार अलग preparations जानने लायक हैं, और examiners conditions पूछते हैं, सिर्फ़ products नहीं। पहली दो अभी लेते हैं।
शुरू करने से पहले एक काम का pattern। कई routes एक ही intermediate से होकर गुज़रते हैं, sodium phenoxide, और आख़िरी step बस उस salt को acidify करके phenol बनाना है।
board पर, ऊपर की row Dow process है और नीचे की row alkali fusion। साथ साथ हर arrow की conditions पढ़ते चलिए।

Dow process chlorobenzene से शुरू होता है। इसे aqueous sodium hydroxide के साथ लगभग six hundred twenty three kelvin पर high pressure में गरम करते हैं, करीब three hundred से three hundred twenty atmospheres।
<whisper>इस route को इसकी conditions से tag कीजिए।</whisper> six hundred twenty three kelvin plus high pressure Dow process का fingerprint है। अगर question ये numbers दे, तो वो Dow चाहता है।
दूसरा route है alkali fusion। पहले benzene को oleum से sulphonate करके benzenesulphonic acid बनाते हैं। फिर उस acid को molten sodium hydroxide के साथ fuse करते हैं, जो sulphonic group को बदल देता है।
और ध्यान दीजिए, ये दोनों sodium phenoxide देते हैं। किसी भी acid से एक quick acidification फिर phenoxide salt को phenol में बदल देता है।
C B S E reliably पूछता है chlorobenzene या benzene से phenol बनाना, दो या तीन marks का। तो ख़ुद को हर एक arrow पर reagent और temperature लिखने की आदत डालिए, क्योंकि marks वहीं रहते हैं।

sections.title: Phenol from diazonium salts and cumene

board_events.text: Four routes to phenol: the last two
Diazonium route: aniline $+$ NaNO$_2$/HCl at 273-278 K gives a diazonium salt; warm with water to get phenol.
The 273-278 K diazotisation is the fingerprint of the diazonium route.
Cumene process: cumene is air-oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide, which dilute acid cleaves to phenol $+$ acetone.
Most of the world's phenol is made this way; acetone as by-product is the giveaway cue.

board_events.text: So the four routes are chlorobenzene/Dow, benzenesulphonic acid, diazonium hydrolysis, and cumene.
Classify a preparation MCQ in one beat by its signature condition or by-product.

segments.text: Now the remaining two phenol routes, and then we will see all four together on one hub diagram.

Route three uses a diazonium salt. Take an aromatic amine like aniline, diazotise it with sodium nitrite and hydrochloric acid held cold at two hundred seventy three to two hundred seventy eight kelvin. Then simply warm the diazonium salt with water and it hydrolyses to phenol, releasing nitrogen gas.

<whisper>Tag this one too.</whisper> That cold diazotisation window, two hundred seventy three to two hundred seventy eight kelvin, is the fingerprint of the diazonium route. Cold and from an amine means diazonium.

Route four is the cumene process, the industrial giant. Cumene, which is isopropylbenzene, is air oxidised to cumene hydroperoxide. Then dilute acid cleaves that hydroperoxide into two products at once, phenol and acetone.

Most of the world's phenol is actually made this way, and the acetone is a valuable by product, not waste. <excited>So if a question mentions acetone appearing alongside phenol, it can only be the cumene process.</excited>

Now step back and see all four converging on the board. Chlorobenzene from the top left, benzenesulphonic acid from the top right, the diazonium salt from below left, and cumene from below right, all four arrows pointing inward at phenol.
So the complete set is four. Chlorobenzene by the Dow process, benzenesulphonic acid by alkali fusion, diazonium salt by hydrolysis, and cumene industrially.

And here is your speed habit. Classify any preparation question in a single beat by its signature. Acetone by product means cumene. Six twenty three kelvin, high pressure means Dow. Cold two seventy three to two seventy eight diazotisation means the diazonium route.
अब बाक़ी दो phenol routes, और फिर चारों को एक साथ एक hub diagram पर देखेंगे।

Route three एक diazonium salt इस्तेमाल करता है। aniline जैसा एक aromatic amine लीजिए, इसे sodium nitrite और hydrochloric acid के साथ two hundred seventy three से two hundred seventy eight kelvin पर ठंडा रखकर diazotise कीजिए। फिर diazonium salt को बस water के साथ गरम कीजिए और वो hydrolyse होकर phenol बन जाता है, nitrogen gas छोड़ते हुए।
<whisper>इसे भी tag कीजिए।</whisper> वो ठंडा diazotisation window, two hundred seventy three से two hundred seventy eight kelvin, diazonium route का fingerprint है। ठंडा और amine से मतलब diazonium।

Route four है cumene process, industrial दिग्गज। cumene, यानी isopropylbenzene, हवा से oxidise होकर cumene hydroperoxide बनता है। फिर dilute acid उस hydroperoxide को एक साथ दो products में तोड़ देता है, phenol और acetone।

दुनिया का ज़्यादातर phenol असल में इसी तरह बनता है, और acetone एक valuable by product है, कचरा नहीं। <excited>तो अगर कोई question phenol के साथ acetone का ज़िक्र करे, तो वो सिर्फ़ cumene process हो सकता है।</excited>
अब पीछे हटकर board पर चारों को phenol पर मिलते देखिए। ऊपर बाएँ से chlorobenzene, ऊपर दाएँ से benzenesulphonic acid, नीचे बाएँ से diazonium salt, और नीचे दाएँ से cumene, चारों arrows phenol की ओर।
तो पूरा set चार का है। chlorobenzene Dow process से, benzenesulphonic acid alkali fusion से, diazonium salt hydrolysis से, और cumene industrially।

और ये आपकी speed habit। किसी भी preparation question को एक ही beat में उसकी signature से classify कीजिए। acetone by product मतलब cumene। six twenty three kelvin, high pressure मतलब Dow। ठंडा two seventy three से two seventy eight diazotisation मतलब diazonium route।

board_events.text: Dehydration: two primary alcohol molecules lose water over conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ at about 413 K to give a symmetrical ether.
Raising the temperature favours intramolecular dehydration to the alkene instead.
Williamson: a sodium alkoxide (or aryloxide) displaces halide from an alkyl halide by S$_N$2.
It is the general route, and the only sensible way to a mixed ether.
Because it is S$_N$2, keep the halide primary; a 3$^\circ$ halide eliminates to an alkene. Put the bulk on the alkoxide.
So: dehydration only for symmetrical 1-degree ethers; Williamson for everything, especially unsymmetrical.

segments.text: To close the preparation section, let us make ethers. Two routes, and they divide the labour neatly.
On the board, dehydration sits on top and the Williamson synthesis below. One is a blunt instrument, the other is the precision tool.

First, dehydration. Take two molecules of a primary alcohol, heat with concentrated sulphuric acid at about four hundred thirteen kelvin, and they lose one water between them to give a symmetrical ether.

<whisper>But watch the temperature.</whisper> Raise it, and the same acid switches from joining two alcohols to tearing water out of a single one, giving the alkene instead. Lower temperature, ether; higher temperature, alkene. That competition is worth flagging.
Second, the Williamson synthesis, the real workhorse. A sodium alkoxide, or an aryloxide from a phenol, displaces the halide from an alkyl halide by an S N two substitution.
This is the general route. It makes symmetrical ethers, and crucially it is the only sensible way to make a mixed, unsymmetrical ether, because you choose the two halves independently.

But there is a design rule you must obey. Since the step is S N two, the alkyl halide has to be primary. A tertiary halide will not substitute, it will just eliminate to an alkene. So always put the bulky group on the alkoxide side and keep the halide primary.
To summarise the two, then. Dehydration only makes symmetrical ethers of primary alcohols. Williamson makes essentially everything, and it is your go to whenever the ether is unsymmetrical.
preparation section बंद करने के लिए, चलिए ethers बनाते हैं। दो routes, और ये काम को साफ़ बाँट लेते हैं।
board पर dehydration ऊपर है और Williamson synthesis नीचे। एक blunt instrument है, दूसरा precision tool।

पहले, dehydration। एक primary alcohol के दो molecules लीजिए, concentrated sulphuric acid के साथ लगभग four hundred thirteen kelvin पर गरम कीजिए, और वो आपस में एक water खोकर एक symmetrical ether बनाते हैं।

<whisper>पर temperature देखते रहिए।</whisper> इसे बढ़ाइए, और वही acid दो alcohols जोड़ने से हटकर एक ही में से water खींचने लगता है, alkene दे देता है। कम temperature, ether; ज़्यादा temperature, alkene। ये competition flag करने लायक है।
दूसरा, Williamson synthesis, असली workhorse। एक sodium alkoxide, या phenol से बना aryloxide, एक alkyl halide से halide को S N two substitution से displace करता है।
ये general route है। ये symmetrical ethers बनाता है, और सबसे अहम, एक mixed, unsymmetrical ether बनाने का यही एकमात्र समझदार तरीक़ा है, क्योंकि आप दोनों halves अलग अलग चुनते हैं।

पर एक design rule माननी ही होगी। चूँकि step S N two है, alkyl halide primary होना चाहिए। tertiary halide substitute नहीं करेगा, वो बस alkene में eliminate हो जाएगा। तो हमेशा bulky group alkoxide side पर रखिए और halide primary रखिए।
तो दोनों का सार। dehydration सिर्फ़ primary alcohols के symmetrical ethers बनाता है। Williamson लगभग सब कुछ बनाता है, और जब भी ether unsymmetrical हो ये आपका go to है।

board_events.text: CBSE: name and classify this alcohol

board_events.caption: Numbering and the final name

board_events.text: Longest chain that contains the OH carbon has 5 carbons, so the parent is pentane, becoming pentanol.
Number from the left: OH sits on C-2 (lowest locant), and a methyl branch sits on C-4.
Assemble the name: 4-methylpentan-2-ol.
The C-2 carbon is bonded to two other carbons, so this is a secondary (2-degree) alcohol.
Two things were asked, the name and the class, so answer both explicitly.

segments.text: Let us put the naming rules to work on a real C B S E board question. Name this alcohol, and also classify it.
Here is the molecule with the working shown. Follow the numbering as we build the name step by step.
First, the parent chain. The longest continuous chain that still contains the carbon carrying the O H has five carbons. So the parent is pentane, and with an O H it becomes pentanol.
Now number to give the oxygen hydrogen the lowest locant. Counting from the left, the O H sits on carbon two, and there is a methyl branch on carbon four.
Assemble it in order. The methyl is a four substituent, and the O H is a two suffix, so the full name is four methylpentan two ol.
Now the classification the question also demanded. Look at carbon two, the one wearing the O H. It is bonded to two other carbons, which by definition makes this a secondary alcohol.
<whisper>And never lose the easy half mark.</whisper> The question asked two things, the name and the class. So write both, four methylpentan two ol, a secondary alcohol, and the answer is complete.
चलिए naming rules को एक असली C B S E board question पर आज़माते हैं। इस alcohol का नाम बताइए, और इसे classify भी कीजिए।
ये रहा molecule, working के साथ। नाम बनाते हुए numbering को follow कीजिए।
पहले parent chain। सबसे लंबी continuous chain जिसमें O H वाला carbon हो, उसमें पाँच carbon हैं। तो parent है pentane, और O H के साथ ये बनता है pentanol।
अब number इस तरह कीजिए कि oxygen hydrogen को lowest locant मिले। बाएँ से गिनने पर O H carbon two पर है, और carbon four पर एक methyl branch है।
इसे क्रम में जोड़िए। methyl एक four substituent है, और O H एक two suffix, तो पूरा नाम है four methylpentan two ol।
अब classification जो question ने भी माँगा। carbon two देखिए, जो O H पहने है। ये दो और carbons से जुड़ा है, जो definition से इसे secondary alcohol बनाता है।
<whisper>और आसान आधा mark कभी मत खोइए।</whisper> question ने दो चीज़ें पूछीं, नाम और class। तो दोनों लिखिए, four methylpentan two ol, एक secondary alcohol, और जवाब पूरा हो गया।

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: how many alcohols, how many tertiary?
Question: how many structurally isomeric alcohols of formula C$_4$H$_{10}$O, and how many are tertiary?
Read carefully: alcohols only. Do NOT draw the isomeric ethers.

board_events.caption: Placing OH on each C4 skeleton

board_events.text: Straight chain butane gives butan-1-ol (1-degree) and butan-2-ol (2-degree): two alcohols.
Branched isobutane gives 2-methylpropan-1-ol (1-degree) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3-degree): two more.
Total is 4 isomeric alcohols; exactly 1 is tertiary, namely 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Speed tip: a 3-degree alcohol needs at least four carbons, so C4 admits exactly one.

segments.text: This one is a classic N E E T speed trap, and it rewards method over drawing. How many structurally isomeric alcohols share the formula C four H ten O, and how many of them are tertiary?
Set the target clearly. We want alcohols of this molecular formula, and then a headcount of the tertiary ones among them.
<whisper>Here is the trap.</whisper> That same formula also fits ethers, but the question said alcohols. So resist the urge to draw any ethers, they would pad your count and cost you the mark.
The clean method is on the board. Instead of drawing every molecule, take each carbon skeleton and slide the oxygen hydrogen to each distinct position.
On the straight chain, the butane skeleton, the O H can sit at the end giving butan one ol, a primary alcohol, or one carbon in giving butan two ol, a secondary alcohol. That is two.
On the branched skeleton, isobutane, the O H on the end carbon gives two methylpropan one ol, primary, and on the central carbon gives two methylpropan two ol, tertiary. That is two more.
Add them up. Four isomeric alcohols in total, and scanning them, exactly one is tertiary, the two methylpropan two ol.

And bank the speed tip for next time. A tertiary alcohol needs a carbon bonded to three other carbons plus the O H, which needs at least four carbons in all. So C four is the very first formula that admits one, and it admits exactly one.
ये एक classic N E E T speed trap है, और ये drawing से ज़्यादा method को reward करता है। formula C four H ten O वाले कितने structurally isomeric alcohols हैं, और उनमें कितने tertiary हैं?
target साफ़ रखिए। हमें इस molecular formula के alcohols चाहिए, और फिर उनमें से tertiary वालों की गिनती।
<whisper>यहाँ trap है।</whisper> यही formula ethers में भी fit होता है, पर question ने alcohols कहा। तो कोई ether खींचने की इच्छा रोकिए, वो आपकी count बढ़ा देंगे और mark ले जाएँगे।
साफ़ method board पर है। हर molecule खींचने के बजाय, हर carbon skeleton लीजिए और oxygen hydrogen को हर अलग position पर सरकाइए।
straight chain पर, butane skeleton, O H सिरे पर बैठकर butan one ol देता है, एक primary alcohol, या एक carbon अंदर बैठकर butan two ol, एक secondary alcohol। ये हुए दो।
branched skeleton पर, isobutane, सिरे वाले carbon पर O H देता है two methylpropan one ol, primary, और बीच वाले carbon पर two methylpropan two ol, tertiary। ये हुए दो और।
जोड़िए। कुल चार isomeric alcohols, और इन्हें scan करने पर, ठीक एक tertiary है, वो two methylpropan two ol।

और speed tip अगली बार के लिए संभाल लीजिए। एक tertiary alcohol को एक ऐसा carbon चाहिए जो तीन और carbons plus O H से जुड़ा हो, यानी कुल कम से कम चार carbon। तो C four पहला formula है जो एक की इजाज़त देता है, और ठीक एक की।

board_events.text: JEE Main: predict and explain the difference
3-methylbut-1-ene, (CH$_3$)$_2$CH-CH=CH$_2$, is treated (i) with dilute H$_2$SO$_4$, and (ii) with BH$_3$ then H$_2$O$_2$/OH$^-$.

board_events.text: Path (i): protonation gives a 2-degree cation at C-2, which rearranges by a 1,2-hydride shift to a 3-degree cation at C-3.
Water captures there, giving 2-methylbutan-2-ol, a 3-degree alcohol whose skeleton looks moved.
Path (ii): boron adds to terminal C-1 with no carbocation, so OH ends on C-1: 3-methylbutan-1-ol, a 1-degree alcohol.
The contrast is the whole point: rearranged 3-degree alcohol versus clean anti-Markovnikov 1-degree alcohol.
Two ideas combine here: carbocation stability and rearrangement, against the regiochemistry of HBO.

segments.text: This J E E Main problem is where the three alkene routes earn their keep. The same starting alkene is pushed two ways, and the two products look startlingly different.
Our substrate is three methylbut one ene, an isopropyl group attached to a terminal double bond. Treatment one is dilute sulphuric acid, treatment two is borane followed by hydrogen peroxide in base.
Watch the board fork into two paths. Read the acid path going down on the left, and the H B O path going down on the right.

Take the acid path first. Protonation puts a secondary carbocation on carbon two. But sitting right next door on carbon three is a tertiary position, so a one two hydride shift slides the positive charge over to the more stable tertiary cation.

Water then captures at that rearranged carbon three, and the product is two methylbutan two ol, a tertiary alcohol. Notice how the skeleton looks moved, because the cation genuinely relocated before water arrived.

Now the H B O path. Boron adds to the terminal carbon one, there is no carbocation at all, so nothing can rearrange, and after oxidation the oxygen hydrogen stays put on carbon one. The product is three methylbutan one ol, a clean primary alcohol.

<excited>That contrast is the entire question.</excited> One route rearranges to a tertiary alcohol, the other stays disciplined and gives the anti Markovnikov primary alcohol on an untouched skeleton.

So two big ideas are being tested at once. Carbocation stability and rearrangement on the acid side, versus the fixed regiochemistry and carbocation free mechanism of H B O on the other. Name both to secure full marks.
ये J E E Main problem वहाँ है जहाँ तीनों alkene routes अपनी कमाई करते हैं। वही starting alkene दो तरह से push किया जाता है, और दोनों products चौंकाने वाले अलग दिखते हैं।
हमारा substrate है three methylbut one ene, एक terminal double bond से जुड़ा isopropyl group। पहला treatment dilute sulphuric acid, दूसरा borane फिर base में hydrogen peroxide।
board को दो paths में बँटते देखिए। acid path बाईं ओर नीचे पढ़िए, और H B O path दाईं ओर नीचे।

पहले acid path लीजिए। protonation carbon two पर एक secondary carbocation डालता है। पर ठीक बगल में carbon three पर एक tertiary position बैठी है, तो एक one two hydride shift positive charge को ज़्यादा stable tertiary cation पर सरका देता है।

फिर water उस rearranged carbon three पर capture करता है, और product है two methylbutan two ol, एक tertiary alcohol। ध्यान दीजिए skeleton कैसे moved दिखता है, क्योंकि water के आने से पहले cation सचमुच जगह बदल चुका था।

अब H B O path। boron terminal carbon one पर add होता है, कोई carbocation है ही नहीं, तो कुछ rearrange नहीं हो सकता, और oxidation के बाद oxygen hydrogen carbon one पर ही रहता है। product है three methylbutan one ol, एक clean primary alcohol।
<excited>यही contrast पूरा question है।</excited> एक route rearrange होकर tertiary alcohol देता है, दूसरा disciplined रहकर एक untouched skeleton पर anti Markovnikov primary alcohol देता है।

तो एक साथ दो बड़े ideas test हो रहे हैं। acid side पर carbocation stability और rearrangement, बनाम दूसरी ओर H B O की fixed regiochemistry और carbocation free mechanism। full marks के लिए दोनों नाम लिखिए।

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: pick reagents and defend the choice
Task: make propan-2-ol from propene with no risk of skeletal rearrangement, and separately make anisole.
