board_events.text: For propan-2-ol, the disciplined choice is oxymercuration-demercuration: a bridged mercurinium ion, so no free cation can rearrange.
Acid hydration gives the same product here, but trains a route that fails on substrates like the previous example.
For anisole, use Williamson: sodium phenoxide $+$ methyl iodide. Bulk and aryl character on the oxide; the SN2 electrophile is unhindered methyl.
The reversed pairing, phenyl halide + sodium methoxide, fails: aryl halides do not undergo ordinary SN2, so no ether forms.
Method selection hinges on which fragment can be the SN2 electrophile.

segments.text: Our final worked example is a J E E Advanced style choice question. It is less about mechanism and more about judgement, picking the right reagent and defending why the obvious alternative is inferior.
Two tasks. First, make propan two ol from propene with no risk of skeletal rearrangement. Second, separately make anisole, that is methoxybenzene.
The two answers sit on the board, oxymercuration up top and a Williamson synthesis below. Let us justify each.

For propan two ol, the requirement is a Markovnikov alcohol with zero rearrangement risk. The disciplined choice is oxymercuration demercuration, because its intermediate is a bridged mercurinium ion, so no free carbocation can ever rearrange.

<whisper>Now defend it against the obvious alternative.</whisper> Acid hydration would actually give the same propan two ol here, since propene has nowhere better to rearrange to. But relying on the open carbocation as a habit is exactly what burned us in the previous example. So oxymercuration is the principled answer.

For anisole, reach for the Williamson synthesis, combining sodium phenoxide with methyl iodide. The bulk and the aryl character sit safely on the oxide side, and the S N two electrophile is the small, unhindered methyl halide. Ideal.
Now the trap you must call out. The reversed pairing, a phenyl halide with sodium methoxide, simply fails. Aryl halides do not undergo ordinary S N two, so no ether ever forms on that route.
So the deep lesson across both parts is one sentence. Method selection hinges on which fragment can serve as the S N two electrophile, and you build your synthesis around protecting that role.
हमारा आख़िरी worked example एक J E E Advanced style choice question है। ये mechanism से कम और judgement से ज़्यादा है, सही reagent चुनना और ये defend करना कि obvious alternative कमतर क्यों है।
दो tasks। पहला, propene से propan two ol बनाइए बिना किसी skeletal rearrangement के risk के। दूसरा, अलग से anisole बनाइए, यानी methoxybenzene।
दोनों जवाब board पर हैं, ऊपर oxymercuration और नीचे एक Williamson synthesis। चलिए हर एक को justify करते हैं।

propan two ol के लिए, ज़रूरत है एक Markovnikov alcohol बिना किसी rearrangement risk के। disciplined choice है oxymercuration demercuration, क्योंकि इसका intermediate एक bridged mercurinium ion है, तो कोई free carbocation कभी rearrange नहीं कर सकता।

<whisper>अब इसे obvious alternative के ख़िलाफ़ defend कीजिए।</whisper> acid hydration यहाँ असल में वही propan two ol देगा, क्योंकि propene के पास rearrange होने के लिए कोई बेहतर जगह नहीं है। पर open carbocation पर आदत के तौर पर भरोसा करना ठीक वही है जिसने पिछले example में हमें जलाया। तो oxymercuration ही principled जवाब है।

anisole के लिए, Williamson synthesis उठाइए, sodium phenoxide को methyl iodide के साथ मिलाकर। bulk और aryl character सुरक्षित रूप से oxide side पर बैठते हैं, और S N two electrophile है छोटा, unhindered methyl halide। ideal।
अब वो trap जो बतानी ज़रूरी है। उलटी pairing, एक phenyl halide sodium methoxide के साथ, बस fail हो जाती है। aryl halides ordinary S N two नहीं करते, तो उस route पर कभी कोई ether नहीं बनता।
तो दोनों हिस्सों की गहरी सीख एक वाक्य में है। method selection इस पर टिका है कि कौन सा fragment S N two electrophile बन सकता है, और आप अपनी synthesis उसी role को बचाने के इर्द गिर्द बनाते हैं।

board_events.text: Traps that cost easy marks
Calling phenol an alcohol: its oxygen sits on an sp2 aromatic carbon, changing acidity, bond length and reactivity.
Markovnikov mix-ups: acid hydration and oxymercuration are Markovnikov; HBO is anti-Markovnikov.
Remember only acid hydration can rearrange; oxymercuration cannot. Forgetting this costs Advanced marks.
Wrong parent chain: the chain must include the OH carbon even if a longer chain exists elsewhere.
Dropping the $-e$ in diols and triols: it is ethane-1,2-diol, not ethandiol.
Williamson: putting the bulky group on the halide (3-degree halide eliminates, no ether).

Pro-tip: classify preparation MCQs by signature. Acetone by-product $\Rightarrow$ cumene; 623 K, high P $\Rightarrow$ Dow; 273-278 K diazotisation $\Rightarrow$ diazonium; syn/anti-Markovnikov/no rearrangement $\Rightarrow$ HBO.

segments.text: Let us close Part one by collecting the traps, the small mistakes that quietly bleed marks even when you understand the chemistry.

Trap one, calling phenol an alcohol. They both show an oxygen hydrogen, yes, but phenol's oxygen sits on an s p two aromatic carbon, and that single fact changes its acidity, its bond length, and its reactivity. Treat them as separate families.
Trap two, the Markovnikov mix up. Lock the table once and for all. Acid hydration and oxymercuration are both Markovnikov. Hydroboration oxidation is the odd one out, anti Markovnikov.

And the finer half of that trap. Among the two Markovnikov routes, only acid hydration can rearrange, because oxymercuration goes through that safe bridged ion. Forgetting this distinction is exactly what costs marks at the Advanced level.

Trap three, choosing the wrong parent chain. The chain you name must run through the carbon bearing the O H, even when a longer carbon chain exists somewhere off to the side. Include the O H first, then worry about length.
Trap four, a spelling trap that examiners genuinely penalise. In diols and triols you keep the letter e. It is ethane one comma two diol, never ethandiol.

Trap five, the Williamson blunder. Never load the bulky group onto the halide. A tertiary halide simply eliminates to an alkene and gives you no ether. Bulk goes on the alkoxide, halide stays primary.

<whisper>And now the pro tip that wins speed rounds.</whisper> Classify preparation questions by their signature in one glance. Acetone by product means cumene. Six twenty three kelvin and high pressure means Dow. Cold diazotisation at two seventy three to two seventy eight means the diazonium route. And syn, or anti Markovnikov, or no rearrangement means hydroboration oxidation. That closes Part one.
Part one बंद करते हैं traps इकट्ठा करके, वो छोटी ग़लतियाँ जो chemistry समझने के बावजूद चुपके से marks बहा देती हैं।

Trap एक, phenol को alcohol कहना। दोनों में oxygen hydrogen दिखता है, सही, पर phenol का oxygen एक s p two aromatic carbon पर बैठा है, और यही एक बात इसकी acidity, bond length और reactivity बदल देती है। इन्हें अलग families मानिए।
Trap दो, Markovnikov का घालमेल। table एक बार में पक्की कर लीजिए। acid hydration और oxymercuration दोनों Markovnikov हैं। hydroboration oxidation अलग है, anti Markovnikov।

और उस trap का बारीक आधा। दो Markovnikov routes में से सिर्फ़ acid hydration rearrange कर सकता है, क्योंकि oxymercuration उस safe bridged ion से गुज़रता है। इस फ़र्क़ को भूलना ठीक वही है जो Advanced level पर marks ले जाता है।
Trap तीन, ग़लत parent chain चुनना। जिस chain का नाम रखें उसे O H वाले carbon से होकर गुज़रना चाहिए, चाहे कहीं किनारे कोई लंबी carbon chain हो। पहले O H शामिल कीजिए, फिर length की सोचिए।
Trap चार, एक spelling trap जिस पर examiners सचमुच marks काटते हैं। diols और triols में e अक्षर रखते हैं। ये ethane one comma two diol है, कभी ethandiol नहीं।
Trap पाँच, Williamson की चूक। bulky group को कभी halide पर मत लादिए। एक tertiary halide बस alkene में eliminate हो जाता है और कोई ether नहीं देता। bulk alkoxide पर जाता है, halide primary रहता है।

<whisper>और अब वो pro tip जो speed rounds जिताती है।</whisper> preparation questions को उनकी signature से एक नज़र में classify कीजिए। acetone by product मतलब cumene। six twenty three kelvin और high pressure मतलब Dow। two seventy three से two seventy eight पर ठंडा diazotisation मतलब diazonium route। और syn, या anti Markovnikov, या no rearrangement मतलब hydroboration oxidation। इसी के साथ Part one पूरा।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Why alcohols boil high and dissolve

board_events.text: Physical properties: it all traces to the O-H

board_events.caption: Boiling points at similar molecular mass
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="340" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Boiling points at comparable mass (~58-60 u)</text><rect x="60" y="160" width="46" height="40" fill="#a0aec0" rx="3"/><text x="83" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">273 K</text><text x="83" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">n-butane</text><rect x="180" y="148" width="46" height="52" fill="#63b3ed" rx="3"/><text x="203" y="142" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">281 K</text><text x="203" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">methoxyethane</text><rect x="300" y="110" width="46" height="90" fill="#4fd1c5" rx="3"/><text x="323" y="104" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">322 K</text><text x="323" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">propanal</text><rect x="420" y="101" width="46" height="99" fill="#48bb78" rx="3"/><text x="443" y="95" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">329 K</text><text x="443" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">propanone</text><rect x="540" y="60" width="46" height="140" fill="#dd6b20" rx="3"/><text x="563" y="54" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#1f2933">370 K</text><text x="563" y="216" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">propan-1-ol</text><text x="563" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#c05621">O-H···O</text><text x="340" y="240" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">the alcohol tops the list: hydrogen bonding must be pried apart</text></svg>

board_events.text: Each O-H is a hand that grips a neighbour's oxygen through a hydrogen bond; boiling must pry all those hands apart.
So an alcohol boils far higher than an alkane, ether or haloalkane of comparable mass.
Ethers have no O-H hand of their own, so they boil low, close to the alkanes.
Small alcohols like ethanol mix with water in all proportions, because the O-H shakes hands with water.
As the carbon tail lengthens, the oily part overwhelms the friendly O-H, so water-solubility falls with chain length.
A polyhydric alcohol carries several hands, so it stays soluble longer.

segments.text: In Part one we built and named these molecules. Now we ask how they behave, and almost everything traces back to that one hard working group, the oxygen hydrogen.
Look at the boiling points on the board, all for molecules of nearly the same mass. Watch how the alcohol towers over everything else.

Here is the picture to keep. Think of a crowded platform. Alkane molecules are strangers who never hold hands, so they drift apart and boil low. But each alcohol carries an oxygen hydrogen, a hand that grips a neighbour's oxygen through a hydrogen bond. To boil the liquid you must pry all those hands apart, and that costs extra energy.
That is why an alcohol boils much higher than an alkane, an ether, or a haloalkane of comparable molecular mass. The hydrogen bonding is the whole story.
An ether, by contrast, has no oxygen hydrogen hand of its own to offer. So ether molecules cannot hold hands with each other, and they boil low, right down near the alkanes.
Now solubility. The oxygen hydrogen end happily shakes hands with water, also through hydrogen bonding. So small alcohols like ethanol mix with water in all proportions.

But as the carbon tail lengthens, the oily, water fearing part of the molecule grows and eventually overwhelms that friendly oxygen hydrogen. So water solubility steadily falls as the chain gets longer.
And a nice corollary. A polyhydric alcohol carries several oxygen hydrogen hands at once, so it can keep gripping water and stays soluble for longer chains than a simple alcohol would.
Part one में हमने ये molecules बनाए और नाम रखे। अब पूछते हैं ये कैसे behave करते हैं, और लगभग सब कुछ उसी एक मेहनती group पर टिका है, oxygen hydrogen।
board पर boiling points देखिए, सब लगभग एक जैसे mass वाले molecules के लिए। ध्यान दीजिए alcohol बाक़ी सबसे कितना ऊपर है।

ये तस्वीर याद रखिए। एक भीड़ भरे platform की सोचिए। alkane molecules अजनबी हैं जो कभी हाथ नहीं मिलाते, तो अलग हो जाते हैं और नीचे boil होते हैं। पर हर alcohol एक oxygen hydrogen रखता है, एक हाथ जो पड़ोसी के oxygen को hydrogen bond से पकड़ता है। liquid को boil करने के लिए वो सारे हाथ छुड़ाने पड़ते हैं, और उसमें extra energy लगती है।
इसीलिए alcohol एक comparable mass वाले alkane, ether, या haloalkane से कहीं ऊँचे boil होता है। पूरी कहानी hydrogen bonding की है।
इसके उलट ether के पास देने को अपना कोई oxygen hydrogen हाथ नहीं है। तो ether molecules आपस में हाथ नहीं मिला सकते, और नीचे boil होते हैं, ठीक alkanes के पास।
अब solubility। oxygen hydrogen सिरा water से ख़ुशी से हाथ मिलाता है, वो भी hydrogen bonding से। तो ethanol जैसे छोटे alcohols water में हर अनुपात में मिल जाते हैं।

पर जैसे carbon tail लंबी होती है, molecule का तैलीय, पानी से डरने वाला हिस्सा बढ़ता है और आख़िरकार उस दोस्ताना oxygen hydrogen पर हावी हो जाता है। तो chain लंबी होते ही water solubility लगातार गिरती है।
और एक अच्छा corollary। एक polyhydric alcohol एक साथ कई oxygen hydrogen हाथ रखता है, तो वो water को पकड़े रह सकता है और एक साधारण alcohol से लंबी chains तक soluble रहता है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: The two seams: how the OH reacts

board_events.text: Two seams, two families of reaction

board_events.caption: The O-H seam and the C-O seam
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 620 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="620" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="310" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">The C-O-H unit has two seams</text><text x="310" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="30" fill="#1f2933">C — O — H</text><line x1="360" y1="95" x2="410" y2="60" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="470" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">O-H seam</text><text x="470" y="73" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">give up H(+) = ACIDITY</text><line x1="255" y1="95" x2="205" y2="60" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="150" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">C-O seam</text><text x="150" y="73" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">give up OH / replace it</text><text x="150" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2b6cb0">substitution (OH → halide)</text><text x="150" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2b6cb0">dehydration (→ alkene)</text><text x="470" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c53030">how easily H(+) leaves,</text><text x="470" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c53030">how stable the anion is</text></svg>

board_events.text: Chemistry attacks the C-O-H unit at one of two seams. Everything in this subtopic sorts into these two.
The O-H seam: give up the hydrogen as a proton. This is acidity.
Acid strength depends on how willingly the proton leaves and how stable the leftover negative ion is.
The C-O seam: give up the whole OH, or replace it.
This underlies substitution (OH becomes a halide, as in the Lucas test) and dehydration (OH plus an adjacent H leave as water).
Sort every reaction ahead into O-H (acidity) or C-O (substitution / dehydration) and it stops feeling like a list.

segments.text: Before we dive into a long list of reactions, let us build the map that organises the whole subtopic. There are only two places chemistry can attack.
Picture the carbon oxygen hydrogen unit on the board. It has exactly two seams, marked in two colours, and every reaction we meet will cut along one of them.
That is the key idea. Chemistry attacks this unit at one of two seams, and if you know which seam a reaction uses, you already understand its logic.
First, the oxygen hydrogen seam. Here the molecule gives up its hydrogen as a proton. That is acidity, plain and simple.

And acid strength has two ingredients. How willingly the proton actually leaves, and how stable the negative ion left behind is. Hold on to that second one, because it explains everything about phenol shortly.
Second, the carbon oxygen seam. Here the molecule gives up the whole oxygen hydrogen group, or swaps it for something else.

This second seam underlies two big reaction types. Substitution, where the oxygen hydrogen is replaced by a halide, exactly what the Lucas test does. And dehydration, where the oxygen hydrogen and an adjacent hydrogen leave together as water, giving an alkene.

<whisper>So here is your organising trick.</whisper> Every reaction ahead sorts into O H seam, which means acidity, or C O seam, which means substitution or dehydration. Do that sorting and this subtopic stops feeling like a list to memorise.
reactions की लंबी list में कूदने से पहले, चलिए वो map बनाते हैं जो पूरे subtopic को व्यवस्थित करती है। chemistry के पास attack करने की सिर्फ़ दो जगहें हैं।
board पर carbon oxygen hydrogen unit की कल्पना कीजिए। इसमें ठीक दो seams हैं, दो रंगों में चिह्नित, और हम जो भी reaction देखेंगे वो इन्हीं में से एक पर कटेगी।
यही मुख्य idea है। chemistry इस unit पर दो में से एक seam पर attack करती है, और अगर आपको पता है कि reaction कौन सी seam इस्तेमाल करती है, तो उसका logic आप पहले ही समझ गए।
पहली, oxygen hydrogen seam। यहाँ molecule अपना hydrogen एक proton के रूप में छोड़ता है। यही acidity है, सीधा सादा।

और acid strength में दो ingredients हैं। proton असल में कितनी ख़ुशी से छूटता है, और पीछे बचा negative ion कितना stable है। इस दूसरे को पकड़े रहिए, क्योंकि थोड़ी देर में यही phenol के बारे में सब कुछ समझाएगा।
दूसरी, carbon oxygen seam। यहाँ molecule पूरा oxygen hydrogen group छोड़ देता है, या उसे किसी और चीज़ से बदल देता है।

ये दूसरी seam दो बड़े reaction types के पीछे है। substitution, जहाँ oxygen hydrogen की जगह halide आता है, ठीक वही जो Lucas test करता है। और dehydration, जहाँ oxygen hydrogen और एक बगल वाला hydrogen साथ में water बनकर निकलते हैं, alkene देते हुए।

<whisper>तो ये आपकी organising trick है।</whisper> आगे की हर reaction दो में बँटती है, O H seam यानी acidity, या C O seam यानी substitution या dehydration। ये छँटाई कीजिए और ये subtopic रटने की list जैसा महसूस होना बंद कर देगा।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Why phenol is the troublemaker

board_events.text: Phenol's dual personality

board_events.caption: Electrons flow both ways
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 620 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="620" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="310" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Phenol: a two-way electron street</text><polygon points="310.0,98.0 282.3,114.0 282.3,146.0 310.0,162.0 337.7,146.0 337.7,114.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="310" cy="130" r="19.2" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="310.0" y1="98.0" x2="310.0" y2="72.0" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><text x="310.0" y="66.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#c05621">O-H</text><text x="470" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">ring tugs e(-) off O</text><text x="470" y="88" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">→ O-H lets H(+) go</text><text x="470" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c53030">MORE ACIDIC</text><defs><marker id="m43080" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#c53030"/></marker></defs><line x1="430" y1="80" x2="360" y2="95" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#m43080)"/><text x="150" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">O-H feeds e(-) in</text><text x="150" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">→ ring electron-rich</text><text x="150" y="210" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2f855a">EAS at ortho / para</text><defs><marker id="m210180" markerWidth="9" markerHeight="9" refX="7" refY="3" orient="auto"><path d="M0,0 L7,3 L0,6 Z" fill="#2f855a"/></marker></defs><line x1="210" y1="180" x2="275" y2="150" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.8" marker-end="url(#m210180)"/><text x="310" y="235" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">two personalities: acidic O-H  +  activated ring</text></svg>

board_events.text: In an alcohol the OH sits on a quiet sp3 carbon. In phenol it sits on a benzene ring, an electron-sharing marketplace.
The ring tugs electron density away from oxygen, so the O-H lets its proton go more readily.
Phenol is markedly more acidic than any alcohol, and even more acidic than water.
The sharing runs the other way too: the OH pumps electron density into the ring, making it electron-rich.
So the ring is strongly activated toward electrophiles, which attack at the ortho and para positions.
Phenol therefore does two families of reaction: acidic O-H reactions, and electrophilic substitution on the ring.

segments.text: Before the reactions, one big idea explains almost all of phenol's behaviour. Phenol is the troublemaker of the family, and it is a troublemaker in two directions at once.
On the board, watch the electrons move. Arrows point both ways between the oxygen and the ring, and each direction gives phenol a different power.

Here is the setup. In an ordinary alcohol the oxygen hydrogen is bolted to a quiet s p three carbon that mostly leaves it alone. But in phenol it sits on a benzene ring, a crowded, electron sharing marketplace.
Look at the first arrow. The ring tugs electron density away from the oxygen. With less electron density holding it, the oxygen hydrogen bond lets its proton go far more readily.
The consequence is one of the most tested facts in the chapter. Phenol is markedly more acidic than any alcohol, and it is even more acidic than water itself.
Now the second arrow, running the other way. The oxygen hydrogen also pumps electron density into the ring, feeding it a lone pair. That makes the ring genuinely electron rich.
And an electron rich ring is catnip for electrophiles. So the ring is strongly activated, and incoming electrophiles attack preferentially at the ortho and para positions.

<whisper>So carry this one sentence into every phenol reaction.</whisper> Phenol does two whole families of chemistry. Acidic reactions at the oxygen hydrogen, and electrophilic substitution on the activated ring. Which arrow is doing the work tells you which family you are in.
reactions से पहले, एक बड़ा idea phenol के लगभग सारे behaviour को समझा देता है। phenol इस family का troublemaker है, और एक साथ दो दिशाओं में troublemaker है।
board पर electrons को हिलते देखिए। oxygen और ring के बीच arrows दोनों तरफ़ इशारा करते हैं, और हर दिशा phenol को एक अलग शक्ति देती है।

setup ये है। एक साधारण alcohol में oxygen hydrogen एक शांत s p three carbon पर लगा है जो उसे ज़्यादातर छोड़े रखता है। पर phenol में वो एक benzene ring पर बैठा है, एक भीड़ भरा, electron share करता बाज़ार।
पहला arrow देखिए। ring oxygen से electron density खींच लेता है। कम electron density के साथ, oxygen hydrogen bond अपना proton कहीं ज़्यादा आसानी से छोड़ता है।
नतीजा chapter के सबसे ज़्यादा पूछे जाने वाले facts में से एक है। phenol किसी भी alcohol से साफ़ ज़्यादा acidic है, और water से भी ज़्यादा acidic है।
अब दूसरा arrow, उलटी दिशा में। oxygen hydrogen ring में electron density भी pump करता है, उसे एक lone pair खिलाते हुए। इससे ring सचमुच electron rich हो जाता है।
और एक electron rich ring electrophiles के लिए catnip है। तो ring ख़ूब activated है, और आने वाले electrophiles ख़ासकर ortho और para positions पर attack करते हैं।

<whisper>तो ये एक वाक्य हर phenol reaction में साथ ले जाइए।</whisper> phenol दो पूरी families की chemistry करता है। oxygen hydrogen पर acidic reactions, और activated ring पर electrophilic substitution। कौन सा arrow काम कर रहा है यही बताता है आप किस family में हैं।

board_events.text: Acidity, strongest first: carboxylic acid, carbonic acid, phenol, water, alcohol.
Anchors: carboxylic acids about 4 to 5, phenol about 10, water about 15.7, ethanol about 16. Smaller pKa is stronger.
Within alcohols the intrinsic order is CH$_3$OH $\gt$ 1$^\circ$ $\gt$ 2$^\circ$ $\gt$ 3$^\circ$, from the electron-releasing $+$I effect of alkyl groups.
Substituted phenols: electron-withdrawing groups ($-$NO$_2$, $-$X, $-$CHO, $-$CN) at ortho/para raise acidity.
Picric acid, 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, is very strong; electron-releasing groups (cresols) lower acidity.
Reagent brackets: NaHCO3 catches only the acids; NaOH reaches through phenol; alcohols yield only to sodium metal.

segments.text: The data worth memorising in this subtopic is not a formula, it is one acidity chain. Learn it as a single ladder and half the questions here answer themselves.
Here it is on the board as a number line. Acid strength on the left, weakness on the right, with the p K a values and, below, brackets showing which reagent each species reacts with.
Say the chain out loud until it is automatic. Carboxylic acid, stronger than carbonic acid, stronger than phenol, stronger than water, stronger than an alcohol.

Now the numerical anchors. Carboxylic acids around four to five, phenol around ten, water around fifteen point seven, ethanol around sixteen. And remember, the smaller the p K a, the stronger the acid.

Zoom in on the alcohols themselves. Their intrinsic order is methanol, then primary, then secondary, then tertiary, from strong to weak. The reason is the electron releasing plus I effect of alkyl groups, which piles electron density onto the anion and destabilises it.
Now zoom in on substituted phenols instead. An electron withdrawing group, such as nitro, a halogen, an aldehyde, or a cyano group, placed at ortho or para, raises acidity.

Push that to the extreme and you get picric acid, two four six trinitrophenol, with three nitro groups, which is a very strong acid indeed. Electron releasing groups do the reverse, so the cresols, being methyl phenols, are weaker than phenol.

Finally read the reagent brackets, because they turn acidity into a lab test. Sodium bicarbonate reacts only with the true acids. Sodium hydroxide reaches all the way through phenol. And the feeble alcohols yield only to sodium metal itself.
इस subtopic में याद रखने लायक data कोई formula नहीं, बल्कि एक acidity chain है। इसे एक ही ladder की तरह सीख लीजिए और यहाँ के आधे सवाल ख़ुद हल हो जाते हैं।
ये रही board पर एक number line के रूप में। बाईं ओर acid strength, दाईं ओर कमज़ोरी, p K a values के साथ, और नीचे brackets जो दिखाते हैं हर species किस reagent से react करती है।
इस chain को तब तक बोलिए जब तक automatic न हो जाए। carboxylic acid, carbonic acid से मज़बूत, phenol से मज़बूत, water से मज़बूत, alcohol से मज़बूत।
अब numerical anchors। carboxylic acids around four to five, phenol around ten, water around fifteen point seven, ethanol around sixteen। और याद रखिए, p K a जितना छोटा, acid उतना मज़बूत।

अब alcohols पर zoom कीजिए। इनका intrinsic order है methanol, फिर primary, फिर secondary, फिर tertiary, मज़बूत से कमज़ोर। कारण है alkyl groups का electron releasing plus I effect, जो anion पर electron density ढेर करके उसे destabilise करता है।
अब substituted phenols पर zoom कीजिए। एक electron withdrawing group, जैसे nitro, एक halogen, एक aldehyde, या cyano group, ortho या para पर लगा हो, तो acidity बढ़ाता है।

इसे चरम पर ले जाइए तो मिलता है picric acid, two four six trinitrophenol, तीन nitro groups के साथ, जो सचमुच बहुत मज़बूत acid है। electron releasing groups उलटा करते हैं, तो cresols, यानी methyl phenols, phenol से कमज़ोर होते हैं।

आख़िर में reagent brackets पढ़िए, क्योंकि ये acidity को एक lab test में बदल देते हैं। sodium bicarbonate सिर्फ़ असली acids से react करता है। sodium hydroxide phenol तक पहुँच जाता है। और कमज़ोर alcohols सिर्फ़ sodium metal के आगे झुकते हैं।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Acidity mechanism: resonance decides

board_events.text: The stability of the anion is everything
Both alcohols and phenols react with active metals (Na, K, Al), releasing hydrogen and forming alkoxides or phenoxides.
But phenol ALSO reacts with aqueous NaOH to give sodium phenoxide; alcohols do not. That single line proves phenol is the stronger acid.

board_events.caption: Phenoxide is resonance-stabilised; alkoxide is not
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="340" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Why phenol beats alcohols</text><polygon points="150.0,100.0 124.0,115.0 124.0,145.0 150.0,160.0 176.0,145.0 176.0,115.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="150" cy="130" r="18.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="150.0" y1="100.0" x2="150.0" y2="76.0" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="70.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="13" fill="#c05621">O(-)</text><text x="150" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">phenoxide</text><text x="150" y="218" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">charge spread over O + o/p carbons</text><circle cx="126" cy="160" r="3" fill="#2f855a"/><circle cx="174" cy="160" r="3" fill="#2f855a"/><circle cx="150" cy="164" r="3" fill="#2f855a"/><text x="360" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="24" fill="#5a6570">vs</text><text x="530" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" fill="#1f2933">CH3–CH2–O(-)</text><text x="530" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">alkoxide</text><text x="530" y="168" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#5a6570">charge stuck on O, no resonance</text><text x="530" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c53030">less stable → barely acidic</text></svg>

board_events.text: On losing a proton, phenol gives the phenoxide ion, whose negative charge is delocalised over oxygen and the ortho/para carbons.
That spreading stabilises the anion, so the proton leaves readily.
An alkoxide has no such resonance; the charge stays localised on oxygen, the anion is less stable, and the alcohol is barely acidic.
Substituent shift: an EWG at ortho/para drains still more charge off, stabilising further and raising acidity; an EDG does the opposite.

segments.text: We stated that phenol beats alcohols on acidity. Now let us prove it, because the reasoning is worth more than the fact. It all comes down to the stability of the anion left behind.

Start with what they share. Both alcohols and phenols react with active metals, sodium, potassium, aluminium, fizzing off hydrogen and forming alkoxides or phenoxides. So both have a weakly acidic oxygen hydrogen.

But here is the line that separates them. Phenol also reacts with ordinary aqueous sodium hydroxide to give sodium phenoxide, whereas alcohols simply do not. That one experimental fact proves phenol is the stronger acid.
The board shows why. On the left, the phenoxide ion. On the right, an alkoxide from an alcohol. The difference between them is the entire explanation.

When phenol loses its proton, the resulting phenoxide ion is special. Its negative charge does not stay put on the oxygen. It is delocalised, spread out over the oxygen and the ortho and para carbons of the ring.
And a spread out charge is a stabilised charge. Because the anion is comfortable, the proton is happy to leave in the first place. Stability of the product drives the acidity of the parent.
Contrast the alkoxide. It has no ring to delocalise into, no resonance at all. The negative charge stays stuck on a single oxygen, the anion is far less stable, and so the alcohol is barely acidic.

And this immediately explains the substituent effects. An electron withdrawing group at ortho or para drains even more charge off the phenoxide, stabilising it further and raising acidity. An electron releasing group pushes charge back on, destabilising the anion and lowering acidity.
हमने कहा phenol acidity में alcohols को हराता है। अब इसे साबित करते हैं, क्योंकि reasoning fact से ज़्यादा क़ीमती है। सब कुछ पीछे बचे anion की stability पर आता है।

जो साझा है उससे शुरू करते हैं। alcohols और phenols दोनों active metals, sodium, potassium, aluminium से react करते हैं, hydrogen छोड़ते हुए और alkoxides या phenoxides बनाते हुए। तो दोनों में एक weakly acidic oxygen hydrogen है।

पर यही line इन्हें अलग करती है। phenol साधारण aqueous sodium hydroxide से भी react करके sodium phenoxide बनाता है, जबकि alcohols नहीं करते। यही एक experimental fact साबित करता है कि phenol मज़बूत acid है।
board दिखाता है क्यों। बाईं ओर phenoxide ion। दाईं ओर एक alcohol से बना alkoxide। इन दोनों का फ़र्क़ ही पूरी व्याख्या है।
जब phenol अपना proton खोता है, बनने वाला phenoxide ion ख़ास होता है। इसका negative charge oxygen पर टिका नहीं रहता। वो delocalise होता है, oxygen और ring के ortho तथा para carbons पर फैल जाता है।
और फैला हुआ charge एक stabilise हुआ charge है। चूँकि anion आरामदेह है, इसलिए proton पहली जगह में ख़ुशी से निकलता है। product की stability parent की acidity चलाती है।

अब alkoxide से तुलना कीजिए। इसके पास delocalise होने के लिए कोई ring नहीं, कोई resonance नहीं। negative charge एक अकेले oxygen पर अटका रहता है, anion कहीं कम stable है, इसलिए alcohol मुश्किल से acidic है।

और यही तुरंत substituent effects समझाता है। ortho या para पर एक electron withdrawing group phenoxide से और ज़्यादा charge खींच लेता है, उसे और stabilise करके acidity बढ़ाता है। एक electron releasing group charge वापस धकेलता है, anion को destabilise करके acidity घटाता है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Esterification: the acid loses its OH

board_events.text: An O-H reaction with the acid's C-O
Alcohols and phenols react with carboxylic acids, acid chlorides or acid anhydrides to give esters.

board_events.caption: Which oxygen ends up in the water

board_events.text: With a carboxylic acid you need conc. H2SO4 as catalyst and dehydrating agent; the reaction is reversible, so water is removed to drive it forward.
Isotopic labelling proves it is the acid's OH, not the alcohol's, that is lost as water.
Bulky groups slow it, so the ease of esterification runs CH$_3$OH $\gt$ 1$^\circ$ $\gt$ 2$^\circ$ $\gt$ 3$^\circ$.
Mechanism: acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen, the alcohol adds to give a tetrahedral intermediate, then water leaves and a proton is lost.
Every step is reversible, which is exactly why removing water or using excess reactant pushes the equilibrium toward the ester.

segments.text: Esterification is a lovely bridge reaction. It uses the oxygen hydrogen seam of the alcohol, but it attacks the carbon oxygen of the acid. Watch which molecule sacrifices what.
The reaction itself is general. Alcohols and phenols react with carboxylic acids, or with acid chlorides, or with acid anhydrides, to give esters.
The board highlights the subtle question examiners love. When water is expelled, whose oxygen ends up in that water molecule?

Take the carboxylic acid version. You need concentrated sulphuric acid, doing double duty as catalyst and as dehydrating agent. The reaction is reversible, so you deliberately remove the water to keep driving it forward.

And here is the classic mechanistic fact. Isotopic labelling shows that the water molecule is built from the acid's oxygen hydrogen, not the alcohol's. The alcohol keeps its own oxygen. This is a nucleophilic acyl substitution.
Bulk matters for the rate. Crowded alcohols react sluggishly, so the ease of esterification runs methanol, then primary, then secondary, then tertiary, the familiar downhill order.

Briefly, the mechanism. The acid protonates its own carbonyl oxygen, which makes the carbonyl carbon more electrophilic. The alcohol oxygen then adds to it, giving a tetrahedral intermediate. A proton shuffle turns the acid's oxygen hydrogen into a good leaving group, water departs, and a final proton is lost to give the ester.

<whisper>And notice the payoff.</whisper> Every single step is reversible. That is precisely why the practical tricks work. Remove the water, or flood the flask with excess reactant, and you shove the equilibrium all the way toward the ester.
Esterification एक प्यारी bridge reaction है। ये alcohol की oxygen hydrogen seam इस्तेमाल करती है, पर acid के carbon oxygen पर attack करती है। देखिए कौन सा molecule क्या क़ुर्बान करता है।
reaction ख़ुद general है। alcohols और phenols carboxylic acids, या acid chlorides, या acid anhydrides से react करके esters बनाते हैं।
board उस बारीक सवाल को उभारता है जो examiners को पसंद है। जब water निकलता है, तो उस water molecule में किसका oxygen जाता है?

carboxylic acid वाला version लीजिए। concentrated sulphuric acid चाहिए, जो catalyst और dehydrating agent दोनों का काम करता है। reaction reversible है, तो आप जानबूझकर water हटाते रहते हैं ताकि ये आगे बढ़ती रहे।

और ये रहा classic mechanistic fact। isotopic labelling दिखाता है कि water molecule acid के oxygen hydrogen से बनता है, alcohol के नहीं। alcohol अपना oxygen अपने पास रखता है। ये एक nucleophilic acyl substitution है।
rate के लिए bulk मायने रखता है। भीड़ वाले alcohols सुस्ती से react करते हैं, तो esterification की आसानी चलती है methanol, फिर primary, फिर secondary, फिर tertiary, वही जाना पहचाना ढलान।

संक्षेप में mechanism। acid अपने ही carbonyl oxygen को protonate करता है, जिससे carbonyl carbon ज़्यादा electrophilic हो जाता है। फिर alcohol oxygen उस पर add होता है, एक tetrahedral intermediate देते हुए। एक proton की अदला बदली acid के oxygen hydrogen को एक अच्छा leaving group बना देती है, water निकलता है, और आख़िर में एक proton खोकर ester बनता है।

<whisper>और payoff देखिए।</whisper> हर एक step reversible है। इसीलिए practical tricks काम करती हैं। water हटा दीजिए, या flask को excess reactant से भर दीजिए, और equilibrium को पूरा ester की ओर धकेल दीजिए।

board_events.text: The alcohol reacts to give an alkyl chloride, R-Cl, which separates as an oily turbidity.
It goes by an S$_N$1 path: ZnCl2 helps the OH leave, so the rate tracks carbocation stability.
Turbidity is immediate for 3-degree (and benzylic/allylic), about 5 minutes for 2-degree, and absent at room temperature for 1-degree.
Rate order is therefore 3$^\circ$ $\gt$ 2$^\circ$ $\gt$ 1$^\circ$, exactly the carbocation-stability order.
Benzylic and allylic alcohols react as fast as tertiary, because their cations are resonance-stabilised.

segments.text: Now we cross to the carbon oxygen seam, the reactions that cleave the whole oxygen hydrogen off. Our first is a diagnostic test you will use again and again, the Lucas test.
The reagent is simple. An equimolar mixture of concentrated hydrochloric acid and anhydrous zinc chloride. Its job is to tell primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols apart.
And the way it tells them apart is on the board, by speed. Read the three rows, from tertiary at the top to primary at the bottom.

Chemically, the alcohol is converted to an alkyl chloride. That chloride is not soluble in the reagent mix, so it separates out as a cloudy, oily turbidity. Turbidity appearing is your positive signal.

The mechanism is S N one. The zinc chloride grips the oxygen hydrogen and helps it leave as the leaving group, generating a carbocation. So the rate of the whole test simply tracks how stable that carbocation is.

Hence the timings. A tertiary alcohol gives turbidity immediately. A secondary alcohol takes about five minutes. And a primary alcohol does not react at all at room temperature, because its carbocation is far too unstable to form.
So the rate order is tertiary, then secondary, then primary, which is nothing but the carbocation stability order written out as reaction speed.

<whisper>One extra case to remember.</whisper> Benzylic and allylic alcohols react as fast as tertiary ones, giving immediate turbidity, because their carbocations are resonance stabilised. Do not misread a benzylic alcohol as secondary just from its structure.
अब हम carbon oxygen seam पर आते हैं, वो reactions जो पूरा oxygen hydrogen काट देती हैं। पहली है एक diagnostic test जिसे आप बार बार इस्तेमाल करेंगे, Lucas test।
reagent simple है। concentrated hydrochloric acid और anhydrous zinc chloride का equimolar mixture। इसका काम है primary, secondary और tertiary alcohols को अलग बताना।
और ये कैसे अलग बताता है वो board पर है, speed से। तीनों rows पढ़िए, ऊपर tertiary से नीचे primary तक।
chemically, alcohol एक alkyl chloride में बदल जाता है। वो chloride reagent mix में घुलता नहीं, तो एक धुँधली, तैलीय turbidity बनकर अलग हो जाता है। turbidity का आना ही आपका positive signal है।

mechanism S N one है। zinc chloride oxygen hydrogen को पकड़कर उसे leaving group के रूप में निकलने में मदद करता है, एक carbocation बनाते हुए। तो पूरे test का rate बस इस पर टिका है कि वो carbocation कितना stable है।

इसलिए timings। एक tertiary alcohol तुरंत turbidity देता है। एक secondary alcohol लगभग पाँच मिनट लेता है। और एक primary alcohol room temperature पर react ही नहीं करता, क्योंकि उसका carbocation बनने के लिए बहुत unstable है।
तो rate order है tertiary, फिर secondary, फिर primary, जो carbocation stability order को reaction speed के रूप में लिखने के सिवा कुछ नहीं है।

<whisper>एक extra case याद रखिए।</whisper> benzylic और allylic alcohols tertiary जितनी तेज़ी से react करते हैं, तुरंत turbidity देते हुए, क्योंकि इनके carbocations resonance stabilised हैं। एक benzylic alcohol को उसकी structure से secondary मत समझ बैठिए।

board_events.text: Dehydration: pull out water, make an alkene

board_events.caption: E1 dehydration follows Saytzeff

board_events.text: Heating an alcohol with conc. H2SO4 removes water to give an alkene, by an E1 mechanism.
The major product follows Saytzeff's rule: the more substituted alkene.
Ease of dehydration is 3$^\circ$ $\gt$ 2$^\circ$ $\gt$ 1$^\circ$, again because a more stable carbocation forms more easily.
Tertiary alcohols dehydrate around 360 K; primary alcohols need about 440 K.
So both the Lucas order and the dehydration order track the same thing: carbocation stability.
This is a C-O seam reaction: the OH and an adjacent hydrogen leave together as water.

segments.text: Our second carbon oxygen reaction is dehydration. Here the alcohol does not swap its oxygen hydrogen for a halide, it throws it away entirely as water and collapses into an alkene.
Follow the board with butan two ol. Heat it with concentrated sulphuric acid and it loses water to give but two ene.

The reagent is concentrated sulphuric acid with heat, and the mechanism is E one. The acid protonates the oxygen hydrogen, water leaves to give a carbocation, and then a neighbouring hydrogen is lost to form the double bond.
Which alkene do you get when there is a choice? The major product follows Saytzeff's rule, the more substituted, more stable alkene. So from butan two ol you get but two ene, not but one ene.
And the ease of dehydration is tertiary, then secondary, then primary. The reason is now familiar. A more stable carbocation forms more easily, and a tertiary alcohol makes the most stable cation.

That difference even shows up in the temperature you need. A tertiary alcohol dehydrates gently, around three hundred sixty kelvin, whereas a stubborn primary alcohol needs roughly four hundred forty kelvin.

<whisper>Notice the pattern repeating.</whisper> The Lucas order and the dehydration order are the very same order, tertiary over secondary over primary, and both are really just carbocation stability wearing two different costumes.
And to keep our map intact, this is squarely a carbon oxygen seam reaction. The oxygen hydrogen and an adjacent hydrogen leave together as one water molecule, which is what generates the double bond.
हमारी दूसरी carbon oxygen reaction है dehydration। यहाँ alcohol अपना oxygen hydrogen halide से नहीं बदलता, बल्कि उसे पूरा water बनाकर फेंक देता है और एक alkene में ढह जाता है।
board पर butan two ol के साथ चलिए। इसे concentrated sulphuric acid के साथ गरम कीजिए और ये water खोकर but two ene बन जाता है।

reagent है concentrated sulphuric acid गरमी के साथ, और mechanism E one है। acid oxygen hydrogen को protonate करता है, water निकलकर एक carbocation देता है, फिर एक पड़ोसी hydrogen निकलकर double bond बनाता है।
choice होने पर कौन सा alkene मिलता है? major product Saytzeff's rule follow करता है, ज़्यादा substituted, ज़्यादा stable alkene। तो butan two ol से but two ene मिलता है, but one ene नहीं।
और dehydration की आसानी है tertiary, फिर secondary, फिर primary। कारण अब जाना पहचाना है। ज़्यादा stable carbocation आसानी से बनता है, और tertiary alcohol सबसे stable cation बनाता है।

ये फ़र्क़ तो ज़रूरी temperature में भी दिखता है। एक tertiary alcohol आराम से dehydrate होता है, लगभग three hundred sixty kelvin पर, जबकि ज़िद्दी primary alcohol को करीब four hundred forty kelvin चाहिए।

<whisper>pattern को दोहराते देखिए।</whisper> Lucas order और dehydration order बिल्कुल एक ही order हैं, tertiary ऊपर secondary ऊपर primary, और दोनों असल में carbocation stability ही हैं जो दो अलग costumes पहने है।
और अपनी map बनाए रखने के लिए, ये सीधे एक carbon oxygen seam reaction है। oxygen hydrogen और एक बगल वाला hydrogen साथ में एक water molecule बनकर निकलते हैं, और यही double bond बनाता है।

board_events.text: A primary alcohol oxidises to an aldehyde with a mild oxidant, and on to a carboxylic acid with a strong one (KMnO4 or acidified K2Cr2O7).
A secondary alcohol gives a ketone.
A tertiary alcohol resists oxidation: there is no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon for the oxidant to pull off.
Catalytic dehydrogenation over hot copper at about 573 K parallels this: 1-degree gives an aldehyde, 2-degree a ketone.
But over hot copper a tertiary alcohol has no C-H to lose, so it dehydrates to an alkene instead.
These differing products are themselves a way to tell the three classes apart.

segments.text: Our third carbon oxygen reaction is oxidation, and it is beautiful because the product literally announces the class of the alcohol.
The whole outcome fits in one table on the board. Three rows for the three classes, with the oxidation product in the middle column and the hot copper result on the right.

Start with a primary alcohol. A mild oxidant takes it up one step to an aldehyde. Push harder with a strong oxidant, potassium permanganate or acidified potassium dichromate, and you overshoot to a carboxylic acid.
A secondary alcohol has only one place to go. It oxidises to a ketone and stops there, because the carbon has no further hydrogen to give up.

And the tertiary alcohol simply refuses. The carbinol carbon, the one bearing the oxygen hydrogen, has no hydrogen at all attached to it. A mild oxidant works by pulling off that hydrogen, so with nothing to pull, there is no ordinary oxidation.

Catalytic dehydrogenation over hot copper at about five hundred seventy three kelvin tells the same story from a different angle. A primary alcohol loses hydrogen to give an aldehyde, a secondary gives a ketone.

But watch the tertiary alcohol over that same hot copper. With no carbon hydrogen bond on the carbinol carbon to break, it cannot dehydrogenate at all, so it takes the other exit and dehydrates to an alkene instead.

<whisper>So bank this as a test in its own right.</whisper> Aldehyde then acid means primary. A ketone means secondary. And a stubborn refusal to oxidise, or an alkene from hot copper, means tertiary. The product is the fingerprint of the class.
हमारी तीसरी carbon oxygen reaction है oxidation, और ये ख़ूबसूरत है क्योंकि product सचमुच alcohol की class का ऐलान कर देता है।
पूरा outcome board पर एक table में आ जाता है। तीन classes के लिए तीन rows, बीच के column में oxidation product और दाईं ओर hot copper का result।

एक primary alcohol से शुरू कीजिए। एक mild oxidant इसे एक step ऊपर aldehyde तक ले जाता है। एक strong oxidant, potassium permanganate या acidified potassium dichromate, से ज़्यादा ज़ोर लगाइए और आप carboxylic acid तक चले जाते हैं।
एक secondary alcohol के पास जाने को सिर्फ़ एक जगह है। ये oxidise होकर ketone बनता है और वहीं रुक जाता है, क्योंकि उस carbon के पास देने को और hydrogen नहीं है।

और tertiary alcohol बस मना कर देता है। carbinol carbon, जो oxygen hydrogen पहने है, उस पर कोई hydrogen लगा ही नहीं है। एक mild oxidant उसी hydrogen को खींचकर काम करता है, तो खींचने को कुछ न हो तो कोई ordinary oxidation नहीं।
hot copper पर लगभग five hundred seventy three kelvin पर catalytic dehydrogenation वही कहानी अलग कोण से बताती है। एक primary alcohol hydrogen खोकर aldehyde देता है, एक secondary ketone देता है।
पर उसी hot copper पर tertiary alcohol देखिए। carbinol carbon पर तोड़ने को कोई carbon hydrogen bond न होने से ये dehydrogenate हो ही नहीं सकता, तो दूसरा रास्ता लेकर dehydrate होकर alkene बन जाता है।

<whisper>तो इसे अपने आप में एक test मानिए।</whisper> aldehyde फिर acid मतलब primary। एक ketone मतलब secondary। और oxidise होने से ज़िद्दी इनकार, या hot copper से alkene, मतलब tertiary। product class का fingerprint है।

board_events.text: Methanol and primary alcohols lacking that unit do not respond, so the test distinguishes ethanol from propan-1-ol.
Reaction with inorganic acids gives inorganic esters: with conc. H2SO4, ethanol gives ethyl hydrogen sulphate; with conc. HNO3, ethyl nitrate.
Reaction with aldehydes: in dry HCl gas an alcohol adds to an aldehyde, first to a hemiacetal, then with a second alcohol to an acetal.
The acetal is a gem-diether, and this is the basis of carbonyl protection met later in the course.
So the iodoform test pins the CH3CH(OH) pattern; keep it ready for the discrimination toolkit next.

segments.text: Three shorter carbon oxygen reactions round out the alcohol chemistry, and the first of them, the iodoform test, is a genuine exam favourite.

Here is the test. Ethanol, and in fact any alcohol carrying the methyl carbon hydrogen oxygen hydrogen unit, when warmed with iodine and sodium hydroxide, throws down a yellow precipitate of iodoform.
The board shows the scan you should run in your head. Look only for that characteristic fragment, a methyl group attached to a carbon that also carries the oxygen hydrogen.

So ethanol is positive, because it hides that unit. But methanol and primary alcohols that lack it, like propan one ol, stay stubbornly negative. That is exactly why the test cleanly distinguishes ethanol from propan one ol.

The second reaction. Alcohols react not only with organic acids but with inorganic oxy acids too, forming inorganic esters. With concentrated sulphuric acid, ethanol gives ethyl hydrogen sulphate. With concentrated nitric acid, it gives ethyl nitrate.
The third reaction. In the presence of dry hydrogen chloride gas, an alcohol adds to an aldehyde. The first alcohol gives a hemiacetal, and a second alcohol converts that into an acetal.

That acetal is effectively a gem diether, and this exact chemistry is the basis of carbonyl protection, a trick you will meet again later in the course when you need to shield an aldehyde temporarily.
<whisper>Keep the iodoform result front of mind.</whisper> It pins down the methyl carbon hydroxyl pattern, and we are about to use it in the full discrimination toolkit in the very next section.
तीन छोटी carbon oxygen reactions alcohol chemistry को पूरा करती हैं, और इनमें से पहली, iodoform test, सचमुच exam की पसंदीदा है।
ये रहा test। ethanol, और असल में कोई भी alcohol जो methyl carbon hydrogen oxygen hydrogen unit रखता हो, जब iodine और sodium hydroxide के साथ गरम हो, तो iodoform का पीला precipitate गिरा देता है।
board वो scan दिखाता है जो आपको मन में चलाना चाहिए। सिर्फ़ उस ख़ास fragment को ढूँढिए, एक methyl group जो एक ऐसे carbon से जुड़ा हो जो oxygen hydrogen भी रखता हो।

तो ethanol positive है, क्योंकि वो उस unit को छुपाए है। पर methanol और वो primary alcohols जिनमें ये नहीं है, जैसे propan one ol, ज़िद्दी negative रहते हैं। इसीलिए ये test ethanol को propan one ol से साफ़ अलग करता है।

दूसरी reaction। alcohols सिर्फ़ organic acids ही नहीं, inorganic oxy acids से भी react करके inorganic esters बनाते हैं। concentrated sulphuric acid के साथ ethanol ethyl hydrogen sulphate देता है। concentrated nitric acid के साथ ये ethyl nitrate देता है।
तीसरी reaction। dry hydrogen chloride gas की मौजूदगी में एक alcohol एक aldehyde पर add होता है। पहला alcohol एक hemiacetal देता है, और दूसरा alcohol उसे acetal में बदल देता है।
वो acetal असल में एक gem diether है, और ठीक यही chemistry carbonyl protection का आधार है, एक trick जो आगे course में फिर मिलेगी जब आपको किसी aldehyde को अस्थायी रूप से बचाना हो।
<whisper>iodoform result को दिमाग़ में सामने रखिए।</whisper> ये methyl carbon hydroxyl pattern पक्का करता है, और हम इसे ठीक अगली section में पूरी discrimination toolkit में इस्तेमाल करने वाले हैं।

board_events.text: Three independent tests separate primary, secondary and tertiary alcohols, and a complete answer names more than one.
Lucas ranks them by turbidity speed: 3-degree immediate, 2-degree about 5 minutes, 1-degree none at room temperature.
Oxidation or catalytic dehydrogenation gives an aldehyde then acid from 1-degree, a ketone from 2-degree, and merely an alkene from 3-degree.
Victor Meyer's test: a 1-degree alcohol gives blood-red, a 2-degree gives blue, and a 3-degree gives no colour.
Victor Meyer works by converting the alcohol stepwise to a nitroalkane, then treating with nitrous acid and making alkaline.
Combine two cheap tests to partition the space: one fixes the class, another confirms it.

segments.text: Now let us collect the tools into one toolkit, because a favourite exam task is to hand you an unknown alcohol and ask you to prove its class. Three independent tests do the job.
The board lays all three across one grid, with the three classes as columns. Read down each test to see how it splits them.
And the strategic point first. A complete, full mark answer names more than one test, because any single test can leave an ambiguity that a second test cleanly removes.
Test one is Lucas, ranking by turbidity speed. Tertiary is immediate, secondary takes about five minutes, and primary shows nothing at room temperature. That mostly separates the three already.

Test two is oxidation, or the hot copper version. A primary alcohol gives an aldehyde and then an acid, a secondary gives a ketone, and a tertiary gives merely an alkene by dehydration. Different product, different class.

Test three is Victor Meyer's, which is pure colour coding. A primary alcohol ends up blood red, a secondary alcohol blue, and a tertiary alcohol gives no colour at all. Memorise those three colours in order.

For completeness, how Victor Meyer works. You convert the alcohol stepwise into a nitroalkane, then treat it with nitrous acid, and finally make the solution alkaline. It is the resulting species whose colour betrays the class.

<whisper>And here is the exam habit that never fails.</whisper> Do not gamble on one test. Combine two cheap ones so that the first fixes the class and the second confirms it. Two simple observations beat one clever guess every time.
अब सारे tools को एक toolkit में इकट्ठा करते हैं, क्योंकि exam का पसंदीदा काम है आपको एक unknown alcohol देना और उसकी class साबित करने को कहना। तीन independent tests ये काम करते हैं।
board तीनों को एक grid पर रखता है, तीन classes columns के रूप में। हर test को नीचे पढ़िए और देखिए वो इन्हें कैसे बाँटता है।
और पहले strategic बात। एक पूरा, full mark जवाब एक से ज़्यादा test नाम लेता है, क्योंकि कोई भी अकेला test एक ambiguity छोड़ सकता है जिसे दूसरा test साफ़ हटा देता है।
Test एक है Lucas, turbidity speed से ranking। tertiary तुरंत, secondary लगभग पाँच मिनट, और primary room temperature पर कुछ नहीं दिखाता। इतने में ही तीनों काफ़ी हद तक अलग हो जाते हैं।
Test दो है oxidation, या hot copper वाला version। एक primary alcohol aldehyde फिर acid देता है, एक secondary ketone देता है, और एक tertiary dehydration से बस alkene देता है। अलग product, अलग class।

Test तीन है Victor Meyer's, जो शुद्ध colour coding है। एक primary alcohol blood red निकलता है, एक secondary alcohol blue, और एक tertiary alcohol कोई colour नहीं देता। इन तीन colours को क्रम में याद कीजिए।

पूरा करने के लिए, Victor Meyer कैसे काम करता है। आप alcohol को step by step एक nitroalkane में बदलते हैं, फिर उसे nitrous acid से treat करते हैं, और आख़िर में solution को alkaline बनाते हैं। बनने वाली species का colour ही class बता देता है।

<whisper>और ये रही exam की आदत जो कभी नाकाम नहीं होती।</whisper> एक test पर जुआ मत खेलिए। दो सस्ते tests मिलाइए ताकि पहला class तय करे और दूसरा confirm करे। दो सरल observations हर बार एक चतुर अनुमान से बेहतर हैं।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Electrophilic substitution I: nitration

board_events.text: The OH activates the ring; electrophiles hit ortho/para
With dilute HNO3 at about 298 K, phenol gives a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenol.

board_events.caption: Ortho vs para hydrogen bonding
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="340" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Nitration: why o- and p-nitrophenol separate</text><polygon points="150.0,90.0 124.0,105.0 124.0,135.0 150.0,150.0 176.0,135.0 176.0,105.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="150" cy="120" r="18.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="118" y="99" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="#c05621">OH</text><text x="156" y="90" text-anchor="start" font-size="10" fill="#2b6cb0">NO2</text><path d="M138 96 Q170 88 188 106" fill="none" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="3,2"/><text x="150" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">ortho: intramolecular H-bond</text><text x="150" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">closed chelate, no association</text><text x="150" y="209" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2f855a">steam-VOLATILE</text><polygon points="500.0,90.0 474.0,105.0 474.0,135.0 500.0,150.0 526.0,135.0 526.0,105.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="500" cy="120" r="18.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><text x="474" y="99" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c05621">OH</text><text x="500" y="166" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#2b6cb0">NO2</text><text x="500" y="175" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">para: intermolecular H-bond</text><text x="500" y="193" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">molecules associate</text><text x="500" y="209" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c53030">far LESS volatile</text><text x="340" y="238" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">dil. HNO3, 298 K → o/p mixture; conc. HNO3 → picric acid</text></svg>

board_events.text: The two are separated by steam distillation, and the reason is hydrogen bonding, not polarity.
Ortho-nitrophenol forms an intramolecular H-bond (a closed chelate), so molecules don't associate; it is steam-volatile.
Para-nitrophenol associates by intermolecular H-bonding, so it is far less volatile and stays behind.
With concentrated HNO3, phenol is converted all the way to 2,4,6-trinitrophenol, which is picric acid.
Picric acid is a strong acid because three nitro groups facilitate proton release.

segments.text: Now we swing over to phenol's second personality, the activated ring. Every reaction here is an electrophilic substitution at the ortho and para positions. We begin with nitration.
Treat phenol with dilute nitric acid at about two hundred ninety eight kelvin, and you get a mixture of two products, ortho nitrophenol and para nitrophenol.
Now the elegant part, which is a genuine exam favourite. These two isomers are separated by steam distillation, and the board shows why, side by side.
Resist the tempting wrong answer. The separation is not about polarity. It is entirely about hydrogen bonding, specifically about which kind of hydrogen bond each isomer forms.

Look at the ortho isomer. Its nitro group sits right next to the oxygen hydrogen, close enough to form a hydrogen bond within the same molecule, a closed chelate ring. Because each molecule satisfies itself internally, the molecules do not cling to one another, and the compound is steam volatile.

Now the para isomer. Its nitro group is across the ring, too far to bond internally, so instead the molecules hydrogen bond to each other, chaining up. That intermolecular gripping makes it far less volatile, so it stays behind while the ortho isomer distils over.

Change the reagent and you change the destination. With concentrated nitric acid, phenol does not stop at one nitro group. It is nitrated all the way to two four six trinitrophenol, the famous picric acid.
And picric acid is not just a curiosity, it is a strong acid. Three electron withdrawing nitro groups drain the phenoxide so effectively that the proton leaves very easily indeed.
अब हम phenol की दूसरी personality पर आते हैं, activated ring। यहाँ हर reaction ortho और para positions पर एक electrophilic substitution है। शुरुआत nitration से।
phenol को dilute nitric acid के साथ लगभग two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर treat कीजिए, और आपको दो products का mixture मिलता है, ortho nitrophenol और para nitrophenol।
अब elegant हिस्सा, जो सचमुच exam की पसंदीदा है। इन दोनों isomers को steam distillation से अलग किया जाता है, और board साथ साथ दिखाता है क्यों।
लुभावने ग़लत जवाब से बचिए। ये separation polarity के बारे में नहीं है। ये पूरी तरह hydrogen bonding के बारे में है, ख़ासकर इस बारे में कि हर isomer किस तरह का hydrogen bond बनाता है।

ortho isomer देखिए। इसका nitro group ठीक oxygen hydrogen के बगल में है, इतने पास कि एक ही molecule के भीतर hydrogen bond बना ले, एक closed chelate ring। चूँकि हर molecule ख़ुद को अंदर ही संतुष्ट कर लेता है, molecules एक दूसरे से चिपकते नहीं, और compound steam volatile होता है।

अब para isomer। इसका nitro group ring के आर पार है, अंदर bond बनाने के लिए बहुत दूर, तो इसके बजाय molecules आपस में hydrogen bond बनाते हैं, chain बनाते हुए। वो intermolecular पकड़ इसे कहीं कम volatile बनाती है, तो जब ortho isomer distil होकर निकल जाता है ये पीछे रह जाता है।
reagent बदलिए और destination बदल जाता है। concentrated nitric acid के साथ phenol एक nitro group पर नहीं रुकता। ये पूरा two four six trinitrophenol तक nitrate हो जाता है, मशहूर picric acid।
और picric acid सिर्फ़ एक curiosity नहीं, ये एक strong acid है। तीन electron withdrawing nitro groups phenoxide को इतनी असरदार तरीक़े से खींचते हैं कि proton सचमुच बहुत आसानी से निकल जाता है।

sections.title: Electrophilic substitution II: halogenation and sulphonation

board_events.text: Bromination and sulphonation

board_events.caption: Tribromophenol, p-bromophenol, and sulphonation

H2SO4)</text><text x="490" y="188" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">low T → ortho product</text><text x="490" y="206" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">higher T → para (thermodynamic)</text></svg>

board_events.text: With bromine water, phenol gives a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol; all three activated positions brominate.
No catalyst is needed, because the OH has already activated the ring so strongly.
With bromine in a low-polarity solvent (CS2) at low temperature, monobromination dominates, giving mainly p-bromophenol.
With concentrated H2SO4, phenol gives o-phenolsulphonic acid at low temperature.
At higher temperature the para isomer predominates, because the para product is the thermodynamically favoured one.
A white precipitate with bromine water is a classic quick identification of phenol.

segments.text: Staying on the activated ring, we meet two more electrophilic substitutions, halogenation and sulphonation. Both showcase just how reactive that ring has become.
The board collects the outcomes. On the left, the dramatic bromine water result, and on the right, the milder conditions and sulphonation.
Start with bromine water. Phenol is so eager that all three activated positions, the two ortho and the one para, brominate at once, giving a white precipitate of two four six tribromophenol.

And here is the contrast with plain benzene that examiners love. Phenol needs no Lewis acid catalyst for this, none at all, because the oxygen hydrogen has already activated the ring far beyond what benzene could ever manage.

If you want to stop at a single bromine, you change the conditions. Bromine in a low polarity solvent like carbon disulphide, at low temperature, calms the reaction so that monobromination dominates, giving mainly para bromophenol.
Now sulphonation, with concentrated sulphuric acid. At low temperature you get mainly the ortho product, ortho phenolsulphonic acid.

But warm it up and the balance shifts to the para isomer. The reason is thermodynamic control. The para product is the more stable, thermodynamically favoured one, and higher temperature lets the system settle into it.

<whisper>One quick identification to bank.</whisper> A white precipitate the instant you add bromine water is a classic, immediate signal for phenol. If a question describes that, phenol is your answer.
activated ring पर ही रहते हुए, हमें दो और electrophilic substitutions मिलती हैं, halogenation और sulphonation। दोनों दिखाती हैं कि वो ring कितना reactive हो चुका है।
board outcomes इकट्ठा करता है। बाईं ओर नाटकीय bromine water का result, और दाईं ओर हल्की conditions तथा sulphonation।
bromine water से शुरू कीजिए। phenol इतना उत्सुक है कि तीनों activated positions, दो ortho और एक para, एक साथ brominate हो जाती हैं, two four six tribromophenol का white precipitate देते हुए।

और यहाँ सादे benzene से वो contrast है जो examiners को पसंद है। phenol को इसके लिए कोई Lewis acid catalyst नहीं चाहिए, बिल्कुल नहीं, क्योंकि oxygen hydrogen ring को पहले ही benzene की क़ाबिलियत से कहीं आगे activate कर चुका है।

अगर एक ही bromine पर रुकना हो, तो conditions बदलिए। carbon disulphide जैसे low polarity solvent में bromine, low temperature पर, reaction को शांत कर देता है ताकि monobromination हावी रहे, मुख्यतः para bromophenol देते हुए।
अब sulphonation, concentrated sulphuric acid के साथ। low temperature पर मुख्यतः ortho product मिलता है, ortho phenolsulphonic acid।

पर इसे गरम कीजिए और संतुलन para isomer की ओर खिसक जाता है। कारण है thermodynamic control। para product ज़्यादा stable, thermodynamically favoured है, और ज़्यादा temperature system को उसमें बैठने देता है।
<whisper>एक quick identification संभाल लीजिए।</whisper> bromine water डालते ही एक white precipitate phenol का classic, तुरंत signal है। अगर कोई question इसे बताए, तो phenol आपका जवाब है।

board_events.text: Reimer-Tiemann: phenol with CHCl3 and aqueous NaOH at about 340 K, then acid hydrolysis, installs a CHO at the ortho position, giving salicylaldehyde.
The true electrophile is dichlorocarbene, formed when NaOH deprotonates chloroform to a trichloromethyl carbanion which loses chloride.
With CCl4 instead of CHCl3, the product is salicylic acid rather than the aldehyde.
Kolbe reaction: sodium phenoxide absorbs CO2 under pressure at about 400 K; after acidification this yields salicylic acid.
Salicylic acid is the gateway to aspirin (its acetyl ester) and to methyl salicylate, oil of wintergreen.
Product cue: a CHO installed ortho means Reimer-Tiemann; a COOH installed ortho means Kolbe.

segments.text: Two named reactions both decorate the ortho position of phenol, and both lead to famous medicines. Let us take Reimer Tiemann first, then Kolbe.
The board pairs them so you can see the parallel. Both start from phenol on the left and end with an ortho substituted product, one with an aldehyde, one with an acid.

Reimer Tiemann. Treat phenol with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide at about three hundred forty kelvin, then hydrolyse with acid. The result is a formyl group installed at the ortho position, giving salicylaldehyde, that is two hydroxybenzaldehyde.

The mechanism has a lovely twist you should be able to state. Sodium hydroxide deprotonates chloroform to a trichloromethyl carbanion, which then loses a chloride to form the real electrophile, dichlorocarbene. That carbene attacks the electron rich phenoxide ring.

And one useful variation. Swap chloroform for carbon tetrachloride, and the same reaction delivers salicylic acid instead of the aldehyde. Same idea, one extra chlorine, a carboxyl instead of a formyl.

Now Kolbe, sometimes called Kolbe Schmidt. Here sodium phenoxide absorbs carbon dioxide under pressure at about four hundred kelvin. After acidification you again arrive at salicylic acid, this time by planting a carboxyl group ortho to the oxygen hydrogen.

And salicylic acid matters enormously in real life. It is the gateway to aspirin, which is its acetyl ester, and to methyl salicylate, the oil of wintergreen. So this ortho carboxyl is a doorway to the medicine cabinet.
<whisper>Read these by their product.</whisper> A formyl group planted ortho means Reimer Tiemann. A carboxyl group planted ortho means Kolbe. Let the installed group name the reaction for you.
दो named reactions दोनों phenol की ortho position सजाती हैं, और दोनों मशहूर दवाओं तक ले जाती हैं। पहले Reimer Tiemann, फिर Kolbe लेते हैं।
board इन्हें जोड़कर रखता है ताकि आप समानता देख सकें। दोनों बाईं ओर phenol से शुरू होकर एक ortho substituted product पर ख़त्म होती हैं, एक aldehyde के साथ, एक acid के साथ।

Reimer Tiemann। phenol को chloroform और aqueous sodium hydroxide के साथ लगभग three hundred forty kelvin पर treat कीजिए, फिर acid से hydrolyse कीजिए। नतीजा है ortho position पर लगा एक formyl group, salicylaldehyde देते हुए, यानी two hydroxybenzaldehyde।

mechanism में एक प्यारा twist है जो आपको बता आना चाहिए। sodium hydroxide chloroform को deprotonate करके एक trichloromethyl carbanion बनाता है, जो फिर एक chloride खोकर असली electrophile बनाता है, dichlorocarbene। वो carbene electron rich phenoxide ring पर attack करता है।
और एक काम की variation। chloroform की जगह carbon tetrachloride लीजिए, और वही reaction aldehyde की जगह salicylic acid देती है। वही idea, एक extra chlorine, formyl की जगह एक carboxyl।

अब Kolbe, जिसे कभी Kolbe Schmidt कहते हैं। यहाँ sodium phenoxide दबाव में लगभग four hundred kelvin पर carbon dioxide सोखता है। acidification के बाद आप फिर salicylic acid पर पहुँचते हैं, इस बार oxygen hydrogen के ortho एक carboxyl group लगाकर।
और salicylic acid असल ज़िंदगी में बेहद अहम है। ये aspirin का द्वार है, जो इसका acetyl ester है, और methyl salicylate का, यानी oil of wintergreen। तो ये ortho carboxyl दवा की अलमारी का दरवाज़ा है।
<whisper>इन्हें इनके product से पढ़िए।</whisper> ortho लगा एक formyl group मतलब Reimer Tiemann। ortho लगा एक carboxyl group मतलब Kolbe। लगा हुआ group ही आपके लिए reaction का नाम बता दे।

board_events.text: Reaction with zinc dust: heating phenol with zinc dust replaces OH by H, giving benzene.
Friedel-Crafts acetylation: with acetyl chloride and anhydrous AlCl3, phenol gives ortho- and para-hydroxyacetophenone.
The OH is usually acetylated first, so the ring product often comes via a Fries-type rearrangement of that ester.
Gattermann formylation: phenol with HCN and HCl gas over anhydrous AlCl3, then hydrolysis, gives mainly para-hydroxybenzaldehyde.
Gattermann is para-selective, complementary to the ortho-selective Reimer-Tiemann.
Oxidation: chromic acid converts phenol to benzoquinone; in air, phenols slowly darken to quinone mixtures.

segments.text: Let us finish phenol's reaction gallery with four more named transformations. Each one installs or removes a specific group, and the board holds all four at once.
Read them clockwise from the top left. Benzene by removal, an acetyl group, a formyl group, and a full oxidation to a diketone.
First, reaction with zinc dust. Heat phenol with zinc dust and the whole oxygen hydrogen is stripped off and replaced by a hydrogen, taking you right back down to plain benzene.
Second, Friedel Crafts acetylation. With acetyl chloride and anhydrous aluminium chloride, phenol picks up an acetyl group on the ring, giving ortho and para hydroxyacetophenone.

There is a subtlety worth stating. The oxygen hydrogen tends to get acetylated first, forming an ester, so the ring product is often reached by a Fries type rearrangement of that ester rather than by direct ring attack.

Third, Gattermann formylation. Treat phenol with hydrogen cyanide and hydrogen chloride gas over anhydrous aluminium chloride, then hydrolyse, and you install a formyl group, giving mainly para hydroxybenzaldehyde.
<whisper>Pair this with Reimer Tiemann in your memory.</whisper> Gattermann is para selective, while Reimer Tiemann was ortho selective. Two ways to add a formyl group, aimed at opposite positions.

Fourth, oxidation. Chromic acid oxidises phenol to the conjugated diketone benzoquinone. And this is the everyday reason a bottle of phenol darkens on standing, as air slowly oxidises it toward quinone mixtures.
phenol की reaction gallery चार और named transformations से पूरी करते हैं। हर एक कोई ख़ास group लगाती या हटाती है, और board चारों को एक साथ रखता है।
इन्हें ऊपर बाएँ से clockwise पढ़िए। हटाकर benzene, एक acetyl group, एक formyl group, और एक पूरा oxidation एक diketone तक।
पहली, zinc dust से reaction। phenol को zinc dust के साथ गरम कीजिए और पूरा oxygen hydrogen उतरकर एक hydrogen से बदल जाता है, आपको सीधे सादे benzene तक ले जाते हुए।
दूसरी, Friedel Crafts acetylation। acetyl chloride और anhydrous aluminium chloride के साथ phenol ring पर एक acetyl group ले लेता है, ortho और para hydroxyacetophenone देते हुए।
एक बारीकी बताने लायक है। oxygen hydrogen पहले acetylate हो जाता है, एक ester बनाते हुए, तो ring product अक्सर सीधे ring attack के बजाय उस ester के Fries type rearrangement से मिलता है।

तीसरी, Gattermann formylation। phenol को hydrogen cyanide और hydrogen chloride gas के साथ anhydrous aluminium chloride पर treat कीजिए, फिर hydrolyse कीजिए, और आप एक formyl group लगाते हैं, मुख्यतः para hydroxybenzaldehyde देते हुए।
<whisper>इसे Reimer Tiemann के साथ याद में जोड़िए।</whisper> Gattermann para selective है, जबकि Reimer Tiemann ortho selective था। formyl group जोड़ने के दो तरीक़े, उलटी positions पर निशाना।

चौथी, oxidation। chromic acid phenol को conjugated diketone benzoquinone में oxidise करता है। और यही वो रोज़मर्रा वजह है कि phenol की बोतल रखे रहने पर काली पड़ती है, जैसे हवा उसे धीरे धीरे quinone mixtures की ओर oxidise करती है।

board_events.text: Part (i): bromine water brominates all three activated positions, giving 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate.
Part (ii): dilute nitric acid at 298 K gives a mixture of ortho- and para-nitrophenol.
The question also asks why phenol needs no Lewis-acid catalyst, unlike benzene.
The OH strongly activates the ring by donating electron density through resonance.
So phenol is reactive enough toward the electrophile without the ring-activating help a Lewis acid would provide.
Benzene, lacking such activation, needs FeBr3 to brominate. That contrast is the whole marking point.

segments.text: Let us apply the ring chemistry to a straightforward C B S E board question. Predict what phenol gives with bromine water and with dilute nitric acid, and then explain a catalyst difference.
The board runs both reactions from the same phenol. Two arrows, two products, one important explanation underneath.
Part one, bromine water. Phenol is so activated that all three available positions brominate at once, so the product is two four six tribromophenol, and it drops out as a white precipitate.
Part two, dilute nitric acid at two hundred ninety eight kelvin. Here the milder conditions give a simple mixture of the two mononitration products, ortho and para nitrophenol.
Now the conceptual half of the question, which is where the real marks are. Why does phenol need no Lewis acid catalyst to brominate, when benzene does?

The answer is one sentence. The oxygen hydrogen strongly activates the ring by donating electron density into it through resonance. The ring is already electron rich before the electrophile even arrives.
So phenol is reactive enough toward the electrophile on its own. It does not need the extra ring activating help that a Lewis acid catalyst would normally provide.

<whisper>And close by naming the contrast explicitly.</whisper> Benzene has no such activation, so benzene genuinely needs iron three bromide to brominate. Stating that comparison is exactly what earns the final mark.
चलिए ring chemistry को एक सीधे C B S E board question पर लगाते हैं। बताइए phenol bromine water और dilute nitric acid के साथ क्या देता है, फिर एक catalyst का फ़र्क़ समझाइए।
board दोनों reactions उसी phenol से चलाता है। दो arrows, दो products, और नीचे एक अहम explanation।
पहला हिस्सा, bromine water। phenol इतना activated है कि तीनों उपलब्ध positions एक साथ brominate हो जाती हैं, तो product है two four six tribromophenol, और ये एक white precipitate बनकर गिरता है।
दूसरा हिस्सा, dilute nitric acid two hundred ninety eight kelvin पर। यहाँ हल्की conditions दो mononitration products का सादा mixture देती हैं, ortho और para nitrophenol।
अब सवाल का conceptual आधा, जहाँ असली marks हैं। phenol को brominate करने के लिए कोई Lewis acid catalyst क्यों नहीं चाहिए, जबकि benzene को चाहिए?
जवाब एक वाक्य है। oxygen hydrogen resonance के ज़रिए ring में electron density देकर उसे ख़ूब activate करता है। electrophile के आने से पहले ही ring electron rich है।
तो phenol ख़ुद ही electrophile के प्रति काफ़ी reactive है। इसे वो extra ring activating मदद नहीं चाहिए जो एक Lewis acid catalyst आम तौर पर देता।
<whisper>और contrast साफ़ नाम लेकर बंद कीजिए।</whisper> benzene में ऐसी कोई activation नहीं, तो benzene को brominate करने के लिए सचमुच iron three bromide चाहिए। यही तुलना बताना आख़िरी mark दिलाता है।
