board_events.text: Methanol has no such unit, so it is negative.
Ethanol is CH3-CH(OH)-H, which contains the unit, so it is positive.
Propan-1-ol is CH3CH2CH2OH, no unit, negative. Propan-2-ol is CH3-CH(OH)-CH3, which has it, positive.
Answer: ethanol and propan-2-ol give a positive test.
Speed tip: only alcohols oxidisable in situ to a CH3-CO- fragment respond.

segments.text: This N E E T speed trap is pure pattern recognition. Which of these four alcohols give a positive iodoform test, and can you decide it in seconds?
The candidates are methanol, ethanol, propan one ol, and propan two ol. The trick is to scan each for the methyl carbon hydroxyl unit, and not to waste time writing any mechanism.
The board lines up all four with a verdict on each. Let us check them left to right.
Methanol first. It has just one carbon, so it cannot possibly contain a methyl attached to a hydroxyl bearing carbon. No unit, negative.
Ethanol next. Write it as methyl, carbon, hydroxyl, hydrogen, and there it is, the required fragment is hiding in plain sight. So ethanol is positive.

Now the two propanols. Propan one ol is a straight three carbon chain with the hydroxyl on the end carbon, no methyl next to the hydroxyl carbon, so negative. But propan two ol is methyl, carbon hydroxyl, methyl, which contains the unit, so it is positive.
So the answer is clean. Ethanol and propan two ol give a positive iodoform test. The other two do not.

<whisper>And here is the one line rule to carry forward.</whisper> Only alcohols that can be oxidised in place to a methyl carbonyl fragment respond. Scan for that pattern and you will never have to draw a mechanism for this test again.
ये N E E T speed trap शुद्ध pattern recognition है। इन चारों alcohols में से कौन positive iodoform test देते हैं, और क्या आप इसे सेकंडों में तय कर सकते हैं?
candidates हैं methanol, ethanol, propan one ol, और propan two ol। trick है हर एक में methyl carbon hydroxyl unit ढूँढना, और कोई mechanism लिखने में समय बर्बाद न करना।
board चारों को एक verdict के साथ क़तार में रखता है। बाएँ से दाएँ जाँचते हैं।
पहले methanol। इसमें सिर्फ़ एक carbon है, तो इसमें एक hydroxyl वाले carbon से जुड़ा methyl हो ही नहीं सकता। कोई unit नहीं, negative।
फिर ethanol। इसे methyl, carbon, hydroxyl, hydrogen लिखिए, और वहीं है, ज़रूरी fragment सामने छुपा है। तो ethanol positive है।

अब दो propanols। propan one ol एक सीधी तीन carbon chain है जिसमें hydroxyl सिरे वाले carbon पर है, hydroxyl carbon के बगल कोई methyl नहीं, तो negative। पर propan two ol है methyl, carbon hydroxyl, methyl, जिसमें unit है, तो ये positive है।
तो जवाब साफ़ है। ethanol और propan two ol positive iodoform test देते हैं। बाक़ी दो नहीं देते।

<whisper>और ये रहा आगे ले जाने वाला एक line का rule।</whisper> सिर्फ़ वो alcohols जो जगह पर एक methyl carbonyl fragment में oxidise हो सकें, react करते हैं। इस pattern को scan कीजिए और इस test के लिए फिर कभी mechanism नहीं खींचना पड़ेगा।

board_events.text: JEE Main: arrange by increasing acidity
Order ethanol, phenol, para-nitrophenol, para-cresol and water by increasing acidity, and justify the two extremes.

board_events.text: Build from the ladder: alcohols are weakest, phenols in the middle, and substituents tune the phenols.
Result, weakest to strongest: ethanol, water, para-cresol, phenol, para-nitrophenol.
Ethanol is weakest: its alkoxide is not resonance-stabilised, and the ethyl group's +I effect destabilises the anion further.
Para-nitrophenol is strongest: the electron-withdrawing nitro at para drains negative charge off the phenoxide by resonance, stabilising the anion.
Para-cresol's methyl is electron-releasing, so it sits just below phenol.

segments.text: This J E E Main question rewards the ladder we built earlier. Arrange five species, ethanol, phenol, para nitrophenol, para cresol and water, in increasing order of acidity, and justify the two extremes.
Do not compute anything. Just place each species on the acidity ladder and then nudge the phenols for their substituents.
The board shows the finished placement. Notice the three phenol type species cluster in the middle, with the two extremes anchored by an alcohol and a nitro phenol.
The strategy is layered. Alcohols are the weakest acids of the set, the plain phenols sit in the middle, and then the substituents on each phenol tune it up or down.
So the increasing order reads ethanol, then water, then para cresol, then phenol, then para nitrophenol. That is the full answer, but the marks are in justifying the ends.

Take the weak end. Ethanol is weakest because its alkoxide has no ring to delocalise into, so it is not resonance stabilised, and the ethyl group's plus I effect pushes even more charge onto the anion, destabilising it further.

Now the strong end. Para nitrophenol is strongest because the electron withdrawing nitro group at the para position drains negative charge off the phenoxide by resonance. The anion is extra stabilised, so its proton leaves most easily of all.

<whisper>And the middle follows the same logic.</whisper> Para cresol carries an electron releasing methyl, which does the opposite of a nitro group, so it sits just below plain phenol. One rule, electron withdrawing up and electron releasing down, orders the whole set.

ये J E E Main question उस ladder को reward करता है जो हमने पहले बनाई। पाँच species, ethanol, phenol, para nitrophenol, para cresol और water, को acidity के बढ़ते क्रम में लगाइए, और दोनों सिरे justify कीजिए।
कुछ compute मत कीजिए। बस हर species को acidity ladder पर रखिए और फिर phenols को उनके substituents के लिए थोड़ा खिसकाइए।
board तैयार placement दिखाता है। ध्यान दीजिए तीन phenol type species बीच में इकट्ठा हैं, और दोनों सिरे एक alcohol तथा एक nitro phenol से बँधे हैं।
strategy परतदार है। alcohols इस set के सबसे कमज़ोर acids हैं, सादे phenols बीच में बैठते हैं, और फिर हर phenol के substituents उसे ऊपर या नीचे tune करते हैं।
तो बढ़ता क्रम पढ़ता है ethanol, फिर water, फिर para cresol, फिर phenol, फिर para nitrophenol। ये पूरा जवाब है, पर marks सिरों को justify करने में हैं।

कमज़ोर सिरा लीजिए। ethanol सबसे कमज़ोर है क्योंकि इसके alkoxide के पास delocalise होने को कोई ring नहीं, तो ये resonance stabilised नहीं है, और ethyl group का plus I effect anion पर और charge धकेलकर उसे और destabilise करता है।

अब मज़बूत सिरा। para nitrophenol सबसे मज़बूत है क्योंकि para position पर electron withdrawing nitro group resonance से phenoxide से negative charge खींच लेता है। anion अतिरिक्त stabilise होता है, तो इसका proton सबसे आसानी से निकलता है।

<whisper>और बीच वाला भी वही logic follow करता है।</whisper> para cresol एक electron releasing methyl रखता है, जो nitro group का उलटा करता है, तो ये सादे phenol से ठीक नीचे बैठता है। एक ही rule, electron withdrawing ऊपर और electron releasing नीचे, पूरे set को क्रम में लगा देता है।

sections.title: Worked example: identify the alcohol from two tests

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: let two tests partition the space
A bottle contains one of butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, or 2-methylpropan-2-ol. Lucas gives turbidity in about four minutes; the iodoform test is positive.

board_events.caption: How each test narrows the field
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 230" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="230" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="340" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Two tests converge on one alcohol</text><rect x="50" y="44" width="300" height="40" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#d0cabb" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="350" y="44" width="280" height="40" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#d0cabb" stroke-width="1"/><text x="200" y="69" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">Test (a): Lucas ~ 4 minutes</text><text x="490" y="69" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#2b6cb0">Test (b): iodoform positive</text><rect x="50" y="84" width="300" height="80" fill="#fff" stroke="#d0cabb" stroke-width="1"/><rect x="350" y="84" width="280" height="80" fill="#fff" stroke="#d0cabb" stroke-width="1"/><text x="200" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">immediate → 3°   |   ~5 min → 2°   |   none → 1°</text><text x="200" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c05621">4 min → SECONDARY</text><text x="200" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">rules out butan-1-ol & 2-methylpropan-2-ol</text><text x="490" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">needs CH3CH(OH)– unit</text><text x="490" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c05621">butan-2-ol has it</text><text x="490" y="154" text-anchor="middle" font-size="9.5" fill="#5a6570">CH3CH(OH)CH2CH3</text><text x="340" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">∴ the alcohol is butan-2-ol</text></svg>

board_events.text: Lucas: immediate is 3-degree/benzylic/allylic, about 5 minutes is 2-degree, none is 1-degree.
A four-minute response points to a secondary alcohol, eliminating butan-1-ol (1-degree) and 2-methylpropan-2-ol (3-degree).
Iodoform positive requires a CH3-CH(OH)- unit.
Butan-2-ol, CH3-CH(OH)-CH2CH3, has exactly that unit and is the only secondary candidate, so it is oxidised in situ and gives iodoform.
Both tests converge on butan-2-ol: (a) fixes the class, (b) fixes the substitution pattern.

segments.text: Our last worked example is the J E E Advanced deduction that ties the whole toolkit together. A bottle holds one of three alcohols, and two test results must pin it down.
The three suspects are butan one ol, butan two ol, and two methylpropan two ol. The clues are that Lucas reagent gives turbidity in about four minutes, and the iodoform test is positive.
The board shows how each clue slices the field. Read the left panel for the Lucas logic and the right panel for the iodoform logic.
Start with Lucas. Immediate turbidity would mean tertiary or benzylic or allylic. About five minutes would mean secondary. No reaction at room temperature would mean primary.

Our reading is four minutes, which lands squarely in the secondary window. That single observation eliminates butan one ol, a primary that would not react, and two methylpropan two ol, a tertiary that would react instantly.
Now the iodoform clue. A positive test requires the methyl carbon hydroxyl unit somewhere in the molecule.

Check the surviving secondary candidate. Butan two ol is methyl, carbon hydroxyl, then ethyl, so it contains exactly that unit. It is oxidised in place to the needed fragment and gives iodoform, confirming the match.

<whisper>And savour the elegance.</whisper> Neither test alone was decisive. Lucas fixed the class as secondary, iodoform fixed the substitution pattern, and only together do they converge cleanly on butan two ol. That is the whole art of identification.
हमारा आख़िरी worked example वो J E E Advanced deduction है जो पूरी toolkit को जोड़ देता है। एक बोतल में तीन alcohols में से एक है, और दो test results को इसे पक्का करना है।
तीन suspects हैं butan one ol, butan two ol, और two methylpropan two ol। clues हैं कि Lucas reagent लगभग चार मिनट में turbidity देता है, और iodoform test positive है।
board दिखाता है हर clue field को कैसे काटता है। बाएँ panel में Lucas का logic और दाएँ panel में iodoform का logic पढ़िए।
Lucas से शुरू। तुरंत turbidity का मतलब tertiary या benzylic या allylic। लगभग पाँच मिनट का मतलब secondary। room temperature पर कोई reaction नहीं का मतलब primary।

हमारा reading है चार मिनट, जो सीधे secondary window में गिरता है। यही एक observation butan one ol को हटा देता है, एक primary जो react नहीं करता, और two methylpropan two ol को, एक tertiary जो तुरंत react करता।
अब iodoform clue। एक positive test के लिए molecule में कहीं methyl carbon hydroxyl unit चाहिए।
बचे secondary candidate को जाँचिए। butan two ol है methyl, carbon hydroxyl, फिर ethyl, तो इसमें ठीक वही unit है। ये जगह पर ज़रूरी fragment में oxidise होकर iodoform देता है, match confirm करते हुए।

<whisper>और eleganceका मज़ा लीजिए।</whisper> कोई भी test अकेला निर्णायक नहीं था। Lucas ने class को secondary तय किया, iodoform ने substitution pattern तय किया, और सिर्फ़ साथ में ही ये साफ़ butan two ol पर मिलते हैं। यही identification की पूरी कला है।

sections.subtopic: Physical & Chemical Properties of Alcohols and Phenols
sections.title: Common pitfalls and pro-tips

board_events.text: Traps in the scoring heart of the chapter
Claiming tertiary alcohols oxidise to a ketone or acid. They resist ordinary oxidation: no alpha-hydrogen on the carbinol carbon.
Saying every alcohol gives the iodoform test. It needs the CH3-CH(OH)- unit; methanol and propan-1-ol fail.
Treating phenol like a carboxylic acid. Phenol reacts with NaOH but not with NaHCO3, because it is weaker than carbonic acid. That bicarbonate test is the standard discriminator.
Inverting the Lucas order or the dehydration order. Both track carbocation stability: 3$^\circ$ $\gt$ 2$^\circ$ $\gt$ 1$^\circ$.
Forgetting why ortho and para nitrophenols separate. It is intramolecular versus intermolecular hydrogen bonding, not a polarity argument.
Pro-tip: for acidity, don't compute. Place on the ladder (acid, carbonic, phenol, water, alcohol, strongest first), then nudge for substituents (EWG up, EDG down).
Named-reaction cue: CHO ortho means Reimer-Tiemann; COOH ortho means Kolbe; white ppt with bromine water means 2,4,6-tribromophenol.

segments.text: Let us close Part two, the scoring heart of the chapter, by gathering the traps. Get these right and this whole section becomes predictable marks.

Trap one, claiming a tertiary alcohol oxidises to a ketone or an acid. It does not. It resists ordinary oxidation, because there is no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon for a mild oxidant to remove. Only drastic conditions can force it, by cleaving the skeleton.
Trap two, assuming every alcohol gives the iodoform test. It does not. The test strictly needs the methyl carbon hydroxyl unit, so methanol and propan one ol both fail it outright.

Trap three, treating phenol as if it were a carboxylic acid. Phenol reacts with sodium hydroxide, yes, but it does not react with sodium bicarbonate, because phenol is weaker than carbonic acid. That very bicarbonate test is the standard way to tell an acid from a phenol.

Trap four, inverting the Lucas order or the dehydration order. Both of them track carbocation stability, tertiary over secondary over primary. If you ever find yourself writing primary as fastest, stop, you have flipped it.

Trap five, forgetting why the ortho and para nitrophenols separate by steam distillation. The reason is intramolecular versus intermolecular hydrogen bonding, the ortho isomer chelating within itself, and it is not a polarity argument. Give the hydrogen bonding reason.

Now the pro tips. For any acidity comparison, do not compute p K a values. Just place the species on the ladder, acid over carbonic over phenol over water over alcohol, then nudge each phenol for its substituents, electron withdrawing up, electron releasing down.

<whisper>And the named reaction shortcut that wins speed rounds.</whisper> Let the installed group name the reaction. A formyl group ortho means Reimer Tiemann. A carboxyl group ortho means Kolbe. A white precipitate with bromine water means two four six tribromophenol. That closes Part two.
चलिए Part two, chapter का scoring heart, traps इकट्ठा करके बंद करते हैं। इन्हें सही कर लीजिए और ये पूरी section predictable marks बन जाती है।

Trap एक, ये कहना कि tertiary alcohol oxidise होकर ketone या acid देता है। नहीं देता। ये ordinary oxidation का विरोध करता है, क्योंकि carbinol carbon पर mild oxidant के हटाने को कोई hydrogen ही नहीं है। सिर्फ़ drastic conditions ही इसे मजबूर कर सकती हैं, skeleton तोड़कर।
Trap दो, ये मान लेना कि हर alcohol iodoform test देता है। नहीं देता। test को सख़्ती से methyl carbon hydroxyl unit चाहिए, तो methanol और propan one ol दोनों इसमें साफ़ fail होते हैं।

Trap तीन, phenol को ऐसे treat करना जैसे वो carboxylic acid हो। phenol sodium hydroxide से react करता है, सही, पर sodium bicarbonate से नहीं, क्योंकि phenol carbonic acid से कमज़ोर है। वही bicarbonate test एक acid को phenol से अलग बताने का standard तरीक़ा है।

Trap चार, Lucas order या dehydration order उलट देना। दोनों carbocation stability follow करते हैं, tertiary ऊपर secondary ऊपर primary। अगर कभी आप primary को सबसे तेज़ लिखते मिलें, रुकिए, आपने इसे पलट दिया है।

Trap पाँच, ये भूल जाना कि ortho और para nitrophenols steam distillation से क्यों अलग होते हैं। कारण है intramolecular बनाम intermolecular hydrogen bonding, ortho isomer अपने भीतर chelate बनाता है, और ये polarity का तर्क नहीं है। hydrogen bonding वाला कारण दीजिए।

अब pro tips। किसी भी acidity comparison के लिए p K a values compute मत कीजिए। बस species को ladder पर रखिए, acid ऊपर carbonic ऊपर phenol ऊपर water ऊपर alcohol, फिर हर phenol को उसके substituents के लिए खिसकाइए, electron withdrawing ऊपर, electron releasing नीचे।

<whisper>और वो named reaction shortcut जो speed rounds जिताती है।</whisper> लगा हुआ group ही reaction का नाम बता दे। ortho एक formyl group मतलब Reimer Tiemann। ortho एक carboxyl group मतलब Kolbe। bromine water के साथ एक white precipitate मतलब two four six tribromophenol। इसी के साथ Part two पूरा।

sections.title: Why ethers are aloof: boiling point

board_events.text: The ether is the quiet sibling
An ether is just R$-$O$-$R$'$, an oxygen bridging two carbon groups, with no O$-$H bond at all.

board_events.caption: Boiling points at comparable mass
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="240" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="320" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Same mass, very different boiling points</text><rect x="70" y="95" width="70" height="100" fill="#a0aec0" rx="3"/><text x="105" y="89" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">309 K</text><text x="105" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">pentane</text><rect x="285" y="96" width="70" height="99" fill="#63b3ed" rx="3"/><text x="320" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">308 K</text><text x="320" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">ethoxyethane</text><rect x="500" y="45" width="70" height="150" fill="#dd6b20" rx="3"/><text x="535" y="39" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">390 K</text><text x="535" y="212" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">butan-1-ol</text><text x="535" y="55" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c05621">O-H···O H-bonds</text><text x="177" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">ether sits by the alkane</text><text x="320" y="232" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">the only difference is the alcohol’s hydrogen bonding</text></svg>

board_events.text: An ether molecule has no O-H hand to offer, so ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other.
They are held only by weak dipole-dipole forces, because the polar C-O bonds give the bent molecule a small net dipole.
So an ether boils close to the alkane of similar mass, and far below the corresponding alcohol.
Pentane, ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol have nearly the same mass, yet boil at 309, 308 and 390 K.
The ether sits right next to the alkane; the alcohol towers above both, and the only difference is hydrogen bonding.

segments.text: Welcome to the third family, the ether, the quiet sibling of the three. Almost everything about an ether flows from one structural fact, so let us start there.

An ether is simply R minus O minus R prime, an oxygen acting as a bridge between two carbon groups. And critically, there is no oxygen hydrogen bond anywhere in it. Hold that absence in mind, because it explains all the physics.
Look at the board. Three molecules of nearly the same mass, and yet their boiling points are wildly different. Read them and ask why.

Here is the reason. Recall the platform image from the alcohols. Alcohols hold hands through hydrogen bonds and boil high. But an ether has no oxygen hydrogen hand to offer, so ether molecules simply cannot hold hands with each other.

What holds them together instead is only weak dipole dipole attraction. The carbon oxygen bonds are polar, so the bent ether molecule carries a small net dipole, but that is a feeble glue compared to a hydrogen bond.
So the consequence is striking. An ether boils at almost the same temperature as an alkane of similar mass, and far, far below the corresponding alcohol.

The numbers on the board make it concrete. Pentane, ethoxyethane, and butan one ol all have nearly the same molecular mass, yet they boil at three hundred nine, three hundred eight, and three hundred ninety kelvin.

<whisper>Notice where each one lands.</whisper> The ether sits right next to the alkane, practically touching it. The alcohol towers seventy or eighty kelvin above both. And the single thing separating them is the alcohol's hydrogen bonding.
तीसरी family में स्वागत है, ether, तीनों में सबसे शांत भाई। ether के बारे में लगभग सब कुछ एक structural fact से बहता है, तो वहीं से शुरू करते हैं।

ether बस R minus O minus R prime है, oxygen दो carbon groups के बीच एक bridge की तरह। और अहम बात, इसमें कहीं कोई oxygen hydrogen bond नहीं है। इस अनुपस्थिति को याद रखिए, क्योंकि यही पूरी physics समझाती है।
board देखिए। लगभग एक जैसे mass के तीन molecules, फिर भी इनके boiling points बहुत अलग हैं। इन्हें पढ़िए और पूछिए क्यों।

कारण ये है। alcohols वाली platform की तस्वीर याद कीजिए। alcohols hydrogen bonds से हाथ मिलाते हैं और ऊँचे boil होते हैं। पर ether के पास देने को कोई oxygen hydrogen हाथ नहीं है, तो ether molecules आपस में हाथ मिला ही नहीं सकते।

इसके बजाय इन्हें बस weak dipole dipole attraction जोड़े रखता है। carbon oxygen bonds polar हैं, तो मुड़ा हुआ ether molecule एक छोटा net dipole रखता है, पर वो एक hydrogen bond के मुक़ाबले कमज़ोर गोंद है।
तो नतीजा चौंकाने वाला है। एक ether एक समान mass वाले alkane के लगभग बराबर temperature पर boil होता है, और corresponding alcohol से बहुत, बहुत नीचे।

board के numbers इसे ठोस बनाते हैं। pentane, ethoxyethane, और butan one ol सबका molecular mass लगभग एक जैसा है, फिर भी ये three hundred nine, three hundred eight, और three hundred ninety kelvin पर boil होते हैं।

<whisper>ध्यान दीजिए हर एक कहाँ गिरता है।</whisper> ether ठीक alkane के बगल बैठता है, लगभग छूते हुए। alcohol दोनों से सत्तर अस्सी kelvin ऊपर खड़ा है। और इन्हें अलग करने वाली एकमात्र चीज़ है alcohol की hydrogen bonding।

sections.title: Why ethers still dissolve like alcohols

board_events.text: The subtlety students miss
An ether cannot hydrogen-bond to another ether, but its oxygen lone pair CAN accept a hydrogen bond from a water molecule.

board_events.caption: Water donates an H-bond to the ether oxygen
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 660 250" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="660" height="250" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="330" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">But ethers still dissolve like alcohols</text><text x="150" y="80" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" fill="#1f2933">R–O–R'</text><text x="150" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">lone pairs on O</text><path d="M180 78 Q230 78 250 100" fill="none" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-dasharray="3,2"/><text x="290" y="105" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#2b6cb0">H–O–H</text><text x="230" y="130" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2f855a">water DONATES an H-bond to the ether O</text><line x1="60" y1="150" x2="600" y2="150" stroke="#d9d4c8" stroke-width="1"/><text x="175" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">ethoxyethane ~ 7.5 g</text><text x="330" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">butan-1-ol ~ 9 g</text><text x="510" y="180" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#c53030">pentane ~ 0</text><text x="330" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">per 100 mL water</text><rect x="90" y="212" width="480" height="30" rx="7" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="330" y="232" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2b6cb0">Solubility needs ONE partner to offer the hand; boiling needs BOTH</text></svg>

board_events.text: So ethers are about as water-miscible as alcohols of the same mass.
Ethoxyethane and butan-1-ol dissolve to roughly 7.5 and 9 grams per 100 millilitres of water.
The all-carbon pentane, having no oxygen, is essentially insoluble.
So the two properties split apart: boiling needs the molecules to hold hands with each other.
Solubility needs only one partner to offer the hand; boiling needs both. An ether can do the first but not the second.

segments.text: Now the twist that catches students off guard. We just said ethers boil low because they cannot hydrogen bond. So surely they should be insoluble in water too? No, and here is why.

The key distinction is about who offers the hand. An ether cannot hydrogen bond to another ether, true. But its oxygen still carries lone pairs, and those lone pairs can accept a hydrogen bond from a water molecule.
The board shows exactly this. Water, which has oxygen hydrogen bonds to donate, reaches out its hand, and the ether oxygen gladly accepts it. The ether does not need to donate anything.
So an ether turns out to be about as water miscible as an alcohol of the same molecular mass. That surprises people who expected it to behave like the alkane.
The numbers confirm it. Ethoxyethane and butan one ol dissolve to roughly seven point five and nine grams per hundred millilitres of water. Very close, despite their very different boiling points.
And the control case seals it. The all carbon pentane, of similar mass but with no oxygen at all, is essentially insoluble. No oxygen, no hand to accept, no solubility.
So the two properties, boiling and dissolving, actually split apart for ethers, and understanding why is the whole lesson. Boiling requires the molecules to hold hands with each other.

<whisper>Here is the one line to carry away.</whisper> Solubility needs only one partner to offer the hand, and water is happy to be that partner. Boiling needs both molecules to hold hands. An ether can do the first but not the second, which is why it dissolves like an alcohol but boils like an alkane.
अब वो twist जो students को चौंका देता है। अभी हमने कहा ethers नीचे boil होते हैं क्योंकि वो hydrogen bond नहीं बना सकते। तो फिर water में भी insoluble होने चाहिए न? नहीं, और यही कारण है।

मुख्य फ़र्क़ इस बात का है कि हाथ कौन देता है। एक ether दूसरे ether से hydrogen bond नहीं बना सकता, सही। पर इसका oxygen फिर भी lone pairs रखता है, और वो lone pairs एक water molecule से hydrogen bond स्वीकार कर सकते हैं।
board ठीक यही दिखाता है। water, जिसके पास देने को oxygen hydrogen bonds हैं, अपना हाथ बढ़ाता है, और ether oxygen ख़ुशी से उसे स्वीकार कर लेता है। ether को कुछ देना ही नहीं पड़ता।
तो एक ether अपने ही molecular mass वाले alcohol जितना ही water miscible निकलता है। ये उन्हें चौंकाता है जो इसे alkane जैसा behave करने की उम्मीद करते थे।
numbers इसकी पुष्टि करते हैं। ethoxyethane और butan one ol करीब seven point five और nine grams प्रति hundred millilitres पानी में घुलते हैं। बहुत क़रीब, अपने बहुत अलग boiling points के बावजूद।
और control case इसे पक्का कर देता है। all carbon pentane, समान mass का पर बिना किसी oxygen के, लगभग insoluble है। कोई oxygen नहीं, स्वीकार करने को कोई हाथ नहीं, कोई solubility नहीं।
तो दोनों properties, boiling और dissolving, ethers के लिए असल में अलग हो जाती हैं, और क्यों समझना ही पूरा सबक़ है। boiling के लिए molecules को आपस में हाथ मिलाना ज़रूरी है।

<whisper>ये एक line साथ ले जाइए।</whisper> solubility को सिर्फ़ एक partner का हाथ देना चाहिए, और water वो partner बनने को तैयार है। boiling को दोनों molecules का हाथ मिलाना चाहिए। एक ether पहला कर सकता है पर दूसरा नहीं, इसीलिए वो alcohol जैसा घुलता है पर alkane जैसा boil होता है।

board_events.text: Definition, geometry and the numbers to quote
An ether is R$-$O$-$R$'$; the $-$OR fragment is an alkoxy group. Simple/symmetrical if the groups are identical, mixed/unsymmetrical if they differ.

board_events.caption: Geometry and reactivity data
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 640 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="640" height="240" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="320" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Ether structure & data</text><text x="200" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#1f2933">C</text><text x="270" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#c05621">O</text><text x="200" y="150" text-anchor="middle" font-size="20" fill="#1f2933">C</text><line x1="212" y1="96" x2="258" y2="114" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="212" y1="144" x2="258" y2="126" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M226 104 Q240 120 226 136" fill="none" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="150" y="120" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#2b6cb0">~111.7°</text><text x="300" y="120" text-anchor="start" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">C–O ≈ 141 pm</text><rect x="380" y="55" width="230" height="60" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="495" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2b6cb0">angle > 109°28': bulky R groups</text><text x="495" y="98" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">repel & push apart; small net dipole</text><rect x="380" y="130" width="230" height="60" rx="8" fill="#fff8ef" stroke="#c05621" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="495" y="153" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#c05621">HX reactivity to C–O:</text><text x="495" y="174" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">HI > HBr > HCl</text><text x="320" y="215" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">simple/symmetrical (R=R') vs mixed/unsymmetrical; –OR = alkoxy</text></svg>

board_events.text: Oxygen carries two bond pairs and two lone pairs in a roughly tetrahedral arrangement.
The C$-$O$-$C angle is slightly greater than $109^\circ 28'$, about $111.7^\circ$, because the two bulky R groups repel each other.
The C$-$O bond length is about $141$ pm, close to that in alcohols. The polar C$-$O bonds give a small net dipole.
Toward C$-$O cleavage, the reactivity of hydrogen halides is HI $\gt$ HBr $\gt$ HCl.
These specific numbers, the angle, the length, and the halide order, are all exam-quotable.

segments.text: With the physics understood, let us pin down the ether's structure and the handful of numbers examiners quote. Nothing here is hard, but the values must be exact.

Start with the definition. An ether is R minus O minus R prime, and the O R fragment on its own is called an alkoxy group. If the two groups on oxygen are identical, the ether is simple or symmetrical. If they differ, it is mixed or unsymmetrical.
The board shows the geometry alongside the key data. Focus on the angle at oxygen and the halide reactivity order.
At the oxygen, there are two bond pairs, going out to the two carbons, and two lone pairs. Together these four electron pairs adopt a roughly tetrahedral arrangement.

But watch the angle carefully, because it goes the opposite way from an alcohol. The carbon oxygen carbon angle is slightly greater than the tetrahedral one hundred nine degrees twenty eight minutes, about one hundred eleven point seven degrees, because the two bulky R groups on oxygen repel each other and push apart.

The carbon oxygen bond length is about one hundred forty one picometres, close to what we saw in alcohols. And because those carbon oxygen bonds are polar, the bent molecule ends up with a small net dipole moment.

One more data point that will matter hugely for the chemistry. When a hydrogen halide attacks the carbon oxygen bond, the reactivity order is hydrogen iodide, then hydrogen bromide, then hydrogen chloride. Iodide is the most aggressive cleaver.

<whisper>Commit these three to memory.</whisper> The opened angle of about one hundred eleven point seven degrees, the carbon oxygen length near one hundred forty one picometres, and the halide order with hydrogen iodide on top. All three are the kind of value a paper asks for directly.
physics समझ लेने के बाद, चलिए ether की structure और वो कुछ numbers पक्के करते हैं जो examiners पूछते हैं। यहाँ कुछ कठिन नहीं, पर values सटीक होनी चाहिए।

definition से शुरू। एक ether R minus O minus R prime है, और अकेले O R fragment को alkoxy group कहते हैं। अगर oxygen पर दोनों groups एक जैसे हों, तो ether simple या symmetrical है। अगर अलग हों, तो mixed या unsymmetrical।
board geometry को key data के साथ दिखाता है। oxygen पर angle और halide reactivity order पर ध्यान दीजिए।
oxygen पर दो bond pairs हैं, दोनों carbons की ओर जाते हुए, और दो lone pairs। ये चारों electron pairs मिलकर एक roughly tetrahedral arrangement लेते हैं।

पर angle को ध्यान से देखिए, क्योंकि ये alcohol से उलटी दिशा में जाता है। carbon oxygen carbon angle tetrahedral one hundred nine degrees twenty eight minutes से थोड़ा ज़्यादा है, लगभग one hundred eleven point seven degrees, क्योंकि oxygen पर दो bulky R groups एक दूसरे को repel करके दूर धकेलते हैं।
carbon oxygen bond length लगभग one hundred forty one picometres है, alcohols जैसी ही। और चूँकि वो carbon oxygen bonds polar हैं, मुड़ा हुआ molecule एक छोटा net dipole moment रखता है।

एक और data point जो chemistry के लिए बहुत मायने रखेगा। जब एक hydrogen halide carbon oxygen bond पर attack करता है, तो reactivity order है hydrogen iodide, फिर hydrogen bromide, फिर hydrogen chloride। iodide सबसे आक्रामक cleaver है।

<whisper>इन तीन को याद कर लीजिए।</whisper> लगभग one hundred eleven point seven degrees का खुला angle, one hundred forty one picometres के पास carbon oxygen length, और hydrogen iodide सबसे ऊपर वाला halide order। तीनों वैसी value हैं जो paper सीधे पूछता है।

board_events.text: Inertness is the point
With no O-H to ionise and a strong, stable C-O-C framework, ethers are the least reactive of the common functional groups.

board_events.caption: Inert to most; one weak point
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 660 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="660" height="240" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="330" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Ethers are chemically sluggish</text><rect x="40" y="45" width="300" height="130" rx="10" fill="#f0fff4" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="190" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">INERT to:</text><text x="190" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">bases · active metals</text><text x="190" y="114" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">reducing agents</text><text x="190" y="134" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">mild oxidants</text><text x="190" y="160" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">prized as inert solvent</text><rect x="360" y="45" width="270" height="130" rx="10" fill="#fff4f2" stroke="#c53030" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="495" y="70" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" font-weight="700" fill="#c53030">One weak point: C–O</text><text x="495" y="94" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#1f2933">only CONCENTRATED HX,</text><text x="495" y="112" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#1f2933">high temperature</text><text x="495" y="140" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c05621">aryl–O NEVER cleaved</text><text x="495" y="158" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#5a6570">aryl ether → always a phenol</text><text x="330" y="205" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">an aryl ether (anisole) also activates its ring toward o/p electrophiles</text></svg>

board_events.text: That is exactly why diethyl ether is prized as an inert reaction solvent, and was historically used as an inhalation anaesthetic.
Ethers do NOT react with bases, active metals, reducing agents, or mild oxidants.
The one weak point is the C-O bond, and only an aggressive reagent, concentrated HX at high temperature, can break it.
An aryl-oxygen bond is NEVER cleaved by the halide, so an alkyl aryl ether always gives a phenol, not an aryl halide.
When an ether carries an aromatic ring, the alkoxy group also activates that ring toward electrophiles at ortho and para.

segments.text: Now the chemistry, and the headline is unusual. For most functional groups we ask what they react with. For ethers, the striking feature is what they refuse to react with.
The reason is structural. There is no oxygen hydrogen to ionise, and the carbon oxygen carbon framework is strong and stable. So ethers are the least reactive of all the common functional groups.
The board splits the story in two. On the left, the long list of reagents ethers ignore. On the right, their one genuine weak point.

And that inertness is not a flaw, it is a feature we exploit. Diethyl ether is prized precisely as an inert reaction solvent, a place where other chemistry can happen undisturbed. It was even used historically as an inhalation anaesthetic, later replaced for its slow action and unpleasant recovery.

So make the negative list explicit, because questions test it. Ethers do not react with bases. They do not react with active metals. They do not react with reducing agents. And they do not react with mild oxidants. Their unreactivity is the whole point.
There is exactly one weak point, the carbon oxygen bond. And even that yields only to an aggressive reagent, a concentrated hydrogen halide at high temperature. Dilute acid simply will not touch it.

<whisper>And burn this rule in.</whisper> When one side is an aromatic ring, that aryl oxygen bond is never cleaved by the halide, because the s p two aromatic carbon resists nucleophilic substitution. So an alkyl aryl ether always gives a phenol, never an aryl halide.

One last preview. When an ether carries an aromatic ring, such as anisole, a second personality wakes up. The alkoxy group feeds electrons into the ring and activates it toward electrophiles at the ortho and para positions, exactly as the oxygen hydrogen did in phenol. We will use that shortly.
अब chemistry, और headline असामान्य है। ज़्यादातर functional groups के लिए हम पूछते हैं वो किससे react करते हैं। ethers के लिए, ख़ास बात ये है कि वो किससे react करने से इनकार करते हैं।
कारण structural है। ionise करने को कोई oxygen hydrogen नहीं, और carbon oxygen carbon framework मज़बूत तथा stable है। तो ethers सभी common functional groups में सबसे कम reactive हैं।
board कहानी को दो में बाँटता है। बाईं ओर reagents की लंबी list जिन्हें ethers नज़रअंदाज़ करते हैं। दाईं ओर उनका एकमात्र असली weak point।

और वो inertness कोई कमी नहीं, एक feature है जिसका हम फ़ायदा उठाते हैं। diethyl ether ठीक इसी वजह से एक inert reaction solvent के रूप में क़ीमती है, एक जगह जहाँ बाक़ी chemistry बेरोक हो सके। इसे इतिहास में inhalation anaesthetic के रूप में भी इस्तेमाल किया गया, बाद में इसकी धीमी action और अप्रिय recovery के कारण बदल दिया गया।

तो negative list साफ़ कीजिए, क्योंकि questions इसे test करते हैं। ethers bases से react नहीं करते। active metals से react नहीं करते। reducing agents से react नहीं करते। और mild oxidants से react नहीं करते। इनकी unreactivity ही पूरी बात है।
ठीक एक weak point है, carbon oxygen bond। और वो भी सिर्फ़ एक आक्रामक reagent के आगे झुकता है, high temperature पर एक concentrated hydrogen halide। dilute acid इसे छू भी नहीं पाएगा।

<whisper>और ये rule पक्की कर लीजिए।</whisper> जब एक तरफ़ aromatic ring हो, वो aryl oxygen bond halide से कभी नहीं टूटता, क्योंकि s p two aromatic carbon nucleophilic substitution का विरोध करता है। तो एक alkyl aryl ether हमेशा एक phenol देता है, कभी aryl halide नहीं।

एक आख़िरी झलक। जब एक ether एक aromatic ring रखता है, जैसे anisole, तो एक दूसरी personality जाग जाती है। alkoxy group ring में electrons खिलाकर उसे ortho और para positions पर electrophiles के प्रति activate करता है, ठीक वैसे जैसे phenol में oxygen hydrogen करता था। हम इसे थोड़ी देर में इस्तेमाल करेंगे।

board_events.text: A protic acid (conc. H$_2$SO$_4$ or H$_3$PO$_4$) removes water; whether you get an ether or an alkene depends on the temperature.
Ethanol with sulphuric acid gives ethoxyethane at 413 K, but ethene at 443 K.
The mechanism is SN2: a second, neutral alcohol attacks the protonated alcohol, displacing water.
Because that step is SN2, the alkyl group must be primary and unhindered, and the temperature low.
With secondary or tertiary alcohols, elimination outruns substitution and you just get the alkene.
So this method is good only for symmetrical ethers of primary alcohols; it cannot sensibly make a mixed ether.

segments.text: There are two routes to an ether, and the first is simply to dehydrate an alcohol. But there is a delicate catch, because the very same acid can also make an alkene.
The board shows the fork. One alcohol, one acid, and the temperature alone decides whether you walk down the ether path or the alkene path.

The reagent is a protic acid, concentrated sulphuric acid or phosphoric acid, which pulls out water. Whether that water loss joins two alcohols into an ether, or tears one alcohol into an alkene, depends entirely on how hot you run it.

The classic example makes it vivid. Ethanol with sulphuric acid gives ethoxyethane at four hundred thirteen kelvin, but push to four hundred forty three kelvin and you get ethene instead. Lower temperature favours the ether, higher temperature favours the alkene.

The ether forming step is S N two. The acid protonates one alcohol, turning its oxygen hydrogen into a good leaving group, and then a second, neutral alcohol molecule attacks the back of that carbon and displaces water.
Because that key step is bimolecular substitution, the alkyl group has to be primary and unhindered, and the temperature has to be kept low so substitution can win.
Switch to a secondary or tertiary alcohol and the plan collapses. Elimination outruns substitution, and you simply get the alkene instead of the ether.

<whisper>So know the limits of this route.</whisper> It is good only for symmetrical ethers of primary alcohols. It cannot sensibly make a mixed ether, because a mixture of two different alcohols would just give a messy mixture of products. For anything unsymmetrical, we need the next method.
ether तक दो routes हैं, और पहला है बस एक alcohol को dehydrate करना। पर एक नाज़ुक catch है, क्योंकि वही acid एक alkene भी बना सकता है।
board fork दिखाता है। एक alcohol, एक acid, और सिर्फ़ temperature तय करता है कि आप ether path पर चलें या alkene path पर।

reagent एक protic acid है, concentrated sulphuric acid या phosphoric acid, जो water खींच लेता है। वो water loss दो alcohols को ether में जोड़े, या एक alcohol को alkene में तोड़े, ये पूरी तरह इस पर निर्भर है कि आप इसे कितना गरम चलाते हैं।

classic example इसे साफ़ करता है। ethanol sulphuric acid के साथ four hundred thirteen kelvin पर ethoxyethane देता है, पर four hundred forty three kelvin तक धकेलिए और इसके बजाय ethene मिलता है। कम temperature ether के हक़ में, ज़्यादा temperature alkene के हक़ में।

ether बनने वाला step S N two है। acid एक alcohol को protonate करता है, उसके oxygen hydrogen को एक अच्छा leaving group बनाते हुए, और फिर एक दूसरा, neutral alcohol molecule उस carbon के पीछे से attack करके water को displace करता है।
चूँकि वो key step bimolecular substitution है, alkyl group को primary और unhindered होना चाहिए, और temperature को कम रखना चाहिए ताकि substitution जीत सके।
एक secondary या tertiary alcohol पर switch कीजिए और plan ढह जाता है। elimination substitution को पीछे छोड़ देता है, और आपको ether की जगह बस alkene मिलता है।

<whisper>तो इस route की सीमाएँ जानिए।</whisper> ये सिर्फ़ primary alcohols के symmetrical ethers के लिए अच्छा है। ये समझदारी से mixed ether नहीं बना सकता, क्योंकि दो अलग alcohols का mixture बस products का गड़बड़ mixture देगा। किसी भी unsymmetrical चीज़ के लिए, हमें अगला method चाहिए।

board_events.text: The general laboratory route

board_events.caption: Williamson synthesis and its design rule

board_events.text: A sodium alkoxide (or aryloxide) displaces halide from an alkyl halide by S$_N$2: R$-$O$^-$Na$^+$ $+$ R$'$-X gives R$-$O$-$R$'$.
Since the alkoxide attacks by SN2, the alkyl halide should be primary.
The alkoxide is also a strong base, so against a 2-degree or 3-degree halide it triggers elimination instead of substitution.
With a 3-degree halide the alkene is the only product and no ether forms.
Design rule: put the bulk on the alkoxide, keep the halide primary. This is why di-tert-butyl ether cannot be made by Williamson.
The method makes symmetrical, unsymmetrical, and aryl ethers; for an aryl ether, use the phenol as its phenoxide.

segments.text: The second route is the real workhorse of the laboratory, the Williamson synthesis. It fixes the great weakness of dehydration, because it can build unsymmetrical ethers on purpose.
The board shows the reaction and, boxed below, the one design rule that governs everything about it.

The reaction is this. A sodium alkoxide, or an aryloxide made from a phenol, displaces the halide from an alkyl halide by an S N two substitution. You pick the two halves independently, so you can join any R to any R prime.
But there is a catch, and it is the same catch as before. Since the alkoxide attacks by S N two, the alkyl halide really should be primary, so the back side attack can proceed cleanly.

Here is the subtlety that trips people up. The alkoxide is not only a nucleophile, it is also a strong base. So against a secondary or, especially, a tertiary halide, it stops substituting and starts eliminating, ripping off a proton to make an alkene.
Push it to a tertiary halide and the ether vanishes entirely. The alkene becomes the only product, and no ether forms at all.

<whisper>So obey the design rule every time.</whisper> Put the bulk on the alkoxide side, and keep the halide primary. This single rule explains a favourite exam fact. Di tert butyl ether cannot be made by Williamson, because it would require a tertiary halide, which only eliminates.

With that rule respected, the method is wonderfully general. It makes symmetrical ethers, unsymmetrical ethers, and even aryl ethers. For an aryl ether, you simply supply the phenol as its phenoxide and let a primary alkyl halide do the S N two.
दूसरा route laboratory का असली workhorse है, Williamson synthesis। ये dehydration की बड़ी कमज़ोरी ठीक करता है, क्योंकि ये जानबूझकर unsymmetrical ethers बना सकता है।
board reaction दिखाता है और नीचे box में वो एक design rule जो इसके बारे में सब कुछ तय करता है।

reaction ये है। एक sodium alkoxide, या एक phenol से बना aryloxide, एक alkyl halide से halide को S N two substitution से displace करता है। आप दोनों halves अलग अलग चुनते हैं, तो किसी भी R को किसी भी R prime से जोड़ सकते हैं।
पर एक catch है, और वही catch है जो पहले था। चूँकि alkoxide S N two से attack करता है, alkyl halide को सचमुच primary होना चाहिए, ताकि back side attack साफ़ हो सके।

यहाँ वो बारीकी है जो लोगों को गिराती है। alkoxide सिर्फ़ एक nucleophile नहीं, एक strong base भी है। तो एक secondary या, ख़ासकर, tertiary halide के ख़िलाफ़, ये substitute करना बंद करके eliminate करने लगता है, एक proton खींचकर alkene बनाते हुए।
इसे tertiary halide तक धकेलिए और ether पूरी तरह ग़ायब हो जाता है। alkene ही एकमात्र product बन जाता है, और कोई ether बनता ही नहीं।

<whisper>तो हर बार design rule मानिए।</whisper> bulk को alkoxide side पर रखिए, और halide को primary रखिए। यही एक rule एक पसंदीदा exam fact समझाता है। di tert butyl ether Williamson से नहीं बन सकता, क्योंकि इसके लिए एक tertiary halide चाहिए, जो सिर्फ़ eliminate करता है।

उस rule के साथ, method शानदार तरीक़े से general है। ये symmetrical ethers, unsymmetrical ethers, और aryl ethers तक बनाता है। एक aryl ether के लिए, आप बस phenol को उसके phenoxide के रूप में देते हैं और एक primary alkyl halide से S N two करवाते हैं।

sections.title: C-O cleavage by HX: the mechanism

board_events.text: The heart of the ether subtopic
Ethers, otherwise inert, are cleaved by excess concentrated HI or HBr at high temperature, with reactivity HI, then HBr, then HCl.

board_events.caption: Protonation then nucleophilic attack

excess hot HI → alcohol → a 2nd R–I</text><text x="330" y="159" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">reactivity: HI > HBr > HCl (needs a sufficiently acidic, good-nucleophile HX)</text><text x="330" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#c05621">Which carbon iodide hits is the whole game (next section)</text></svg>

board_events.text: Step 1, protonation: the acid protonates the ether oxygen to give an oxonium ion. This is why a sufficiently acidic HX is needed.
Step 2, nucleophilic attack: iodide, a good nucleophile, attacks a carbon and displaces an alcohol.
A dialkyl ether gives, in general, an alkyl halide and an alcohol.
With excess HI at high temperature, the alcohol is converted onward to a second alkyl iodide, so two alkyl iodide molecules result.
The real question, which carbon the iodide attacks, decides the products, and that is the next section.

segments.text: We have made ethers. Now we break them, and this is the single most important reaction of the subtopic. Cleavage of the carbon oxygen bond by a hydrogen halide.

Recall that ethers are otherwise inert. It takes an aggressive reagent, excess concentrated hydrogen iodide or hydrogen bromide at high temperature, to cleave them. The reactivity runs hydrogen iodide, then hydrogen bromide, then hydrogen chloride.
The mechanism has two clean steps on the board. Protonation first, then nucleophilic attack. Learn these two moves and the whole subtopic opens up.

Step one, protonation. The acid protonates the ether oxygen, giving an oxonium ion, a positively charged oxygen now bearing three groups. This is precisely why you need a sufficiently acidic hydrogen halide, one strong enough to protonate that oxygen in the first place.
Step two, nucleophilic attack. Iodide, which is a good nucleophile, now attacks one of the carbons attached to that oxonium oxygen and displaces the rest as an alcohol.
So in general, a dialkyl ether gives one alkyl halide and one alcohol. One carbon walks away as the iodide, the other leaves as the alcohol.

But add a twist. With excess hydrogen iodide at high temperature, that alcohol product does not survive. It is itself converted onward to a second alkyl iodide. So the net result of excess hot hydrogen iodide is two alkyl iodide molecules.

<whisper>And here is the cliffhanger.</whisper> The one thing we have not yet decided is which carbon the iodide chooses to attack. That single choice decides all the products, and it is exactly what the next section resolves.
हमने ethers बना लिए। अब इन्हें तोड़ते हैं, और ये subtopic की सबसे अहम reaction है। एक hydrogen halide से carbon oxygen bond का cleavage।

याद रखिए ethers वरना inert हैं। इन्हें तोड़ने के लिए एक आक्रामक reagent चाहिए, high temperature पर excess concentrated hydrogen iodide या hydrogen bromide। reactivity चलती है hydrogen iodide, फिर hydrogen bromide, फिर hydrogen chloride।
mechanism में board पर दो साफ़ steps हैं। पहले protonation, फिर nucleophilic attack। ये दो moves सीख लीजिए और पूरा subtopic खुल जाता है।

Step one, protonation। acid ether oxygen को protonate करता है, एक oxonium ion देते हुए, एक positively charged oxygen जो अब तीन groups रखता है। इसीलिए एक काफ़ी acidic hydrogen halide चाहिए, इतना मज़बूत कि उस oxygen को पहली जगह में protonate कर सके।
Step two, nucleophilic attack। iodide, जो एक अच्छा nucleophile है, अब उस oxonium oxygen से जुड़े carbons में से एक पर attack करके बाक़ी को एक alcohol के रूप में displace करता है।
तो आम तौर पर, एक dialkyl ether एक alkyl halide और एक alcohol देता है। एक carbon iodide बनकर चला जाता है, दूसरा alcohol बनकर निकलता है।

पर एक twist जोड़िए। high temperature पर excess hydrogen iodide के साथ, वो alcohol product बचता नहीं। ये ख़ुद आगे एक दूसरे alkyl iodide में बदल जाता है। तो excess hot hydrogen iodide का net result है दो alkyl iodide molecules।

<whisper>और ये रहा cliffhanger।</whisper> एकमात्र चीज़ जो हमने अभी तय नहीं की वो है iodide किस carbon पर attack करना चुनता है। वही एक choice सारे products तय करती है, और ठीक यही अगली section सुलझाती है।

ALKYL → phenol + R–I</text><text x="560" y="224" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10" fill="#c53030">aryl–O never breaks</text></svg>

board_events.text: For primary or secondary alkyl groups the attack is SN2, so iodide hits the less hindered, lower alkyl group, which becomes the alkyl iodide.
The bulkier group leaves as the alcohol (and onward to a second iodide with excess hot HI).
When one group is tertiary, the ether loses the alcohol to form a stable 3-degree carbocation (SN1), and iodide bonds to that tertiary carbon.
So (CH$_3$)$_3$C$-$O$-$CH$_3$ $+$ HI gives CH$_3$OH and (CH$_3$)$_3$C$-$I: the iodide lands on the tertiary carbon, opposite to the SN2 rule.
Alkyl aryl ethers ALWAYS cleave at the alkyl-oxygen bond, giving a phenol plus alkyl halide, never an aryl halide.
Anisole plus HI gives phenol and iodomethane; the aryl-O bond has partial double-bond character and the sp2 carbon resists substitution, so the phenol does not react further.

segments.text: Here is the section that decides every product in the whole subtopic. Given an ether and hydrogen iodide, exactly which carbon does the iodide attack? There are three cases, and the board lays them out.
Read the three rows. A dialkyl ether with only primary or secondary groups. An ether with a tertiary group. And an alkyl aryl ether. Each obeys a different logic.
Case one, primary or secondary. The attack is S N two, so the iodide goes for the less hindered, smaller alkyl group, and that smaller group becomes the alkyl iodide.
Meanwhile the bulkier group is displaced and leaves as the alcohol. And remember, with excess hot hydrogen iodide, that alcohol is then pushed onward to a second alkyl iodide as well.

Case two, when one group is tertiary. Now the mechanism flips to S N one. The protonated ether prefers to lose the alcohol first, generating a stable tertiary carbocation, and then the iodide bonds to that tertiary carbon.

So take tert butyl methyl ether with hydrogen iodide. It gives methanol and tert butyl iodide. Notice the iodide landed on the tertiary carbon, which is the exact opposite of the S N two lower group rule. The mechanism switch reverses the outcome.
<whisper>And case three is the one examiners love.</whisper> An alkyl aryl ether always cleaves at the alkyl oxygen bond, giving a phenol plus an alkyl halide, and never an aryl halide.

So anisole plus hydrogen iodide gives phenol and iodomethane. The reason is that the aryl oxygen bond has partial double bond character, because the ring conjugates with an oxygen lone pair, and the s p two aromatic carbon resists nucleophilic substitution. For the same reason, the phenol produced does not react any further with the acid.
ये वो section है जो पूरे subtopic का हर product तय करता है। एक ether और hydrogen iodide दिए हों, तो iodide ठीक किस carbon पर attack करता है? तीन cases हैं, और board उन्हें रखता है।
तीनों rows पढ़िए। सिर्फ़ primary या secondary groups वाला एक dialkyl ether। एक tertiary group वाला ether। और एक alkyl aryl ether। हर एक अलग logic मानता है।
Case एक, primary या secondary। attack S N two है, तो iodide कम hindered, छोटे alkyl group की ओर जाता है, और वही छोटा group alkyl iodide बन जाता है।
इस बीच bulkier group displace होकर alcohol बनकर निकलता है। और याद रखिए, excess hot hydrogen iodide के साथ, वो alcohol भी आगे एक दूसरे alkyl iodide में धकेल दिया जाता है।

Case दो, जब एक group tertiary हो। अब mechanism S N one पर पलट जाता है। protonated ether पहले alcohol खोना पसंद करता है, एक stable tertiary carbocation बनाते हुए, और फिर iodide उस tertiary carbon से bond बनाता है।

तो tert butyl methyl ether को hydrogen iodide के साथ लीजिए। ये methanol और tert butyl iodide देता है। ध्यान दीजिए iodide tertiary carbon पर आया, जो S N two के lower group rule का ठीक उलटा है। mechanism switch outcome को पलट देता है।
<whisper>और case तीन वो है जो examiners को पसंद है।</whisper> एक alkyl aryl ether हमेशा alkyl oxygen bond पर टूटता है, एक phenol plus एक alkyl halide देते हुए, और कभी aryl halide नहीं।

तो anisole plus hydrogen iodide phenol और iodomethane देता है। कारण ये है कि aryl oxygen bond में partial double bond character है, क्योंकि ring एक oxygen lone pair से conjugate करता है, और s p two aromatic carbon nucleophilic substitution का विरोध करता है। इसी कारण, बना हुआ phenol acid के साथ आगे react नहीं करता।

board_events.text: The aryl ether's second personality

board_events.caption: Anisole activated at ortho and para
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 660 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="660" height="240" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="330" y="22" text-anchor="middle" font-size="15" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">Electrophilic substitution on aromatic ethers</text><polygon points="150.0,88.0 122.3,104.0 122.3,136.0 150.0,152.0 177.7,136.0 177.7,104.0" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="150" cy="120" r="19.2" fill="none" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="1.6"/><line x1="150.0" y1="88.0" x2="150.0" y2="66.0" stroke="#1f2933" stroke-width="2"/><text x="150.0" y="60.0" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#c05621">OCH3</text><circle cx="122.3" cy="104.0" r="4" fill="#2f855a"/><circle cx="177.7" cy="104.0" r="4" fill="#2f855a"/><circle cx="150.0" cy="152.0" r="5" fill="#2b6cb0"/><text x="150" y="185" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">anisole: OCH3 activates o / p</text><rect x="330" y="50" width="300" height="55" rx="8" fill="#eef2f7" stroke="#2b6cb0" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="480" y="72" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2b6cb0">Br2 in ethanoic acid, NO FeBr3</text><text x="480" y="92" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">para product dominates (~90%)</text><rect x="330" y="115" width="300" height="55" rx="8" fill="#fff8ef" stroke="#c05621" stroke-width="1.2"/><text x="480" y="137" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#c05621">HNO3/H2SO4 → o/p-nitroanisole</text><text x="480" y="157" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">Friedel-Crafts → o/p alkyl or acyl</text><text x="330" y="200" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">same ortho/para-activating logic as the –OH in phenol</text></svg>

board_events.text: The alkoxy group activates the ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions, exactly as the OH does in phenol.
Halogenation: anisole reacts with bromine in ethanoic acid without any iron(III) bromide catalyst, because the methoxy group has already activated the ring.
The para product dominates, about 90 percent.
Nitration: anisole with HNO3 and H2SO4 gives ortho- and para-nitroanisole.
Friedel-Crafts: anisole with an alkyl or acyl halide and anhydrous AlCl3 gives the ortho and para alkyl or acyl product.
All of these follow the same ortho/para-activating logic as the halogenation above.

segments.text: We saw that an aryl ether has a second personality waiting in its ring. Now let us use it. This is electrophilic substitution on aromatic ethers, and it will feel very familiar.
Take anisole as our example, on the board. Its methoxy group is an electron donor, so the ring lights up at the ortho and para positions, ready for electrophiles.

The general rule is a direct echo of phenol. The alkoxy group activates the ring and directs incoming electrophiles to the ortho and para positions, exactly as the oxygen hydrogen did in phenol. Same donation, same directing.

Take halogenation as the grounded example. Anisole reacts with bromine in ethanoic acid without any iron three bromide catalyst at all, because the methoxy group has already activated the ring far beyond what plain benzene offers.
And there is a regiochemical detail worth quoting. The para product dominates, roughly ninety percent of the mixture, because the para position is the least crowded of the two activated sites.
The pattern repeats for nitration. Anisole with nitric acid and sulphuric acid gives a mixture of ortho and para nitroanisole, the two activated positions again.
And it repeats once more for Friedel Crafts. Anisole with an alkyl or acyl halide over anhydrous aluminium chloride gives the ortho and para alkyl or acyl product.

<whisper>So there is really nothing new to memorise here.</whisper> Every one of these follows the identical ortho para activating logic we established for phenol. An alkoxy group on a ring behaves just like an oxygen hydrogen would, pushing electrophiles to ortho and para.
हमने देखा कि एक aryl ether की ring में एक दूसरी personality इंतज़ार कर रही है। अब इसे इस्तेमाल करते हैं। ये aromatic ethers पर electrophilic substitution है, और ये बहुत जाना पहचाना लगेगा।
board पर anisole को example मानिए। इसका methoxy group एक electron donor है, तो ring ortho और para positions पर जगमगा उठता है, electrophiles के लिए तैयार।

general rule phenol की सीधी गूँज है। alkoxy group ring को activate करता है और आने वाले electrophiles को ortho तथा para positions की ओर directs करता है, ठीक वैसे जैसे phenol में oxygen hydrogen करता था। वही donation, वही directing।

grounded example के रूप में halogenation लीजिए। anisole bromine के साथ ethanoic acid में बिल्कुल बिना किसी iron three bromide catalyst के react करता है, क्योंकि methoxy group ring को सादे benzene से कहीं आगे पहले ही activate कर चुका है।
और एक regiochemical detail quote करने लायक है। para product हावी रहता है, mixture का करीब ninety percent, क्योंकि para position दोनों activated sites में सबसे कम भीड़ वाली है।
pattern nitration के लिए दोहराता है। anisole nitric acid और sulphuric acid के साथ ortho और para nitroanisole का mixture देता है, फिर वही दो activated positions।
और ये Friedel Crafts के लिए एक बार और दोहराता है। anisole एक alkyl या acyl halide के साथ anhydrous aluminium chloride पर ortho और para alkyl या acyl product देता है।

<whisper>तो यहाँ याद करने को सचमुच कुछ नया नहीं है।</whisper> इनमें से हर एक वही ortho para activating logic follow करता है जो हमने phenol के लिए स्थापित किया। एक ring पर alkoxy group बिल्कुल oxygen hydrogen जैसा behave करता है, electrophiles को ortho और para की ओर धकेलते हुए।

board_events.text: CBSE: reagents, equation, and the better pairing
Target: CH$_3$-O-CH$_2$CH$_2$CH$_3$. Two Williamson pairings are conceivable; explain why one is cleaner.

board_events.caption: Two ways to split the ether
board_events.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 680 230" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="system-ui, sans-serif"><rect x="0" y="0" width="680" height="230" fill="#fbfaf7"/><text x="340" y="24" text-anchor="middle" font-size="14" font-weight="700" fill="#1f2933">1-methoxypropane by Williamson</text><text x="340" y="50" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12" fill="#1f2933">target: CH3–O–CH2CH2CH3</text><rect x="40" y="66" width="290" height="130" rx="10" fill="#f0fff4" stroke="#2f855a" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="185" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#2f855a">Preferred</text><text x="185" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">CH3CH2CH2O(-)Na(+)</text><text x="185" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">+ CH3I</text><text x="185" y="165" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">methyl halide = unhindered</text><text x="185" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#2f855a">cleanest SN2</text><rect x="350" y="66" width="290" height="130" rx="10" fill="#fff8ef" stroke="#c05621" stroke-width="1.4"/><text x="495" y="90" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11.5" font-weight="700" fill="#c05621">Workable but poorer</text><text x="495" y="115" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">CH3O(-)Na(+)</text><text x="495" y="135" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="#1f2933">+ CH3CH2CH2Br</text><text x="495" y="165" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">both halides primary, so it works</text><text x="495" y="182" text-anchor="middle" font-size="10.5" fill="#5a6570">methyl pairing is simply cleaner</text></svg>

board_events.text: Preferred: sodium propoxide plus methyl iodide, because the SN2 electrophile is the unhindered methyl halide.
Workable but poorer: sodium methoxide plus 1-bromopropane.
Here both halides are primary, so the second pairing also succeeds; the methyl-halide pairing is simply the cleaner SN2.
The general design rule still bites when a partner is tertiary; then only the primary-halide pairing works at all.
So state both pairings, name the preferred one, and justify it by which fragment is the SN2 electrophile.

segments.text: Let us put the Williamson design rule to work on a C B S E question. Prepare one methoxypropane, and explain why one pairing is better than the other.
The target is methyl minus O minus propyl. In Williamson you always split the ether at the oxygen into an alkoxide and an alkyl halide, and here there are two ways to do that split.
The board shows both splits side by side. The green one on the left is preferred, the amber one on the right is workable but poorer. Let us see why.

The preferred pairing is sodium propoxide plus methyl iodide. The reason is clean. The S N two electrophile is the methyl halide, and a methyl halide is the most unhindered electrophile there is, so the substitution runs smoothly.
The alternative pairing is sodium methoxide plus one bromopropane. This is workable, not wrong.

And here is the honest nuance. In this particular case both halides are primary, so the second pairing also succeeds. The methyl halide pairing is simply the cleaner S N two, not the only possible one.

But do not forget the general rule, because it bites the moment a partner is tertiary. If one fragment were tertiary, only the pairing that keeps the tertiary group as the alkoxide, and the primary group as the halide, would work at all.

<whisper>So structure your answer in three moves.</whisper> Write both conceivable pairings, name the preferred one, and justify it by asking which fragment can safely be the S N two electrophile. That reasoning is what earns full marks.
चलिए Williamson design rule को एक C B S E question पर लगाते हैं। one methoxypropane बनाइए, और समझाइए एक pairing दूसरी से बेहतर क्यों है।
target है methyl minus O minus propyl। Williamson में आप ether को oxygen पर हमेशा एक alkoxide और एक alkyl halide में बाँटते हैं, और यहाँ उस बँटवारे के दो तरीक़े हैं।
board दोनों बँटवारे साथ साथ दिखाता है। बाईं ओर हरा वाला preferred है, दाईं ओर amber वाला workable पर कमतर है। देखते हैं क्यों।
preferred pairing है sodium propoxide plus methyl iodide। कारण साफ़ है। S N two electrophile methyl halide है, और methyl halide सबसे unhindered electrophile है, तो substitution आराम से चलती है।
दूसरी pairing है sodium methoxide plus one bromopropane। ये workable है, ग़लत नहीं।
और ये रही ईमानदार बारीकी। इस ख़ास case में दोनों halides primary हैं, तो दूसरी pairing भी सफल होती है। methyl halide pairing बस cleaner S N two है, एकमात्र संभव नहीं।

पर general rule मत भूलिए, क्योंकि जैसे ही कोई partner tertiary हो ये काट खाती है। अगर एक fragment tertiary होता, तो सिर्फ़ वही pairing काम करती जो tertiary group को alkoxide और primary group को halide रखे।

<whisper>तो अपने जवाब को तीन moves में structure कीजिए।</whisper> दोनों संभव pairings लिखिए, preferred नाम लीजिए, और ये पूछकर justify कीजिए कि कौन सा fragment सुरक्षित रूप से S N two electrophile बन सकता है। यही reasoning full marks दिलाती है।

board_events.text: NEET speed trap: name the products
What are the products when ethoxyethane is heated with excess concentrated HI?

board_events.caption: A symmetric primary ether, cleaved twice

board_events.text: Ethoxyethane is a symmetrical dialkyl ether, both groups primary and identical.
So the first cleavage gives one ethyl iodide and one ethanol.
The excess HI at high temperature converts that ethanol on to a second ethyl iodide.
Answer: two molecules of ethyl iodide, plus water.
Speed tip: excess HI at high temperature is the cue that any alcohol intermediate is pushed all the way to the iodide.

segments.text: A quick N E E T style product question, and it tests whether you remember the two stage cleavage. What comes out when ethoxyethane is heated with excess concentrated hydrogen iodide?
Read the substrate carefully first. Ethoxyethane is a symmetrical dialkyl ether. Both groups are ethyl, both primary, both identical.
The board walks it through. Because the groups are identical and primary, the S N two cleavage is completely straightforward, and then the conditions do a second job.
So set it up. This is a symmetrical dialkyl ether with two primary ethyl groups, which means simple S N two cleavage with no ambiguity about which carbon gets hit.
The first cleavage gives exactly one ethyl iodide and one ethanol. That is the general dialkyl ether result, one halide and one alcohol.
But the conditions say excess hydrogen iodide at high temperature, and that changes the endgame. That leftover ethanol does not survive. It is itself converted on to a second ethyl iodide.
So the final answer is clean. Two molecules of ethyl iodide, plus water. Both halves of the ether end up as the same iodide.

<whisper>And bank the cue.</whisper> The phrase excess hydrogen iodide at high temperature is your signal that any alcohol intermediate will be pushed all the way to the iodide. Whenever you see it, take the alcohol one more step.
एक quick N E E T style product question, और ये जाँचता है कि आपको two stage cleavage याद है या नहीं। जब ethoxyethane को excess concentrated hydrogen iodide के साथ गरम करें तो क्या निकलता है?
पहले substrate ध्यान से पढ़िए। ethoxyethane एक symmetrical dialkyl ether है। दोनों groups ethyl, दोनों primary, दोनों एक जैसे।
board इसे चला देता है। चूँकि groups एक जैसे और primary हैं, S N two cleavage बिल्कुल सीधा है, और फिर conditions एक दूसरा काम करती हैं।
तो इसे set कीजिए। ये दो primary ethyl groups वाला एक symmetrical dialkyl ether है, यानी बिना किसी ambiguity के simple S N two cleavage कि कौन सा carbon hit होगा।
पहला cleavage ठीक एक ethyl iodide और एक ethanol देता है। यही general dialkyl ether का result है, एक halide और एक alcohol।
पर conditions कहती हैं high temperature पर excess hydrogen iodide, और ये endgame बदल देता है। वो बचा ethanol बचता नहीं। ये ख़ुद आगे एक दूसरे ethyl iodide में बदल जाता है।
तो अंतिम जवाब साफ़ है। दो ethyl iodide molecules, plus water। ether के दोनों halves वही iodide बन जाते हैं।

<whisper>और cue संभाल लीजिए।</whisper> high temperature पर excess hydrogen iodide वाक्यांश आपका signal है कि कोई भी alcohol intermediate पूरा iodide तक धकेला जाएगा। जब भी दिखे, alcohol को एक step और ले जाइए।

board_events.text: Part (i): one group is tertiary, so cleavage goes SN1. The protonated ether sheds methanol to give the stable 3-degree carbocation, which captures iodide.
Products: 2-iodo-2-methylpropane plus methanol. The iodide ends on the tertiary carbon, opposite to the SN2 lower-group rule.
Part (ii): anisole has the aryl-oxygen bond protected, so iodide attacks the methyl instead.
Products: phenol plus iodomethane. The aryl halide is never formed.
The two parts contrast the SN1 (tertiary) outcome with the aryl-protected outcome, exactly the discrimination JEE Main rewards.

segments.text: This J E E Main problem is designed to test the cleavage switch we just built. Two ethers, each given one equivalent of hydrogen iodide, and you must predict the major products of each.
The two ethers are tert butyl methyl ether and anisole. They look similar, both a small group joined through oxygen to a bulkier one, but they cleave by completely different logic.
The board runs both in parallel. The top row is the tertiary case, the bottom row is the aryl case. Watch where the iodide lands in each.

Part one, tert butyl methyl ether. One group here is tertiary, which flips the mechanism to S N one. The protonated ether sheds methanol first, generating the stable tertiary carbocation, and that cation then captures the iodide.

So the products are two iodo two methylpropane and methanol. Note carefully, the iodide has ended up on the tertiary carbon, which is the exact opposite of the S N two lower group rule. That reversal is the whole point of part one.
Part two, anisole. Here the aryl oxygen bond is protected and can never break, so the iodide has no choice but to attack the methyl group instead.
So the products are phenol and iodomethane. The aryl halide is never formed, because the s p two aromatic carbon simply will not undergo the substitution.

<whisper>And that is the elegance of the question.</whisper> Two parts, deliberately contrasting the S N one tertiary outcome with the aryl protected outcome. Recognise which case you are in, and the products follow immediately. That discrimination is exactly what J E E Main rewards.
ये J E E Main problem उस cleavage switch को test करने के लिए बना है जो हमने अभी बनाया। दो ethers, हर एक को hydrogen iodide का एक equivalent दिया, और आपको हर एक के major products बताने हैं।
दो ethers हैं tert butyl methyl ether और anisole। ये एक जैसे दिखते हैं, दोनों में एक छोटा group oxygen के ज़रिए एक bulkier से जुड़ा, पर ये बिल्कुल अलग logic से टूटते हैं।
board दोनों को साथ चलाता है। ऊपर की row tertiary case है, नीचे की row aryl case। देखिए हर एक में iodide कहाँ आता है।

पहला हिस्सा, tert butyl methyl ether। यहाँ एक group tertiary है, जो mechanism को S N one पर पलट देता है। protonated ether पहले methanol छोड़ता है, stable tertiary carbocation बनाते हुए, और फिर वो cation iodide को पकड़ लेता है।
तो products हैं two iodo two methylpropane और methanol। ध्यान से देखिए, iodide tertiary carbon पर आया है, जो S N two के lower group rule का ठीक उलटा है। वही पलटाव पहले हिस्से की पूरी बात है।
दूसरा हिस्सा, anisole। यहाँ aryl oxygen bond protected है और कभी नहीं टूट सकता, तो iodide के पास कोई चारा नहीं सिवाय methyl group पर attack करने के।
तो products हैं phenol और iodomethane। aryl halide कभी नहीं बनता, क्योंकि s p two aromatic carbon वो substitution करेगा ही नहीं।

<whisper>और यही इस question की elegance है।</whisper> दो हिस्से, जानबूझकर S N one tertiary outcome को aryl protected outcome से contrast करते हुए। पहचानिए आप किस case में हैं, और products तुरंत आ जाते हैं। यही discrimination J E E Main reward करता है।

sections.title: Worked example: deducing an ether from its cleavage

board_events.text: JEE Advanced: work backward from the products
An ether C4H10O, on cleavage with excess hot HI, gives a single alkyl iodide. Deduce the ether.
